name: PostgreSQL and SQL in Depth
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Developers and architects who use PostgreSQL (directly or via Supabase/Neon) as the main database and want expert-level SQL, schema design and performance skills.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of predict-the-result, read-the-plan, schema design and concurrency questions.

domains.name: SQL querying in depth
domains.summary: Writing SQL that returns exactly what you mean: outer, semi and anti joins (and the NOT IN NULL trap), LATERAL, GROUP BY with FILTER and grouping sets, DISTINCT ON, window functions with frames and gaps-and-islands, recursive CTEs, three-valued logic, casting and set operations.

domains.name: Schema design and data modelling
domains.summary: Modelling data so the database enforces correctness: normalization and when to denormalize, identity versus UUID keys (uuidv7() in 18), foreign keys and ON DELETE, CHECK, UNIQUE and exclusion constraints, choosing column types including generated columns, and declarative partitioning with pruning.

domains.name: Indexes and query performance
domains.summary: Making queries fast and knowing why: B-tree internals, column order and skip scan in 18, partial, expression and covering indexes, GIN, GiST, BRIN and hash, reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and planner statistics, and the anti-patterns that defeat indexes.

domains.name: Transactions, MVCC and concurrency
domains.summary: How PostgreSQL keeps concurrent work correct: MVCC row versions and snapshots, read committed, repeatable read and serializable (SSI), VACUUM, bloat, HOT updates and wraparound, row and table locks with SKIP LOCKED and deadlocks, and upserts, MERGE, advisory locks and retry loops.

domains.name: PostgreSQL as an application platform
domains.summary: Using Postgres for more than tables: jsonb operators and GIN indexes, full-text and trigram search, vector search with pgvector (HNSW vs IVFFlat, filtering, hybrid search), SKIP LOCKED queues, LISTEN/NOTIFY and the outbox, and roles, row-level security and SECURITY DEFINER in Supabase-style apps.

domains.name: Operating PostgreSQL in production
domains.summary: Running PostgreSQL in production: connection budgets and pooling with PgBouncer and Supabase poolers, zero-downtime migrations with lock timeouts and NOT VALID constraints, backups and point-in-time recovery, streaming and logical replication, and monitoring, key settings and upgrades.

scenarios.title: A slow query in production
scenarios.description: A dashboard endpoint went from 40 ms to 4 s after the orders table grew. Read the EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output, spot the misestimate or missing index, and fix it without blocking writes.

scenarios.title: Designing a multi-tenant schema with row-level security
scenarios.description: Many customers share one database. Pick keys and constraints that carry tenant_id, write RLS policies that isolate tenants, and make sure the policies are indexed and cannot be bypassed by the app role.

scenarios.title: A job queue in Postgres
scenarios.description: Workers claim jobs from a table with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, retry failures with backoff, and publish events through an outbox, while keeping the table small enough that VACUUM keeps up.

scenarios.title: Adding vector search to an app
scenarios.description: Store embeddings with pgvector, choose between HNSW and IVFFlat, combine similarity with tenant and metadata filters, and blend vector and full-text ranking into one hybrid search.

scenarios.title: A zero-downtime migration
scenarios.description: Add a column, a foreign key and an index to a busy table without an outage: set lock_timeout, build indexes CONCURRENTLY, add constraints NOT VALID then VALIDATE, and backfill in batches.

lessons.title: Joins in depth: outer, semi, anti and LATERAL
lessons.summary: How inner and outer joins really behave, why EXISTS and NOT EXISTS express semi and anti joins, the NOT IN NULL trap, and when LATERAL is the right tool.

sections.heading: Inner and outer joins
sections.body:
An inner join keeps only row pairs for which the join condition is true. A `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left side; where no right row matches, the right-side columns are filled with NULL. `RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror image and `FULL JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from both sides. `CROSS JOIN` is every pair with no condition.

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

A customer with no orders appears once, with `order_id` NULL. A customer with three orders appears three times: joins multiply rows, which is the usual source of inflated sums and counts.

sections.heading: ON versus WHERE in an outer join
sections.body:
The `ON` clause decides which right rows match. The `WHERE` clause runs after the join and removes whole result rows. Putting a condition on the right table in `WHERE` therefore throws away the NULL-extended rows and silently turns the outer join into an inner join:

```sql
-- Drops customers with no 2026 orders (WHERE sees NULL created_at)
SELECT c.id, count(o.id)
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id;

-- Keeps every customer; only the matching rule changes
SELECT c.id, count(o.id)
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id;
```

Note `count(o.id)` rather than `count(*)`: the NULL-extended row would otherwise count as 1.

sections.heading: Semi joins with EXISTS
sections.body:
A semi join asks "does at least one match exist?" and returns each left row at most once. Write it with `EXISTS`:

```sql
SELECT c.*
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
```

The result of `EXISTS` depends only on whether the subquery returns any row, not on what it selects, so `SELECT 1` is the convention. Rewriting this as an inner join plus `DISTINCT` works but forces a de-duplication step and can hide fan-out bugs.

sections.heading: Anti joins and the NOT IN trap
sections.body:
An anti join keeps rows that have **no** match. Two correct forms:

```sql
SELECT p.* FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id);

SELECT p.* FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;
```

`NOT IN (subquery)` looks equivalent but is not. If the subquery yields even one NULL, `x NOT IN (...)` is never true: it is false or NULL for every row, so the query returns **nothing**. For example, `2 NOT IN (1, NULL)` is NULL, not true. The PostgreSQL wiki's "Don't Do This" page says not to use `NOT IN` with subqueries, both for this NULL behaviour and because it can perform very poorly on large subqueries. Use `NOT EXISTS`.

sections.heading: LATERAL joins
sections.body:
A subquery in `FROM` normally cannot see other `FROM` items. Marking it `LATERAL` lets it reference columns of items that appear earlier, so it is evaluated per left row. The classic use is "top N per group":

```sql
SELECT c.id, o.id AS order_id, o.created_at
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
  WHERE orders.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC  -- id breaks ties
  LIMIT 3
) o ON true;
```

Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` to keep customers with no orders, or `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` (or a comma) to drop them. The lateral item must be joined with INNER or LEFT: in a `RIGHT JOIN LATERAL` it cannot reference the left side. For a function call in `FROM`, `LATERAL` is optional because functions may already reference earlier items.

keyPoints: Conditions on the nullable side of an outer join belong in `ON`; in `WHERE` they turn it into an inner join.
`EXISTS` is a semi join and returns each outer row at most once; `NOT EXISTS` is the safe anti join.
`x NOT IN (subquery)` returns no rows as soon as the subquery yields a NULL.
`LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... LIMIT n) ON true` is the standard top-N-per-group pattern.
Joins multiply rows: aggregate after checking the join cardinality, and use `count(col)` on the nullable side.

gotchas.trap: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` where `customer_id` is nullable.
gotchas.correct: Use `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`; NULLs in the subquery make `NOT IN` return nothing.

gotchas.trap: Filtering the right table of a LEFT JOIN in `WHERE`.
gotchas.correct: Move the filter into the `ON` clause, or filter in a subquery before joining.

gotchas.trap: Writing `JOIN (SELECT ... WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)` without `LATERAL`.
gotchas.correct: Without `LATERAL` the subquery cannot reference `c` and the query fails; add `LATERAL`.

lessons.lab:
Create `customers(id, name)` with three rows and `orders(id, customer_id, created_at)` where one order has `customer_id` NULL and one customer has no orders.
1. Run `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` and note that it returns zero rows.
2. Rewrite it with `NOT EXISTS` and with `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.id IS NULL`; both return the customer with no orders.
3. Write a `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` query that returns each customer's two most recent orders, adding `id` as a tiebreaker in `ORDER BY`.

lessons.title: Aggregation: GROUP BY, HAVING, FILTER and grouping sets
lessons.summary: Where WHERE and HAVING run, conditional aggregates with FILTER, subtotals with GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE, and picking one row per group with DISTINCT ON.

sections.heading: WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING
sections.body:
Logically, `WHERE` filters input rows before grouping, `GROUP BY` forms groups, aggregates are computed per group, and `HAVING` filters whole groups. So an aggregate cannot appear in `WHERE` (`ERROR: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE`), and row-level conditions belong in `WHERE`, where they also reduce the work done before grouping.

```sql
SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'          -- rows
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING sum(amount) > 1000;     -- groups
```

Every non-aggregated column in the select list must be grouped (or functionally dependent on a grouped primary key). Aggregates ignore NULL inputs, with `count(*)` as the exception: it counts rows. On the values `(1), (NULL)`, `count(*)` is 2 and `count(x)` is 1.

sections.heading: Conditional aggregates with FILTER
sections.body:
`FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts which rows feed one aggregate, so several conditional counts come out of a single pass:

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day,
       count(*)                                  AS all_orders,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS paid,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refunded_amt
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1;
```

A common bug is `count(status = 'paid')`. The boolean is non-NULL for both true and false, so it counts every row with a status. On `'paid', 'refunded', 'paid'` it returns 3, while the FILTER form returns 2.

sections.heading: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE
sections.body:
Grouping sets compute several groupings in one query. The result behaves like a `UNION ALL` of one `GROUP BY` per set, with columns that are not in the current set shown as NULL.

- `GROUPING SETS ((region), (product), ())` gives per-region rows, per-product rows and a grand total.
- `ROLLUP (region, product)` is `GROUPING SETS ((region, product), (region), ())`: detail, subtotals, grand total.
- `CUBE (a, b)` is every subset: `(a, b), (a), (b), ()`.

On EU a 10, EU b 20, US a 5, `ROLLUP(region, product)` returns (EU,a,10), (EU,b,20), (EU,NULL,30), (US,a,5), (US,NULL,5), (NULL,NULL,35).

If a grouped column can itself contain NULL, a subtotal row and a real NULL group look the same. The `GROUPING(col)` function returns 1 when `col` is not part of the current grouping set, so use it to label subtotal rows. `GROUP BY DISTINCT` removes duplicate grouping sets (not duplicate output rows) when combined sets overlap.

sections.heading: One row per group with DISTINCT ON
sections.body:
`DISTINCT ON (expr)` keeps the first row of each set of rows that share `expr`, where "first" is defined by `ORDER BY`. The `DISTINCT ON` expressions must match the leftmost `ORDER BY` expressions; the rest of the `ORDER BY` picks the winner.

```sql
-- Latest order per customer
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, id, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC;
```

Without `ORDER BY` the kept row is unpredictable. `ORDER BY created_at DESC` alone fails with `SELECT DISTINCT ON expressions must match initial ORDER BY expressions`. For top N greater than 1, use a window function or `LATERAL`.

keyPoints: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE cond)` is the clean way to compute several conditional aggregates in one pass.
`count(*)` counts rows; `count(expr)` counts non-NULL values, so `count(bool_expr)` counts false too.
`ROLLUP(a, b)` = `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())`; `CUBE(a, b)` produces four grouping sets.
Use `GROUPING(col)` to tell subtotal rows from groups whose key is really NULL.
`DISTINCT ON` needs a matching leading `ORDER BY`; the remaining sort keys choose which row survives.

gotchas.trap: `WHERE sum(amount) > 1000`.
gotchas.correct: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE; use `HAVING sum(amount) > 1000`.

gotchas.trap: `count(status = 'paid')` to count paid orders.
gotchas.correct: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')`; the boolean form counts false values as well.

gotchas.trap: `COALESCE(product, 'Total')` to label ROLLUP subtotals when product can be NULL.
gotchas.correct: Use `CASE WHEN GROUPING(product) = 1 THEN 'Total' ELSE product END`.

gotchas.trap: `SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY created_at DESC`.
gotchas.correct: Lead with the DISTINCT ON key: `ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC`.

lessons.lab:
Using `VALUES ('EU','a',10), ('EU','b',20), ('US','a',5)` as `sales(region, product, amt)`:
1. Run `GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product)` and confirm the six rows, including (NULL, NULL, 35).
2. Add `GROUPING(region), GROUPING(product)` to the select list and label subtotal and total rows.
3. Compute `count(*) FILTER (WHERE amt > 6)` per region (EU 2, US 0) and compare with `count(amt > 6)`.
4. Use `DISTINCT ON (region)` to return the largest sale per region (EU b 20, US a 5).

lessons.title: Window functions: partitions, frames and gaps and islands
lessons.summary: Ranking, running totals, lag and lead, the default frame trap with last_value and ties, and the row_number difference trick for gaps and islands, as of PostgreSQL 18.

sections.heading: How a window works
sections.body:
A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows, without collapsing them as `GROUP BY` does. `PARTITION BY` splits rows into independent groups; `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` orders rows within each partition and defines **peers** (rows equal on the ORDER BY keys).

```sql
SELECT customer_id, created_at, amount,
       sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id) AS running_total
FROM orders;
```

Window functions run after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, and are allowed only in the select list and `ORDER BY`. A filter such as "keep row_number = 1" must go in an outer query:

```sql
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT o.*, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders o
) t WHERE rn = 1;
```

Putting the window call in `WHERE` fails with `window functions are not allowed in WHERE`. A `WINDOW w AS (...)` clause lets several calls share one definition.

sections.heading: Ranking functions
sections.body:
On `x` = 10, 20, 20, 30 with `OVER (ORDER BY x)`:

| x | row_number | rank | dense_rank |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 20 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 20 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| 30 | 4 | 4 | 3 |

- `row_number` numbers rows uniquely; among peers the order is not deterministic, so add a tiebreaker.
- `rank` gives peers the same rank and leaves gaps.
- `dense_rank` gives peers the same rank without gaps.
- `percent_rank` = (rank − 1)/(N − 1), `cume_dist` = (rows preceding or peer)/N, and `ntile(n)` splits rows into n buckets as evenly as possible.

sections.heading: Frames and the default frame trap
sections.body:
Aggregates and `first_value`/`last_value`/`nth_value` work over a **frame** within the partition. Frame modes are `ROWS` (physical rows), `RANGE` (by ORDER BY value, peers together) and `GROUPS` (counted in peer groups), with optional `EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW | GROUP | TIES | NO OTHERS`.

With `ORDER BY`, the default frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which **includes all peers of the current row**. Without `ORDER BY`, every row is a peer, so the frame is the whole partition. Two consequences, from the 10, 20, 20, 30 data:

| x | sum, default RANGE frame | sum, ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING | last_value, default frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 |
| 20 | 50 | 30 | 20 |
| 20 | 50 | 50 | 20 |
| 30 | 80 | 80 | 30 |

A running total over tied keys repeats the same value for peers; use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` plus a unique tiebreaker for a strictly per-row total. `last_value` with the default frame just returns the current row's peer group's last value, which the docs say "is likely to give unhelpful results"; use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.

sections.heading: lag, lead and offsets
sections.body:
`lag(value [, offset [, default]])` reads a row earlier in the partition and `lead` a row later. The offset defaults to 1 and the default to NULL:

```sql
SELECT month, revenue,
       revenue - lag(revenue, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly;
```

As of PostgreSQL 18, the SQL-standard `RESPECT NULLS`/`IGNORE NULLS` options for `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `last_value` and `nth_value`, and `nth_value ... FROM LAST`, are **not implemented**. Do not rely on `IGNORE NULLS` to skip NULLs in 18 (it is planned for 19).

sections.heading: Gaps and islands
sections.body:
"Islands" are runs of consecutive values, such as consecutive login days. Subtract a `row_number` from the value: inside one run both increase by 1, so the difference stays constant and becomes a group key.

```sql
SELECT user_id, min(day) AS streak_start, max(day) AS streak_end, count(*) AS days
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, day,
         day - (row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day))::int AS grp
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, day FROM logins) d
) t
GROUP BY user_id, grp
ORDER BY user_id, streak_start;
```

On days Jan 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 this returns two islands: Jan 1–2 (2 days) and Jan 4–6 (3 days). De-duplicate first: repeated days would break the arithmetic. "Gaps" are found with `lead(day) OVER (...) - day > 1`.

keyPoints: Window functions keep every row; `PARTITION BY` groups, `ORDER BY` orders and defines peers.
Window functions are allowed only in the select list and `ORDER BY`; filter on them in an outer query.
Default frame with `ORDER BY` is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` and includes peers.
For `last_value` use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.
`rank` leaves gaps after ties, `dense_rank` does not, `row_number` is unique but arbitrary among peers.
`IGNORE NULLS` is not available in PostgreSQL 18.
Gaps and islands: value minus `row_number()` is constant within a run.

gotchas.trap: `sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY day)` as a per-row running total when days repeat.
gotchas.correct: Peers share a value under the default RANGE frame; use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` and a unique tiebreaker.

gotchas.trap: `last_value(x) OVER (ORDER BY t)` to get the partition's last value.
gotchas.correct: Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.

gotchas.trap: `WHERE row_number() OVER (...) = 1`.
gotchas.correct: Compute `row_number` in a subquery or CTE and filter outside it.

gotchas.trap: `lag(x) IGNORE NULLS OVER (...)` in PostgreSQL 18.
gotchas.correct: Not implemented in 18; carry the last non-NULL value with a grouping trick or a correlated lookup.

lessons.lab:
1. On `VALUES (10),(20),(20),(30)` compute `row_number`, `rank`, `dense_rank`, `last_value` and two running sums (default frame and `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING`). Confirm the 50/50 versus 30/50 difference.
2. Build `logins(user_id, day date)` with days Jan 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and run the gaps-and-islands query; cast dates to `::text` when checking output.
3. Rewrite "latest order per customer" with `row_number()` in a subquery and compare it with the `DISTINCT ON` version.

lessons.title: CTEs and recursive queries
lessons.summary: WITH queries for readability, recursive CTEs for hierarchies and graphs, SEARCH and CYCLE clauses, materialization control, and data-modifying CTEs.

sections.heading: Plain CTEs and materialization
sections.body:
`WITH name AS (...)` names a subquery for the main statement. Whether it is computed separately or folded into the outer query matters for performance:

- A non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced **once** is inlined, so outer filters can be pushed into it.
- A CTE referenced **more than once** is materialized by default: computed once, with outer conditions not pushed down.
- `WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...)` forces a single computation (useful for an expensive expression used many times). `WITH x AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...)` forces inlining so each reference can use an index.
- Recursive CTEs and CTEs that call volatile functions are never folded.

sections.heading: Recursive CTEs for hierarchies
sections.body:
A recursive CTE has a non-recursive term, `UNION [ALL]`, and a recursive term that references the CTE itself. It is evaluated iteratively: the working table starts with the non-recursive rows, the recursive term runs against the rows produced in the previous step, and evaluation stops when a step produces no rows. `UNION` discards duplicate rows; `UNION ALL` keeps them.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, name, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE id = 42            -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, e.name, c.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id   -- step
)
SELECT * FROM chain;
```

A quick sanity check: `WITH RECURSIVE t(n) AS (VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM t WHERE n < 100) SELECT sum(n) FROM t` returns 5050.

sections.heading: Ordering and cycle detection
sections.body:
The `SEARCH` clause adds an ordering column: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ordercol` lists each node directly followed by its descendants (good for indented trees), and `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ordercol` lists level by level. Then `ORDER BY ordercol` in the outer query.

Graphs can contain cycles, and a recursive query over a cycle never terminates. Switching to `UNION` helps only when whole rows repeat; once you carry a depth or path column, each lap produces a new distinct row. The `CYCLE` clause tracks visited keys for you:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE walk(id, next_id) AS (
  SELECT id, next_id FROM links WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT l.id, l.next_id FROM links l JOIN walk w ON l.id = w.next_id
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT * FROM walk WHERE NOT is_cycle;
```

Adding `LIMIT` to the outer query to stop runaway recursion is a testing trick only, not a safeguard.

sections.heading: Data-modifying CTEs
sections.body:
`INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` can appear in `WITH`. All sub-statements run with the same snapshot, so they cannot see each other's changes to the tables; the only channel between them is `RETURNING`.

```sql
WITH moved AS (
  DELETE FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2025-01-01' RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
```

Because of the shared snapshot, `WITH t AS (UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.05 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM products` shows the **original** prices; select from `t` to see the new ones. Each data-modifying sub-statement runs exactly once, to completion, even if the main query never reads its output.

keyPoints: A CTE referenced once is inlined; referenced twice it is materialized by default. Override with `[NOT] MATERIALIZED`.
Recursive CTE = anchor `UNION [ALL]` recursive term, evaluated iteratively until a step yields no rows.
`SEARCH DEPTH FIRST / BREADTH FIRST BY ... SET col` gives a sort column for tree output.
Use `CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path` for graphs; `UNION` alone fails once rows carry depth or path.
Data-modifying CTEs share one snapshot; read their results through `RETURNING`.

gotchas.trap: A CTE used twice with a selective outer filter that no longer uses an index.
gotchas.correct: It is materialized by default; mark it `NOT MATERIALIZED` or reference it once.

gotchas.trap: Relying on `UNION` or an outer `LIMIT` to stop recursion over cyclic data.
gotchas.correct: Use the `CYCLE` clause (or track a path array) and filter `NOT is_cycle`.

gotchas.trap: Selecting from the base table after an UPDATE in a CTE and expecting new values.
gotchas.correct: Select from the CTE's `RETURNING` output; the main query sees the pre-statement snapshot.

lessons.lab:
1. Build `employees(id, manager_id, name)` with three levels and list the subtree under one manager, with depth.
2. Add `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` and order by `ord`; then try `BREADTH FIRST` and compare.
3. Create `links(id, next_id)` forming a loop 1→2→3→1 and use `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path` so the query terminates.
4. Run `WITH t AS (UPDATE ... RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM base_table` and observe the old values.

lessons.title: NULL, three-valued logic, casting and set operations
lessons.summary: How NULL propagates through comparisons and boolean logic, null-safe comparison, integer division and casts, NULL ordering, and UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT semantics.

sections.heading: Three-valued logic
sections.body:
SQL booleans have three values: true, false and NULL (unknown). Any ordinary comparison with NULL yields NULL, including `NULL = NULL`. `WHERE` and `HAVING` keep a row only when the condition is **true**, so NULL behaves like false there. The truth tables follow "unknown" reasoning:

| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `NULL AND false` | false |
| `NULL AND true` | NULL |
| `NULL OR true` | true |
| `NOT NULL::boolean` | NULL |
| `(NULL = NULL) IS NULL` | true |

So `WHERE discount <> 0` silently drops rows whose discount is NULL. Test NULL with `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`, never `= NULL`.

sections.heading: Null-safe comparison and NULL helpers
sections.body:
`a IS DISTINCT FROM b` treats NULL as a comparable value: it returns true or false, never NULL. `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL` is false and `1 IS DISTINCT FROM NULL` is true. `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` is the null-safe equality.

Other tools: `COALESCE(a, b, ...)` returns the first non-NULL argument, and `NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when `a = b` (handy for `x / NULLIF(y, 0)`). Remember that most aggregates skip NULLs and `count(*)` does not.

sections.heading: Casting and integer arithmetic
sections.body:
`CAST(x AS type)` and the PostgreSQL shorthand `x::type` convert values; a cast of malformed input such as `'abc'::int` raises an error rather than returning NULL.

Integer division truncates toward zero: `7/2` = 3 and `-7/2` = -3, and `7 % -3` = 1. Mixing in a numeric operand gives an exact result: `7/2.0` = 3.5. To compute a ratio of two integer counts, cast an **operand** before dividing: `paid::numeric / total`. Casting the result, `(paid / total)::numeric`, is too late; the integer division already produced 0.

Floating point is inexact: `0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8` is false, while the same test in `numeric` is true.

sections.heading: NULLs in ORDER BY
sections.body: NULLs sort as if larger than any value, so the default is `NULLS LAST` for ascending order and `NULLS FIRST` for descending order. A "latest first" list with `ORDER BY shipped_at DESC` therefore starts with the unshipped rows; write `ORDER BY shipped_at DESC NULLS LAST`. Also, each sort key has its own direction: `ORDER BY x, y DESC` is not the same as `ORDER BY x DESC, y DESC`.

sections.heading: Set operations
sections.body:
`UNION`, `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` combine the results of two queries with the same number of columns and compatible types. Without `ALL` they remove duplicates. With `ALL`, a row that appears m times on the left and n times on the right appears:

- m + n times in `UNION ALL`,
- min(m, n) times in `INTERSECT ALL`,
- max(m − n, 0) times in `EXCEPT ALL`.

So with 'x' three times on the left and once on the right, `EXCEPT ALL` returns 'x' twice, `EXCEPT` returns nothing, and `INTERSECT ALL` returns it once. Duplicate elimination treats NULLs as equal, unlike `=`.

`INTERSECT` binds tighter than `UNION`; `UNION` and `EXCEPT` share precedence and evaluate left to right. An operand needs parentheses to carry its own `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT`. Prefer `UNION ALL` when duplicates are impossible or wanted, since it skips the de-duplication work.

keyPoints: Comparisons with NULL yield NULL; WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true.
`NULL AND false` is false and `NULL OR true` is true; everything else involving NULL tends to stay NULL.
`IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM` is the null-safe comparison.
Integer division truncates toward zero; cast an operand, not the result.
Default NULL ordering: last for ASC, first for DESC.
`INTERSECT ALL` = min(m, n), `EXCEPT ALL` = max(m − n, 0); plain set operations remove duplicates.

gotchas.trap: `WHERE col = NULL`.
gotchas.correct: Always NULL, never true; use `WHERE col IS NULL`.

gotchas.trap: `WHERE discount <> 0` to find rows that are not exactly 0, including unknown discounts.
gotchas.correct: `WHERE discount IS DISTINCT FROM 0`.

gotchas.trap: `(paid / total)::numeric` for a ratio of integers.
gotchas.correct: `paid::numeric / total` (and `NULLIF(total, 0)` to avoid division by zero).

gotchas.trap: `UNION` by habit when the inputs cannot overlap.
gotchas.correct: `UNION ALL` avoids an unnecessary de-duplication step.

1. Evaluate `NULL AND false`, `NULL OR true`, `NOT NULL::boolean`, `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL` and `(NULL = NULL) IS NULL`.
2. Compute `7/2`, `-7/2`, `7 % -3`, `7/2.0`, `(3/4)::numeric` and `3::numeric/4`.
3. With 'x' three times on the left and once on the right, run `EXCEPT`, `EXCEPT ALL` and `INTERSECT ALL` and count the rows.

lessons.title: Normalization, relationships and hierarchies
lessons.summary: Store each fact once, model one-to-many and many-to-many relationships with foreign keys and junction tables, represent trees with an adjacency list, and denormalize only for a measured reason.

sections.heading: Why normalize
sections.body:
Normalization means each fact lives in exactly one place. When the same fact is copied into many rows, an update must find every copy, and a missed copy leaves the database disagreeing with itself (an *update anomaly*).

A practical working rule for third normal form: every non-key column depends on **the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key**.

- A `customer_email` column on `orders` depends on the customer, not on the order. It belongs on `customers`.
- A `product_name` on `order_lines` keyed by `(order_id, product_id)` depends only on part of the key. It belongs on `products`.

Exception: a value that is deliberately a *snapshot*, such as the unit price charged at the time of the order, is a fact about the order line and is correctly stored there.

sections.heading: One-to-many and many-to-many
sections.body:
**One-to-many:** put a foreign key on the "many" side.

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id);  -- not created automatically
```

**Many-to-many:** use a junction (link) table whose primary key is the pair of foreign keys. Attributes of the relationship itself (enrolled_at, role, grade) go on the link table.

```sql
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id bigint REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  course_id  bigint REFERENCES courses(id)  ON DELETE CASCADE,
  enrolled_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON enrollments (course_id);  -- reverse direction lookups
```

The composite PK index serves lookups that start from `student_id`. The extra index on `course_id` serves "who is in this course" and makes deletes from `courses` cheap.

Avoid storing the relationship as an array of ids: PostgreSQL cannot put a foreign key on array elements, and the Arrays docs warn that searching for specific elements "can be a sign of database misdesign" and suggest a separate table with one row per item.

sections.heading: Hierarchies
sections.body:
The default model for a tree is an **adjacency list**: each row has a nullable `parent_id` referencing the same table. Walk it with a recursive CTE:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 1 AS depth FROM categories WHERE id = 42
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, s.depth + 1
  FROM categories c JOIN sub s ON c.parent_id = s.id
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT * FROM sub;
```

- The `CYCLE` clause stops runaway recursion if bad data creates a loop. `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY ...` or `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY ...` gives a stable ordering.
- Alternatives when reads dominate: a **materialized path** (the `ltree` extension) makes "all descendants" a single indexed predicate, at the cost of rewriting paths when a subtree moves; a **closure table** stores every ancestor/descendant pair and makes moves expensive.
- Arbitrary depth is the reason to use recursion. A fixed chain of self-joins only works up to the depth you hard-code.

sections.heading: When to denormalize
sections.body:
Denormalize for a **measured** read problem, and choose a mechanism that keeps the copy correct:

- **Generated column** for a value derived from other columns *in the same row*. Make it `STORED` if you need to index it (see the types lesson).
- **Materialized view** for expensive aggregates where some staleness is acceptable. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` keeps it readable during refresh (it needs a unique index on the view).
- **Trigger-maintained summary** (for example a counter) when the copy must be current. Watch for row-lock contention on a hot summary row.
- **jsonb** for attributes that are genuinely variable per row. Keep frequently filtered, joined or constrained fields as typed columns.

Copying a parent's mutable attribute into child rows "to avoid a join" before measuring anything is the classic premature denormalization.

keyPoints: Every non-key column should depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
One-to-many: foreign key on the many side, and index that column yourself.
Many-to-many: a junction table with a composite primary key plus an index for the reverse direction.
Arrays of ids cannot carry foreign keys; prefer a row per item.
Trees: adjacency list plus WITH RECURSIVE (with CYCLE); ltree or closure tables trade write cost for read speed.
Denormalize only for a measured read problem, using a mechanism that keeps the copy correct.

gotchas.trap: Storing a many-to-many relationship as an int[] column to avoid an extra table.
gotchas.correct: Use a junction table: it allows foreign keys, per-link attributes and ordinary B-tree indexes in both directions.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the composite primary key on (a_id, b_id) also serves lookups by b_id.
gotchas.correct: A B-tree on (a_id, b_id) is driven by a_id; add a separate index on b_id for the reverse direction.

gotchas.trap: Treating every copied value as denormalization.
gotchas.correct: A deliberate snapshot (price at time of sale) is a fact about the child row and belongs there.

2. Build a `categories(id, parent_id, name)` tree four levels deep, and write a `WITH RECURSIVE` query with `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` that lists every descendant of the root in depth-first order.

lessons.title: Keys: identity, UUIDs, natural keys and foreign keys
lessons.summary: Choose between bigint identity and UUID keys (including uuidv7 in PostgreSQL 18), decide when a natural key is safe, and pick foreign key ON DELETE actions deliberately.

sections.heading: Surrogate vs natural keys
sections.body:
- A **natural key** is a real-world value (ISO country code, email, SKU). It is safe as a primary key only if it is truly unique, always present and **never changes**.
- A **surrogate key** is a system-generated value with no meaning. It never needs to change, so foreign keys pointing at it never need to be rewritten.

A common, robust pattern: a surrogate primary key **plus** a `UNIQUE` constraint on the natural key. You get stable references and still enforce the business rule.

Emails, usernames and phone numbers fail the "never changes" test. Short, standardised codes (currency, country) usually pass.

sections.heading: Identity columns, not serial
sections.body:
Use SQL-standard identity columns. The PostgreSQL wiki's "Don't Do This" page lists `serial` as something to avoid in new code.

```sql
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY      -- explicit values rejected
id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY  -- explicit values allowed
```

- `ALWAYS` rejects an explicit value in `INSERT` unless the statement says `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`. This protects against application code inventing ids.
- `BY DEFAULT` allows explicit values, which helps for data migrations but lets ids collide with the sequence later.
- Prefer `bigint` over `int` for tables that may grow large: running out of a 32-bit key space forces a painful type change on a hot table.

sections.heading: UUID keys and uuidv7 in PostgreSQL 18
sections.body:
UUIDs are useful when ids must be generated without a central sequence (by clients, by several services, offline) or when you do not want ids to be guessable counters.

As of PostgreSQL 18 the built-in functions are:

| Function | Notes |
|---|---|
| `gen_random_uuid()` / `uuidv4()` | Version 4, random. `uuidv4()` is new in 18 and is an alias. |
| `uuidv7([shift interval])` | **New in 18.** Contains a Unix timestamp with millisecond precision, a sub-millisecond component and random bits. The release notes call these timestamp-ordered. |
| `uuid_extract_timestamp(uuid)` | Returns the embedded timestamp for version 1 and 7 UUIDs. |
| `uuid_extract_version(uuid)` | Returns the version number. |

Trade-offs to weigh:

- A `uuid` is 16 bytes versus 8 for `bigint`, in the table and in every index and foreign key that references it.
- Version 4 values are random, so consecutive inserts land at random places in the primary key index. Version 7 values are ordered by creation time, so new keys sort near each other and "newest first by id" roughly works.
- A uuidv7 **reveals its creation time** to anyone who can see it (`uuid_extract_timestamp`). Do not use it where that leaks something sensitive.
- The docs do not promise strict monotonic ordering between values generated in the same millisecond across sessions. Do not depend on it for correctness; use a timestamp column if you need exact ordering.

sections.heading: Foreign keys and ON DELETE
sections.body:
```sql
author_id bigint REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
```

| Action | Effect when the parent row is deleted |
|---|---|
| `NO ACTION` (default) | Error if children exist. The check can be **deferred** to commit. |
| `RESTRICT` | Error if children exist. **Cannot be deferred.** |
| `CASCADE` | Delete the children too. |
| `SET NULL [(cols)]` | Set the referencing columns to NULL. |
| `SET DEFAULT [(cols)]` | Set them to their defaults. |

Since PostgreSQL 15, `SET NULL` and `SET DEFAULT` accept a column list (for `ON DELETE` only), which matters for composite keys such as `(tenant_id, author_id)` where only `author_id` should be cleared.

Two facts that bite in production:

1. **The referencing column is not indexed automatically.** A delete or key update on the parent must find matching child rows, so without an index on the child column every parent delete scans the child table.
2. With the default `MATCH SIMPLE`, a row whose foreign key has **any** NULL column is not checked at all. Use `NOT NULL` on FK columns that are mandatory, or `MATCH FULL` for composite keys that must be all-or-nothing.

keyPoints: Natural keys only if unique, always present and never changing; otherwise surrogate PK plus UNIQUE on the natural key.
Use GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (bigint) rather than serial.
PostgreSQL 18 adds uuidv7() (timestamp-ordered) and uuidv4(); uuid_extract_timestamp() reads the time from v1/v7.
uuidv7 exposes creation time; uuid costs 16 bytes vs 8 for bigint in every index and FK.
NO ACTION is the default and deferrable; RESTRICT is not deferrable.
Index foreign key columns yourself; PostgreSQL does not.
MATCH SIMPLE skips the check when any FK column is NULL.

gotchas.trap: Using email as the primary key because it is unique.
gotchas.correct: Emails change. Use a surrogate key and a UNIQUE constraint on email.

gotchas.trap: Believing a FOREIGN KEY creates an index on the referencing column.
gotchas.correct: Only the referenced side must have a unique index. Create the child index yourself.

gotchas.trap: Treating NO ACTION and RESTRICT as identical.
gotchas.correct: Both reject the delete, but NO ACTION can be deferred to commit while RESTRICT is checked immediately.

gotchas.trap: Relying on uuidv7 values being strictly increasing.
gotchas.correct: They are timestamp-ordered, but the docs do not guarantee strict monotonicity across sessions.

lessons.lab:
On PostgreSQL 18:

1. Run `SELECT uuidv7() AS a, uuidv4() AS b;` then `SELECT uuid_extract_version(uuidv7()), uuid_extract_timestamp(uuidv7())::text;` and confirm version 7 and a current timestamp.
2. Create `users(id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY)` and try `INSERT INTO users (id) VALUES (5)`. Read the error, then retry with `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`.
3. Create `comments(author_id bigint REFERENCES users ON DELETE SET NULL)`, delete a user, and confirm the comment remains with a NULL author.

lessons.title: Constraints as correctness
lessons.summary: Push rules into the schema with NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE (including NULLS NOT DISTINCT) and exclusion constraints, and add them to live tables safely.

sections.heading: NOT NULL and CHECK
sections.body:
Constraints are rules that every writer obeys, including scripts, other services and manual fixes. Application validation is not a substitute.

- `NOT NULL` is the cheapest, most valuable constraint. A `PRIMARY KEY` implies it.
- A `CHECK` constraint passes when its expression is **true or NULL**. So `CHECK (discount_pct BETWEEN 0 AND 100)` accepts a NULL discount. Add `NOT NULL` if the value is required.
- Name constraints (`CONSTRAINT price_positive CHECK (price > 0)`) so error messages and later `ALTER` statements are readable.
- In PostgreSQL 18 NOT NULL constraints are stored in `pg_constraint`, can be named, and can be added `NOT VALID`.

sections.heading: UNIQUE and NULLs
sections.body:
By default a `UNIQUE` constraint treats NULLs as **distinct**, so any number of rows may have NULL in a unique column.

```sql
-- at most one row per tenant may have no external_ref
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT one_ref_per_tenant
  UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (tenant_id, external_ref);
```

- `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (since PostgreSQL 15) treats NULLs as equal, so only one NULL is allowed per key.
- A **partial unique index** enforces uniqueness only on a subset, for example "one active subscription per user": `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON subscriptions (user_id) WHERE status = 'active';`
- Uniqueness on case-insensitive values: a unique index on an expression such as `lower(email)`.

sections.heading: Exclusion constraints and WITHOUT OVERLAPS
sections.body:
A unique constraint says "no two rows are *equal*". An **exclusion constraint** generalises it to "no two rows satisfy this operator", which is how you forbid overlapping ranges.

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;  -- lets GiST handle the plain = on room_id
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  room_id int NOT NULL,
  during  tstzrange NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
```

- `&&` means "overlaps". Mixing a scalar equality column into a GiST exclusion constraint requires the `btree_gist` extension. A range-only constraint (`EXCLUDE USING gist (during WITH &&)`) does not.
- An application-side "SELECT for overlaps, then INSERT" check races under concurrency. The constraint does not.
- **New in 18:** temporal keys. `PRIMARY KEY (room_id, during WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` or `UNIQUE (...)` expresses the same rule declaratively, and foreign keys can use `PERIOD`. The `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` column must be last, and scalar columns still need `btree_gist`.

sections.heading: Adding constraints to live tables
sections.body:
Adding a constraint normally checks every existing row while holding a lock. On a large table, split it:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id) NOT VALID;  -- quick: new rows checked from now on
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk;     -- scans old rows, SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE
```

- `NOT VALID` still enforces the constraint for new and updated rows. It only skips checking existing rows.
- `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, so normal reads and writes continue.
- Works for foreign keys and CHECK constraints, and in PostgreSQL 18 also for NOT NULL.
- PostgreSQL 18 also allows CHECK and foreign key constraints to be declared `NOT ENFORCED`: they are recorded but not checked, so they document intent without protecting data.
- Deferrable constraints (`DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED`) are checked at commit, which helps when rows that reference each other are inserted in one transaction.

keyPoints: CHECK passes on true or NULL; pair it with NOT NULL for required values.
UNIQUE allows many NULLs by default; NULLS NOT DISTINCT (15+) allows only one.
Partial unique indexes enforce uniqueness on a subset of rows.
Exclusion constraints with && forbid overlapping ranges; scalar = columns need btree_gist.
PostgreSQL 18 adds WITHOUT OVERLAPS keys and PERIOD foreign keys.
NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT avoids a long blocking check on big tables.

gotchas.trap: Expecting CHECK (x > 0) to reject NULL.
gotchas.correct: NULL makes the expression NULL, which passes. Add NOT NULL.

gotchas.trap: Using a partial unique index WHERE col IS NOT NULL to allow at most one NULL.
gotchas.correct: That index ignores NULL rows entirely. Use UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT.

gotchas.trap: Preventing double bookings with a SELECT-then-INSERT check in application code.
gotchas.correct: Two concurrent transactions can both pass the check. Use an exclusion constraint.

gotchas.trap: Thinking a NOT VALID constraint is not enforced at all.
gotchas.correct: It is enforced for new writes; only existing rows are unchecked until VALIDATE.

lessons.lab:
1. Create `t(x int CHECK (x > 0))` and insert `NULL`; note that it succeeds. Add `NOT NULL` and retry.
2. Create `u(a int, b int, UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (a, b))` and insert `(1, NULL)` twice; observe the second insert fail.
3. Create `r(during tstzrange, EXCLUDE USING gist (during WITH &&))` (no extension needed) and insert two overlapping ranges, then two adjacent ranges such as `[10:00,11:00)` and `[11:00,12:00)`.

lessons.title: Choosing column types
lessons.summary: Pick timestamptz, numeric, text, jsonb, arrays, enums or lookup tables for the right reasons, and use generated columns knowing that PostgreSQL 18 makes them virtual by default.

sections.heading: Time: timestamptz vs timestamp
sections.body:
- `timestamptz` stores an absolute **point in time**. Input with an offset or zone is converted to UTC on the way in, and output is shown in the session's `TimeZone`.
- `timestamp` (without time zone) stores a wall-clock reading and **ignores** any zone information. The same value means different instants in different zones.
- The PostgreSQL wiki's advice: use `timestamptz` for points in time, **even if you only ever store UTC**. Use `timestamp` only for abstract wall-clock values (a recurring "09:00 local" schedule).
- Query ranges with `>= start AND < end`, not `BETWEEN`, which includes the end boundary and double counts it.

sections.heading: Numbers and text
sections.body:
- `numeric` is exact decimal arithmetic. `real`/`double precision` are binary floating point and inexact: `0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8` is **false**, while the same comparison with `numeric` is true. Use `numeric` for money and anything that must add up exactly.
- Avoid the `money` type; the wiki recommends `numeric` (and storing the currency in its own column).
- Use `text` by default. The docs state there is no performance difference among `text`, `varchar(n)` and `char(n)` apart from padding costs for `char(n)`. If a length limit is a real business rule, express it as a `CHECK (length(code) <= 10)`, which is easier to change.
- Avoid `char(n)`: it pads with spaces.

sections.heading: jsonb and arrays
sections.body:
**jsonb** is good for genuinely variable or externally defined data (payloads, per-category attributes).

- Keep fields that you filter, join, sort or constrain on as typed columns. jsonb fields cannot carry foreign keys, and type checks need extra CHECK constraints.
- A GIN index supports containment and existence (`@>`, `?`) queries.
- Any update to a jsonb value rewrites the whole row version, so keep documents small rather than growing one large document per entity.

**Arrays** suit small, ordered, value-like lists that are read and written as a unit (tags on a post, a handful of phone numbers). They are a poor fit for relationships to other tables, because elements cannot be foreign keys.

sections.heading: Enums vs lookup tables
sections.body:
An **enum** type is compact and orders by declaration order.

- You can add values (`ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE`) and rename them, but **existing values cannot be removed and their sort order cannot be changed** without dropping and recreating the type.
- Enums hold only a label: no extra attributes.

A **lookup table** (`order_status(code text PRIMARY KEY, label text, is_terminal boolean, sort_order int)`) referenced by a foreign key costs a join, but values can be added, retired and described with metadata using ordinary DML.

Rule of thumb: enum for small sets that are truly stable; lookup table when the business owns the list or needs metadata. A `CHECK (status IN (...))` is a middle ground that is easy to read but needs DDL to change.

sections.heading: Generated columns in PostgreSQL 18
sections.body:
```sql
ALTER TABLE order_lines ADD COLUMN total numeric
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * unit_price) STORED;   -- computed on write, can be indexed
ALTER TABLE order_lines ADD COLUMN total_v numeric
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * unit_price);          -- 18 default: VIRTUAL, computed on read
```

- **In PostgreSQL 18, VIRTUAL is the default** when neither keyword is given. Virtual columns are computed when read and take no storage.
- **Virtual generated columns cannot be indexed** (`indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported`). Use `STORED`, or an expression index on the same expression.
- Adding a virtual column does not rewrite the table. Adding a stored one does.
- The expression may use only immutable functions and same-row columns, and cannot reference another generated column. Virtual columns cannot use user-defined types or functions.
- You cannot write to a generated column (`cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value`), and a generated column cannot be part of a partition key.
- Logical replication can publish **stored** generated columns only.

keyPoints: timestamptz for points in time, even for UTC-only data; >= and < for ranges.
numeric for exact amounts; floats are inexact; avoid money.
text by default; length rules as CHECK constraints.
Typed columns for fields you filter, join or constrain; jsonb for genuinely variable data.
Enum values cannot be removed or reordered; lookup tables can carry metadata and change by DML.
PostgreSQL 18 generated columns default to VIRTUAL, which cannot be indexed; use STORED for indexing.

gotchas.trap: Using timestamp without time zone because "we always store UTC".
gotchas.correct: Use timestamptz; it represents an instant and converts correctly for every client zone.

gotchas.trap: Summing prices stored as double precision.
gotchas.correct: Floating point is inexact; use numeric.

gotchas.trap: Choosing varchar(255) for performance.
gotchas.correct: There is no performance difference vs text; use text plus a CHECK if a limit is a real rule.

gotchas.trap: Writing GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) on PostgreSQL 18 and then indexing it.
gotchas.correct: Without STORED the column is virtual and cannot be indexed.

lessons.lab:
On PostgreSQL 18:

1. Run `SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8 AS f, 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric = 0.3::numeric AS n;`
2. Create `t(a int, b int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (a * 2))`, try `CREATE INDEX ON t (b)`, and read the error. Check `SELECT attgenerated FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 't'::regclass AND attname = 'b';` (expect `v`).
3. Recreate the column with `STORED` and create the index successfully.
4. Create an enum `mood` with three values, add a fourth with `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE`, and look for a way to drop one (there is none short of recreating the type).

lessons.title: Declarative partitioning
lessons.summary: How range, list and hash partitioning work, what partition pruning needs from your queries, the constraints partitioning imposes, and when it actually helps.

sections.heading: Range, list and hash
sections.body:
```sql
CREATE TABLE events (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  user_id bigint NOT NULL,
  payload jsonb,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE events_2026_11 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-11-01') TO ('2026-12-01');
CREATE TABLE events_default PARTITION OF events DEFAULT;
```

- **Range**: contiguous, non-overlapping ranges. The lower bound is **inclusive** and the upper bound **exclusive**, so monthly partitions meet exactly. Typical for time series.
- **List**: explicit key values per partition (region, tenant tier).
- **Hash**: `FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0)` spreads rows evenly when there is no natural range or list, for example many tenants.
- A **DEFAULT** partition catches rows that fit no other partition.

sections.heading: Partition pruning
sections.body:
Pruning removes partitions that cannot contain matching rows.

- It happens at **plan time** for constants and at **execution time** for parameters and values from subqueries (shown as `Subplans Removed` in EXPLAIN).
- It needs a predicate on the **partition key**. A query on `events` filtered only by `user_id` must visit every partition.
- `enable_partition_pruning` is on by default.
- Within a partition, ordinary indexes still do the work. Pruning picks partitions; indexes find rows.

sections.heading: Constraints and limitations
sections.body:
- A `PRIMARY KEY` or `UNIQUE` constraint on a partitioned table must **include all partition key columns**. There is no global unique index across partitions, so "`id` unique across all months" cannot be enforced directly.
- `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` is not supported on the parent. Create the index `ON ONLY` the parent, build it concurrently on each partition, then `ALTER INDEX ... ATTACH PARTITION`.
- A generated column cannot be part of the partition key.
- Partitioned parents are not processed by autovacuum's ANALYZE, so run `ANALYZE` on the parent yourself when queries need its statistics.
- PostgreSQL 18 does not allow unlogged partitioned tables.

sections.heading: When partitioning helps
sections.body:
Partitioning is a tool for **data lifecycle and very large tables**, not a general speed-up.

Good reasons:

- **Retention**: removing a month is `DROP TABLE events_2025_10` or `ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2025_10 CONCURRENTLY`, instead of a huge `DELETE` that creates dead tuples for vacuum to clean.
- **Huge tables with locality**: the docs' rule of thumb is that benefits appear when a table would otherwise be larger than the server's physical memory, and most queries touch one or a few partitions.
- **Bulk loading**: load a new table, add a CHECK that matches the bounds, then `ATTACH PARTITION`; the matching CHECK lets PostgreSQL skip the validation scan.

Poor reasons: a table of a few gigabytes queried by primary key, or queries that never filter on the partition key. Too many partitions also cost planning time; a few thousand is workable when pruning keeps the touched set small.

keyPoints: Range bounds: lower inclusive, upper exclusive; list for discrete values; hash for even spread.
Pruning needs a predicate on the partition key; it works at plan time and execution time.
PK/UNIQUE must include the partition key; there is no global unique index.
Retention by DROP or DETACH PARTITION [CONCURRENTLY] avoids massive DELETEs.
Partition for lifecycle and tables larger than memory with locality, not for small tables.
CIC is not supported on the parent: ON ONLY parent, CIC per partition, then ATTACH.

gotchas.trap: Declaring PRIMARY KEY (id) on a table partitioned by created_at.
gotchas.correct: The key must include created_at, for example PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at).

gotchas.trap: Expecting partitioning to speed up queries that do not filter on the partition key.
gotchas.correct: Without a key predicate every partition is scanned; it can be slower than one table.

gotchas.trap: Using BETWEEN-style inclusive upper bounds for monthly partitions.
gotchas.correct: Upper bounds are exclusive: FROM (2026-11-01) TO (2026-12-01).

lessons.lab:
1. Create `events` partitioned by month as shown, with three monthly partitions and a DEFAULT partition, and insert rows across them.
2. Run `EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-01' AND created_at < '2026-12-01';` and confirm only one partition appears.
3. Run `EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 1;` and note every partition is listed.
4. Try `CREATE TABLE bad (id int PRIMARY KEY, d date) PARTITION BY RANGE (d);` and read the error.
5. Detach the oldest partition and drop it.

lessons.title: B-tree indexes in depth
lessons.summary: How a B-tree index narrows a search, why column order in a multicolumn index matters, how indexes deliver sorted output, and what an index-only scan needs.

sections.heading: What a B-tree is good at
sections.body:
A B-tree is PostgreSQL's default index type. It keeps keys in sorted order, so it can answer:

- equality and range comparisons: `<`, `<=`, `=`, `>=`, `>`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`
- `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`
- anchored pattern matches such as `LIKE 'abc%'`, but only when the column uses the C collation or the index uses a pattern operator class such as `text_pattern_ops`

Because the keys are sorted, a B-tree can also return rows already in order. That lets the planner skip a separate Sort step.

sections.heading: Multicolumn column order
sections.body:
In a multicolumn B-tree on `(a, b, c)`, the conditions that narrow the scanned part of the index are:

1. equality conditions on the leading columns, plus
2. one inequality on the first column that has no equality condition.

Conditions on later columns are still checked inside the index, which saves heap visits. But they do not shrink the range of index entries that has to be read.

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created_at);
-- Good: equality on the leading column, then a range on the next
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= now() - interval '30 days';
```

Rule of thumb: put the columns you filter by equality first. Put the range or sort column after them.

An index can have up to 32 columns, INCLUDE columns counted.

sections.heading: Skip scan in PostgreSQL 18
sections.body:
Before 18, a query that filtered only on a non-leading column, such as `WHERE b = 7` against an index on `(a, b)`, could not search that index efficiently.

PostgreSQL 18 adds **B-tree skip scan**. The planner can run one search for each distinct value of `a`. This pays off only when `a` has few distinct values. When `a` has many, the planner still prefers another plan, such as a sequential scan.

Skip scan is a help, not a design strategy. If a query filters on `b` alone and runs often, give it an index that leads with `b`.

sections.heading: Sort order and ORDER BY
sections.body:
A B-tree can be scanned forwards or backwards. So an index on `(x)` serves both `ORDER BY x` and `ORDER BY x DESC`.

Mixed directions need a matching index. `ORDER BY x ASC, y DESC` cannot come from an index on `(x, y)`. It needs `(x ASC, y DESC)`, or `(x DESC, y ASC)` read backwards.

NULL placement is part of the order. By default NULLs sort as larger than every value. That means `NULLS LAST` for ascending and `NULLS FIRST` for descending.

Index order matters most with `LIMIT`. When the query needs every row, a sequential scan followed by a sort is often cheaper than reading the whole table in index order.

sections.heading: Index-only scans
sections.body:
An index-only scan answers a query from the index without visiting the table (the heap). It needs two things:

1. The index type supports it. B-tree always does, GiST and SP-GiST do for some operator classes, and **GIN never does**.
2. Every column the query references is stored in the index.

There is a catch. MVCC visibility is stored in the heap, not the index. PostgreSQL checks the **visibility map** and visits the heap only for pages that are not marked all-visible. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` reports these visits as `Heap Fetches`.

A table that changes a lot, and that VACUUM has not processed recently, can show an "Index Only Scan" that still fetches most rows from the heap.

keyPoints: Put equality columns first and the range or sort column after them in a multicolumn B-tree.
Conditions on later columns are checked in the index but do not shrink the scanned range.
PostgreSQL 18 skip scan helps a non-leading-column filter only when the leading column has few distinct values.
One B-tree serves both ORDER BY x and ORDER BY x DESC. Mixed directions need a matching index.
Index-only scans need every referenced column in the index and pages marked all-visible. Heap Fetches shows the shortfall.

gotchas.trap: An index on (a, b) is just as good for WHERE b = ? as an index on (b).
gotchas.correct: Without equality on a, the scan is not bounded by b. Skip scan in 18 helps only when a has few distinct values, so add an index that leads with b if that query matters.

gotchas.trap: Index Only Scan in the plan means the heap was never touched.
gotchas.correct: Check Heap Fetches. Pages that are not all-visible in the visibility map still need a heap visit, so VACUUM affects index-only performance.

gotchas.trap: An index on (x, y) serves ORDER BY x, y DESC.
gotchas.correct: Mixed directions need an index declared with matching directions, such as (x, y DESC).

lessons.lab: Create a table with 100k rows and an index on (customer_id, created_at). Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE for WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10. Then try WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day' alone and compare the plans. Finally run SELECT customer_id, created_at with and without a preceding VACUUM, and watch Heap Fetches.

lessons.title: Partial, expression and covering indexes
lessons.summary: Three ways to shape an index around a query: index only some rows, index a computed value, or carry extra payload columns so the heap is never visited.

sections.heading: Why a function on a column skips the index
sections.body:
An index on `email` stores the values of `email`. A query that filters on `lower(email)` asks about a different value, so the plain index cannot be searched:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON users (email);
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'ann@example.com';  -- cannot use the index above
```

The same applies to casts and arithmetic on the column, such as `created_at::date = '2026-01-01'` or `price * 1.2 > 100`. There are two fixes:

- Rewrite the predicate so the bare column is compared. For example, use `created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-02'`.
- Build an **expression index** on exactly the expression the query uses.

sections.heading: Expression indexes
sections.body:
```sql
CREATE INDEX users_lower_email ON users (lower(email));
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'ann@example.com';  -- can use it
```

The rules:

- The query has to use the same expression that was indexed.
- The functions in the expression have to be IMMUTABLE.
- The expression is computed on every INSERT and on every UPDATE that changes it, so writes cost more.
- Wrap anything more than a bare function call in extra parentheses, as in `CREATE INDEX ON t ((a || ' ' || b))`.

A unique expression index can enforce rules that a plain constraint cannot. For example, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` makes emails unique regardless of case.

For an index-only scan on `f(x)`, the planner may still want `x` itself in the index. Adding `INCLUDE (x)` helps.

sections.heading: Partial indexes
sections.body:
A partial index covers only the rows that match a `WHERE` predicate:

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_pending ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
```

This is smaller and cheaper to maintain than a full index when the queries only ever look at a small subset, such as unprocessed rows or non-deleted rows.

- The planner uses the index only when it can prove the query's WHERE clause implies the index predicate.
- That check happens at **plan time**. A parameterized clause like `status = $1` in a generic plan does not match a partial index on `status = 'pending'`.
- Functions in the predicate must be IMMUTABLE.
- A **partial unique index** enforces uniqueness only among matching rows. For example, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON subscriptions (user_id) WHERE active` allows one active subscription per user.

sections.heading: Covering indexes with INCLUDE
sections.body:
`INCLUDE` adds payload columns to the leaf entries. They are not part of the search key:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON accounts (account_no) INCLUDE (balance);
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_no = 'A-100';  -- index-only scan candidate
```

- INCLUDE columns can be returned by an index-only scan, but they cannot be searched or used for ordering.
- They are ignored for uniqueness. Here only `account_no` must be unique.
- They cannot be expressions.
- They are supported by B-tree, GiST and SP-GiST.
- They are never deduplicated.

Do not use INCLUDE to pile wide columns into an index. Every extra column makes the index larger and slows writes.

keyPoints: A function or cast applied to an indexed column stops a plain index on that column from being searched.
An expression index must match the query's expression exactly and use only IMMUTABLE functions.
A partial index is used only when the planner can prove at plan time that the query implies its predicate.
A partial unique index enforces uniqueness within a subset, such as one active row per user.
INCLUDE columns enable index-only scans but are not searchable and do not count for uniqueness.

gotchas.trap: WHERE created_at::date = '2026-01-01' will use the index on created_at.
gotchas.correct: The cast hides the column. Use a half-open range (>= day AND < next day) or an expression index on the cast.

gotchas.trap: A partial index on status = 'pending' will serve a prepared statement WHERE status = $1.
gotchas.correct: Predicate matching happens at plan time, so a generic plan with a parameter cannot use it. Use a literal or a full index.

gotchas.trap: UNIQUE (a) INCLUDE (b) makes the pair (a, b) unique.
gotchas.correct: INCLUDE columns are ignored for uniqueness. Only a must be unique.

lessons.lab: On a users table, run EXPLAIN for WHERE lower(email) = 'x' with only an index on email, then add an index on lower(email) and compare. Create a partial index WHERE status = 'pending' and check that a query with status = 'done' does not use it.

lessons.title: GIN, GiST, BRIN and hash: picking the index type
lessons.summary: Which index access method fits which operator: inverted indexes for containment, GiST for ranges and nearest-neighbour search, BRIN for huge naturally ordered tables, and hash for equality only.

sections.heading: Start from the operator
sections.body:
An index type only helps a query when it supports the operator that query uses. Choose by the operator, not by the column's type:

| Type | Operators it supports | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| B-tree | `< <= = >= >`, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, anchored LIKE | Equality, ranges, sorted output |
| Hash | `=` only | Equality only |
| GiST | geometric operators, range `&&` and containment, KNN `<->` | Ranges, geometry, nearest neighbour, exclusion constraints |
| SP-GiST | space-partitioned operators | Quadtrees, tries |
| GIN | `@> <@ = &&` and more, per operator class | Arrays, jsonb, full-text tsvector, trigrams |
| BRIN | min/max (or other) summaries per block range | Very large tables whose values follow physical order |

sections.heading: GIN: the inverted index
sections.body:
GIN stores each element (an array item, a jsonb key or value, a lexeme) with the list of rows that contain it. This makes it the default choice for:

- jsonb containment (`@>`) and key existence (`?`). The default `jsonb_ops` supports `?`. `jsonb_path_ops` is smaller but supports only `@>`, `@?` and `@@`.
- array overlap and containment (`&&`, `@>`)
- full-text search on `tsvector`
- unanchored `LIKE '%foo%'` and similarity searches, through pg_trgm's `gin_trgm_ops`

Trade-offs:

- GIN **never supports index-only scans**.
- Updates cost more than for a B-tree.
- PostgreSQL 18 can build GIN indexes in parallel.

sections.heading: GiST: ranges, geometry and nearest neighbour
sections.body:
GiST is a balanced framework for "overlaps", "contains" and distance operators. Use it for:

- range types (`tstzrange && tstzrange`)
- geometric types
- exclusion constraints such as `EXCLUDE USING gist (during WITH &&)`
- **KNN ordering** with `ORDER BY col <-> value LIMIT n`

With pg_trgm, nearest-neighbour `ORDER BY <->` on text works with GiST (`gist_trgm_ops`), not GIN.

sections.heading: BRIN and hash
sections.body:
**BRIN** stores a small summary, such as the min and max, for each range of table blocks. A query skips every block range whose summary cannot match.

BRIN is tiny and cheap to maintain. It only works well when values correlate with physical row order, such as an append-only events table filtered by `created_at`. On randomly ordered data almost every range matches, so BRIN saves nothing. Results come back through a bitmap heap scan with a recheck.

**Hash** indexes support only `=`. They cannot serve ranges or sorting, and they cannot back a unique constraint. A B-tree also handles equality, so pick hash only when you have a measured reason.

keyPoints: Pick the index type by the operator the query uses.
GIN fits containment and membership: jsonb @>, arrays, tsvector, trigram LIKE '%x%'.
GiST fits ranges, geometry, exclusion constraints and KNN ORDER BY <->.
BRIN is tiny but only useful when values correlate with physical order.
Hash supports only equality. B-tree is usually the safer default.

gotchas.trap: A B-tree on a jsonb column will speed up WHERE doc @> '{"tag":"x"}'.
gotchas.correct: B-tree does not support @>. Use a GIN index (jsonb_ops or jsonb_path_ops).

gotchas.trap: BRIN is a smaller B-tree that works on any column.
gotchas.correct: BRIN only summarizes block ranges. On data not correlated with physical order it skips almost nothing.

gotchas.trap: A GIN trigram index supports ORDER BY name <-> 'x' LIMIT 10.
gotchas.correct: KNN distance ordering with pg_trgm needs a GiST index (gist_trgm_ops).

lessons.lab: Create a jsonb table, query it with @> using a B-tree and then a GIN index, and compare EXPLAIN output. Build a BRIN index on an append-only created_at column and on a random column, and compare how many rows each range filter rechecks.

lessons.title: Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and planner statistics
lessons.summary: How to read a plan: node types, estimated against actual rows, per-loop numbers, buffers, and how statistics and ANALYZE drive the planner's choices.

sections.heading: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE
sections.body:
`EXPLAIN` shows the plan the planner chose and its **estimates**. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` **runs** the statement and adds actual times and row counts. For an UPDATE or DELETE that really modifies data, wrap it:

```sql
BEGIN;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) DELETE FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2020-01-01';
ROLLBACK;
```

How to read a node line:

- Costs are in arbitrary units, anchored on `seq_page_cost = 1.0`. The docs' example is 345 pages × 1.0 + 10000 rows × 0.01 = 445.
- `rows` is the number of rows the node emits.
- Actual time and rows are **per loop**. Multiply by `loops` to get the totals.

In PostgreSQL 18, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` includes buffer counts by default (turn them off with `BUFFERS OFF`). Row counts are shown with fractions, and index scan nodes report `Index Searches`.

sections.heading: Scan and join nodes
sections.body:
**Scans:**

- **Seq Scan** reads the whole table. It is the right choice when a large fraction of rows match.
- **Index Scan** walks the index and visits the heap for each match.
- **Index Only Scan** answers from the index. Check `Heap Fetches`.
- **Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan** collects matching row locations, then reads heap pages in physical order. Several bitmaps can be combined with BitmapAnd or BitmapOr. `Recheck Cond` and `Heap Blocks: exact=… lossy=…` show up here. Lossy blocks appear when the bitmap does not fit in work_mem.

**Joins:**

- **Nested Loop** runs the inner side once per outer row, so watch `loops`. It is good when the outer side is small and the inner side is indexed.
- **Hash Join** builds a hash table from one input. It is good for large unsorted equality joins.
- **Merge Join** merges two inputs that are sorted on the join key.

Lines such as `Rows Removed by Filter` show work spent reading rows that were then discarded. Don't draw conclusions from tiny test tables: a one-page table almost always gets a seq scan.

sections.heading: Estimates vs actuals
sections.body:
The most useful check is to compare the estimated `rows=` with the actual rows at each node. A large mismatch, such as an estimate of 10 against 50,000 actual, usually explains a bad plan. A typical example is a Nested Loop chosen because the planner thought the outer side was tiny.

Common causes:

- **Stale statistics.** The table changed a lot since the last ANALYZE.
- **Correlated columns.** The planner assumes conditions are independent, so `city = 'Paris' AND country = 'FR'` is underestimated. `CREATE STATISTICS` (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) can teach it the correlation.
- **Skewed values** that the sampled most-common-values list does not capture. Raise the column's statistics target with `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN … SET STATISTICS`, then ANALYZE.
- **Expressions and functions** with no statistics. An expression index gets its own statistics after ANALYZE.

sections.heading: ANALYZE and autovacuum
sections.body:
The planner's row estimates come from statistics in `pg_statistic`, which `ANALYZE` collects from a sample.

- Autovacuum runs ANALYZE on a table after about 50 + 10% of its rows have changed (the default thresholds).
- Run ANALYZE yourself after a bulk load or a large delete, before the next queries depend on good estimates.
- Partitioned **parent** tables are not analyzed by autovacuum. Run ANALYZE on them manually so queries that span partitions get good estimates.
- In 18, `pg_upgrade` keeps optimizer statistics (extended statistics excepted), so a freshly upgraded cluster no longer starts without them.

keyPoints: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Wrap DML in BEGIN/ROLLBACK.
Actual time and rows are per loop. Multiply by loops.
A large gap between estimated and actual rows is the first clue to a bad plan.
Stale stats call for ANALYZE. Correlated columns call for CREATE STATISTICS.
In 18, EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports buffers by default and index nodes show Index Searches.

gotchas.trap: The plan says actual rows=5 loops=2000, so the node produced 5 rows.
gotchas.correct: Actual rows are per loop. The node produced about 10,000 rows in total.

gotchas.trap: Autovacuum keeps the partitioned parent's statistics current.
gotchas.correct: Autovacuum does not analyze partitioned parents. Run ANALYZE on the parent manually.

gotchas.trap: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DELETE is safe because it only explains.
gotchas.correct: It runs the DELETE. Use BEGIN … ROLLBACK.

lessons.lab: Load 1M rows with two correlated columns (city, country). Compare estimated and actual rows for a filter on both. Run CREATE STATISTICS (dependencies) ON city, country, then ANALYZE, and re-check the estimate.
