lessons.title: Query anti-patterns that defeat indexes
lessons.summary: Patterns that make otherwise good indexes useless or waste work: deep OFFSET pagination, N+1 queries, SELECT *, hidden casts and functions on columns, and OR across different columns.

sections.heading: OFFSET pagination vs keyset pagination
sections.body:
The docs warn that rows skipped by `OFFSET` "still have to be computed inside the server". So `OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20` reads and throws away 100,000 rows, and each page is slower than the one before. Rows inserted or deleted between requests can also shift a row onto two pages, or skip it entirely.

**Keyset (seek) pagination** remembers where the last page ended and seeks past it:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON posts (created_at DESC, id DESC);
SELECT id, title, created_at FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_created_at, $last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

The `id` tiebreaker makes the order unique. The row comparison maps onto the index, so every page costs the same. Also, `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns an unpredictable subset.

sections.heading: N+1 queries
sections.body:
An N+1 pattern runs one query for a list, then one more query per row:

```text
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;   -- 1 query
SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ?;   -- N more queries, one per order
```

Each query may be fast, but N network round trips and N statement executions add up. Fixes:

- a single join
- `WHERE order_id = ANY($1)` with an array of ids
- `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` when you need the top few child rows per parent

These show up in query statistics as one cheap statement with a huge call count.

sections.heading: SELECT * and wide rows
sections.body:
`SELECT *`:

- ships columns the caller does not need, including large TOASTed values
- breaks when columns are added or reordered
- **rules out index-only scans**, because an index-only scan needs every referenced column in the index

Name the columns you need. A narrow query such as `SELECT id, status` can be served by a covering index.

sections.heading: Hidden casts, functions and OR across columns
sections.body:
**Casts and functions.** Wrapping the column in a cast or function, such as `created_at::date`, `lower(email)` or `col + 0`, means a plain index on the column can't be searched. Compare the bare column against a range or constant of the column's type, or add an expression index. The wiki also recommends `>=` and `<` over `BETWEEN` for time ranges.

**OR across different columns.** `WHERE email = $1 OR phone = $2` cannot be answered by one B-tree on either column. The planner can combine two separate indexes with a **BitmapOr**. If it does not, rewrite the query as a `UNION` of two indexed queries.

PostgreSQL 18 turns ORs on the **same** column into an `= ANY(array)` search, which softens that older anti-pattern. ORs across **different** columns still need one of the fixes above.

keyPoints: Deep OFFSET computes and discards every skipped row. Keyset pagination costs the same on every page.
Keyset pagination needs a unique sort key (add id as a tiebreaker) and a matching index.
Replace N+1 loops with a join, = ANY(array) or LATERAL.
SELECT * rules out index-only scans and ships unneeded data.
OR across different columns needs a BitmapOr of two indexes or a UNION rewrite.

gotchas.trap: OFFSET is cheap because the skipped rows are not returned.
gotchas.correct: Skipped rows are still computed inside the server, so cost grows with the offset.

gotchas.trap: Keyset pagination on created_at alone is safe.
gotchas.correct: Without a unique tiebreaker such as id, rows with equal timestamps can be skipped or repeated.

gotchas.trap: A composite index on (email, phone) serves WHERE email = ? OR phone = ?.
gotchas.correct: It cannot bound the phone branch. Use separate indexes (BitmapOr) or a UNION.

lessons.lab: Fill a posts table with 1M rows. Time OFFSET 0, 10000 and 500000 with LIMIT 20, then the keyset version at the same positions. Compare buffer counts in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE).

lessons.title: Isolation levels and MVCC visibility
lessons.summary: How PostgreSQL keeps several row versions, decides which one each snapshot sees, and what each isolation level does and does not protect against (as of PostgreSQL 18).

sections.heading: MVCC: every UPDATE writes a new row version
sections.body:
PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control. A row is stored as one or more **tuple versions**. Each version carries system columns:

- `xmin`: the ID of the transaction that inserted this version.
- `xmax`: the ID of the transaction that deleted or updated it (zero while it is live and unlocked).
- `ctid`: the physical location `(page, item)` of this version.

An `UPDATE` never overwrites a row in place. It writes a **new version** with a new `xmin` and marks the old version with `xmax`. You can see this yourself:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id int PRIMARY KEY, v int);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 10);
SELECT ctid, xmin, * FROM t;   -- (0,1)
UPDATE t SET v = 11 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT ctid, xmin, * FROM t;   -- (0,2), new xmin
```

Because `ctid` moves on UPDATE (and on `VACUUM FULL`), it is never a durable row identifier. Use the primary key.

sections.heading: Snapshots: readers never block writers
sections.body:
Each statement (or transaction) reads through a **snapshot**: a record of which transactions had committed when it was taken. A version is visible if its `xmin` committed before the snapshot and its `xmax` did not. The old version stays on disk, so a reader keeps seeing it while a writer creates the new one.

The practical result: reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading. Writers only wait for other writers to the **same row**. The cost is that old versions pile up as **dead tuples** until VACUUM removes them (see the VACUUM lesson).

sections.heading: Read committed: a new snapshot per statement
sections.body:
`READ COMMITTED` is the default. Each statement sees data committed before **that statement** began, so two `SELECT`s in one transaction can return different results.

For `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `SELECT FOR UPDATE`, if a target row was changed by a concurrent transaction, the statement **waits**, then **re-evaluates its WHERE clause on the new version**. The docs example: `hits` holds 9 and 10, session A runs `UPDATE website SET hits = hits + 1`, and a concurrent `DELETE FROM website WHERE hits = 10` deletes **nothing**: its snapshot saw 9 for the first row, and the row it waited on is now 11.

The classic bug at this level is the **lost update**: read a value in the app, compute, then write it back. Two sessions both read 5 and both write 4. Fix it with an atomic `UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1`, with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or with a stricter level plus retries. `READ UNCOMMITTED` is accepted but behaves exactly like read committed.

sections.heading: Repeatable read: one snapshot for the whole transaction
sections.body:
`REPEATABLE READ` takes its snapshot at the first non-transaction-control statement and keeps it. In PostgreSQL this level also prevents **phantom reads**, which the SQL standard would allow.

If the transaction tries to update or lock a row that a concurrent transaction changed and committed after the snapshot, it fails:

```
ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
```

The SQLSTATE is `40001`. The only correct response is to roll back and **retry the whole transaction**, including the reads that led to the write.

Repeatable read still allows **serialization anomalies** such as **write skew**: two transactions each read an overlapping set, each writes a different row based on what it read, and the combined result matches no serial order.

sections.heading: Serializable: SSI and read-only deferrable
sections.body:
`SERIALIZABLE` uses **serializable snapshot isolation (SSI)**. It runs like repeatable read but also tracks read/write dependencies with predicate locks (`SIReadLock` in `pg_locks`). These locks **never block** and cannot cause deadlocks. When a dangerous pattern appears, one transaction fails with:

```
ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
```

Again SQLSTATE `40001`. SSI can report false positives, so every serializable transaction needs a retry loop. Declaring transactions `READ ONLY` where possible helps.

For long reports, `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` may wait for a **safe snapshot** when it starts. After that it runs without the risk of being cancelled by a serialization failure.

| Level | Dirty read | Nonrepeatable read | Phantom | Serialization anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read committed | No | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| Repeatable read | No | No | No (in PG) | Possible |
| Serializable | No | No | No | No |

keyPoints: UPDATE writes a new tuple version (new xmin, new ctid); the old one is marked with xmax and becomes dead after commit.
Readers and writers do not block each other; writers wait only for writers to the same row.
Read committed is the default and re-evaluates WHERE on the newest row version after waiting.
Repeatable read in PostgreSQL prevents phantoms but still allows write skew.
Serializable (SSI) aborts instead of blocking; both RR and serializable errors use SQLSTATE 40001 and need a whole-transaction retry.

gotchas.trap: Wrapping read-then-write logic in BEGIN/COMMIT makes it safe.
gotchas.correct: Under read committed a transaction block alone does not stop lost updates. Use an atomic UPDATE, a row lock, or a stricter level with retries.

gotchas.trap: Serializable makes the second transaction wait until the first commits.
gotchas.correct: SSI predicate locks never block. A conflicting transaction is aborted with 40001 and must be retried.

gotchas.trap: ctid is a handy stable row ID.
gotchas.correct: ctid changes on every UPDATE and on VACUUM FULL. Store primary keys instead.

lessons.lab: Open two psql sessions on a scratch table `acct(id int primary key, bal int)`. (1) In both sessions, at read committed, SELECT a balance and then UPDATE it to the value you computed; observe the lost update. (2) Repeat with `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ` and watch the second writer get SQLSTATE 40001. (3) Build the on-call doctors write-skew example under repeatable read and then serializable, and note which session fails. Note: the single-connection SQL runner cannot run this; use a real server.

lessons.title: VACUUM, bloat, HOT and wraparound
lessons.summary: Why dead tuples accumulate, how autovacuum decides when to run, how HOT updates avoid index churn, and how to respond to transaction ID wraparound warnings.

sections.heading: What VACUUM does
sections.body:
Plain `VACUUM` removes dead row versions from tables and indexes and marks the space as **reusable**. It runs alongside normal reads and writes (it takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`). It generally does **not** return space to the operating system, except for fully empty pages at the end of the table.

`VACUUM FULL` writes a complete new copy of the table with no dead space and returns space to the OS. It takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, which blocks even plain `SELECT`, and it needs extra disk for the new copy. The docs recommend frequent plain vacuums over occasional `VACUUM FULL` for heavily updated tables. Autovacuum never issues `VACUUM FULL`.

VACUUM also maintains the visibility map (which makes index-only scans cheap) and **freezes** old tuples.

sections.heading: Why bloat grows: the xmin horizon
Autovacuum thresholds and tuning
sections.body:
Autovacuum vacuums a table when its dead tuples exceed

```
min(autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold,
    autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor * reltuples)
```

In PostgreSQL 18 the defaults are 50 + 0.2 × rows, capped by the new `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` (100 million). Inserts have their own threshold so insert-only tables still get vacuumed and frozen. On a huge, busy table, 20% can be a lot of dead rows, so tune **that table**:

```sql
ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01);
```

Other levers: `autovacuum_max_workers` (3 by default; 18 adds `autovacuum_worker_slots` so it can be raised without a restart) and the cost-based delay settings that throttle each worker.

sections.heading: HOT updates
sections.body:
Because UPDATE writes a new version, every index normally needs a new entry pointing to it. A **heap-only tuple (HOT)** update skips that when both conditions hold:

1. The update changes **no column referenced by any index** on the table (summarizing indexes such as BRIN excepted). `INCLUDE` columns count as referenced.
2. The page holding the old version has **enough free space** for the new one.

HOT updates add no index entries, and old versions in the chain can be pruned during normal page access, without waiting for VACUUM. To get more of them, avoid indexing frequently updated columns and lower the table `fillfactor` (for example 80 or 90) so pages keep room. Monitor `n_tup_hot_upd` against `n_tup_upd` in `pg_stat_all_tables`.

sections.heading: Transaction ID wraparound and freezing
sections.body:
Transaction IDs are **32-bit**, so comparisons work on a circle of about four billion IDs. VACUUM **freezes** old tuples so they count as visible to everyone regardless of their `xmin`. If a table goes about two billion transactions without freezing, data loss could result.

Safeguards:

- When a table's oldest unfrozen XID exceeds `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` (200 million by default), an anti-wraparound autovacuum runs **even if autovacuum is disabled**.
- `vacuum_failsafe_age` makes VACUUM skip non-essential work to finish freezing faster.
- About 40 million XIDs before the limit, the server warns. At about 3 million left, it refuses to assign new XIDs.

The response: resolve whatever holds the horizon back (old prepared transactions, stale replication slots, long transactions), then run a **database-wide plain VACUUM** as a superuser. The docs say single-user mode is no longer needed in typical cases and should be avoided.

keyPoints: Plain VACUUM makes dead space reusable without blocking reads or writes; VACUUM FULL rewrites under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.
Long or idle-in-transaction sessions, old prepared transactions and stale replication slots stop VACUUM from removing dead tuples.
Tune autovacuum per table with storage parameters such as autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor.
HOT needs no indexed column to change and free space on the same page; lower fillfactor helps.
Wraparound is prevented by freezing; anti-wraparound vacuums run even with autovacuum disabled; fix warnings with a plain database-wide VACUUM.

gotchas.trap: Run VACUUM FULL to fix bloat caused by a long idle transaction.
gotchas.correct: Neither VACUUM nor VACUUM FULL can remove versions an open snapshot still sees. End the transaction first, then let plain VACUUM work.

gotchas.trap: Disabling autovacuum on a table stops all vacuuming of it.
gotchas.correct: Anti-wraparound autovacuum still runs once the table passes autovacuum_freeze_max_age.

gotchas.trap: Wraparound warnings require restarting in single-user mode.
gotchas.correct: Current docs say to run a normal database-wide VACUUM; single-user mode is riskier and should be avoided.

lessons.lab: On a test server: create a table, update every row several times, and compare `n_live_tup`, `n_dead_tup` and `pg_relation_size` before and after plain VACUUM and VACUUM FULL. Open a second session with `BEGIN; SELECT 1;` and leave it idle, then show that VACUUM reports dead rows it "cannot remove yet". Finally set `fillfactor = 80`, repeat non-indexed updates, and compare `n_tup_hot_upd`.

lessons.title: Row locks, table locks and deadlocks
lessons.summary: The table lock levels each command takes, the four row-lock strengths, queue patterns with SKIP LOCKED and NOWAIT, and how deadlocks are detected and prevented.

sections.heading: Table lock levels
sections.body:
Every statement takes a table-level lock. The ones to remember:

| Lock | Taken by |
|---|---|
| ACCESS SHARE | `SELECT` |
| ROW SHARE | `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE/SHARE` |
| ROW EXCLUSIVE | `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE` |
| SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE | `VACUUM`, `ANALYZE`, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` |
| SHARE | `CREATE INDEX` (blocks writes, allows reads) |
| SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE | `CREATE TRIGGER`, adding a foreign key |
| EXCLUSIVE | `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` |
| ACCESS EXCLUSIVE | `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `VACUUM FULL`, most `ALTER TABLE` |

Only **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE** blocks a plain `SELECT`. Lock requests wait in a queue, so a pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request can stall later readers too; pair DDL with `lock_timeout`.

sections.heading: Row-level locks
sections.body:
Row locks are stored in the tuple itself, so there is no memory limit on how many rows you can lock. There are four strengths:

| Requested | Conflicts with |
|---|---|
| `FOR KEY SHARE` | `FOR UPDATE` |
| `FOR SHARE` | `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, `FOR UPDATE` |
| `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` | `FOR SHARE`, `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, `FOR UPDATE` |
| `FOR UPDATE` | all four |

A plain `UPDATE` takes `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` unless it changes a key column that a foreign key could reference. Foreign-key checks on a child insert take `FOR KEY SHARE` on the parent row. So locking a parent with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` blocks child inserts, while `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` does not.

sections.heading: NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED
sections.body:
- `NOWAIT` raises an error immediately instead of waiting for a row lock.
- `SKIP LOCKED` skips rows that are already locked. The docs describe it as giving an inconsistent view of the data, suited to avoiding contention when **multiple consumers read a queue-like table**.

A work-queue claim:

```sql
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'pending'
  ORDER BY id
  LIMIT 10
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running'
FROM next WHERE jobs.id = next.id
RETURNING jobs.id;
```

The locking clause must be **inside** the CTE. A locking clause in the main query does not lock rows produced by a WITH query.

sections.heading: Deadlocks
sections.body:
A deadlock happens when two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds, for example two transfers that update accounts 1 and 2 in opposite order. After `deadlock_timeout` (1s by default) of waiting, PostgreSQL checks for a cycle and aborts one of the transactions with `deadlock detected` (SQLSTATE `40P01`). Which one is aborted is not predictable.

Prevention:

- Acquire locks in a **consistent order** (for example lowest id first, or `SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`).
- Keep transactions short.
- Treat 40P01 as retryable.

Raising `deadlock_timeout` only delays detection. It is not a fix.

keyPoints: Only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, most ALTER TABLE) blocks plain SELECT; plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes.
Plain UPDATE takes FOR NO KEY UPDATE; FK checks take FOR KEY SHARE, and the two do not conflict.
SKIP LOCKED is for queue consumers; NOWAIT errors instead of waiting.
Put FOR UPDATE inside the CTE that selects the rows to lock.
Deadlocks are detected and one victim is aborted (40P01); prevent them with a consistent lock order.

gotchas.trap: Use NOWAIT so queue workers do not block each other.
gotchas.correct: NOWAIT makes every contended worker fail. SKIP LOCKED lets each worker take different rows.

gotchas.trap: Raise deadlock_timeout to make deadlocks go away.
gotchas.correct: It only changes how long PostgreSQL waits before checking. Fix the lock ordering.

gotchas.trap: SELECT FOR UPDATE is the right lock before updating a non-key column.
gotchas.correct: FOR NO KEY UPDATE is enough and does not block foreign-key checks from child inserts.

lessons.lab: With two sessions: (1) run `BEGIN; SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;` in one and try `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` and then `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` in the other. (2) Lock a parent row with FOR UPDATE and insert a child row referencing it from the other session; repeat with FOR NO KEY UPDATE. (3) Update two rows in opposite order in the two sessions and read the deadlock error. Inspect `pg_locks` joined to `pg_stat_activity` while sessions wait.

lessons.title: Upserts, MERGE, advisory locks and retries
lessons.summary: Concurrency-safe write patterns: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, when MERGE fits, advisory locks for application-level mutual exclusion, and retry loops for serialization failures.

sections.heading: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT
sections.body:
`ON CONFLICT` guarantees an **atomic INSERT-or-UPDATE outcome** even under high concurrency, which a SELECT-then-INSERT in application code cannot.

```sql
INSERT INTO page_views (page, n) VALUES ($1, 1)
ON CONFLICT (page) DO UPDATE
  SET n = page_views.n + EXCLUDED.n
RETURNING n;
```

Rules to know:

- `DO UPDATE` needs a conflict target (columns or `ON CONSTRAINT`). `DO NOTHING` may omit it.
- `EXCLUDED` holds the row proposed for insertion.
- One statement cannot update the same row twice. Duplicate keys in a batch raise a cardinality violation (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`), so deduplicate the input first.
- A `WHERE` on `DO UPDATE` still locks conflicting rows it chooses not to update.
- To infer a partial unique index, repeat its predicate: `ON CONFLICT (did) WHERE is_active`.
- Exclusion constraints cannot be arbiters for `DO UPDATE`.
- In 18, `RETURNING old.*, new.*` shows before and after values (old values are NULL for a fresh insert).

sections.heading: MERGE
sections.body:
`MERGE` joins a source to a target and runs the first matching `WHEN` clause per row:

- `WHEN MATCHED` can UPDATE, DELETE or DO NOTHING.
- `WHEN NOT MATCHED [BY TARGET]` can INSERT.
- `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE` (17) acts on target rows with no source row, for example to delete them in a sync.

Clauses are checked in order. A clause without `AND` is the last reachable one of its kind, and adding another after it is an error. `RETURNING merge_action()` (17) reports what happened to each row.

If more than one source row matches the same target row, MERGE raises a cardinality violation for updates and deletes. MERGE follows normal isolation rules under concurrency. The docs point to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` as the alternative that can run an UPDATE when a concurrent INSERT occurs. The two are **not interchangeable**: use ON CONFLICT for concurrent upserts and MERGE for batch syncs with richer logic.

sections.heading: Advisory locks
sections.body:
Advisory locks lock an application-defined number, not a row. Use them for things like "only one worker may run this job".

- **Session level** (`pg_advisory_lock`, `pg_try_advisory_lock`): held until explicitly unlocked or the session ends, and **not released by ROLLBACK**.
- **Transaction level** (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`, `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock`): released automatically at commit or rollback.

Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, session-level advisory locks are not supported because consecutive transactions can run on different server connections. Use the transaction-level variants there.

Docs pitfall: `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100` can take locks on more rows than it returns, because LIMIT is not guaranteed to apply before the function runs. Apply the LIMIT in a subquery first.

sections.heading: Retrying serialization failures
sections.body:
Under repeatable read and serializable, conflicts show up as errors, not waits. A correct client:

1. Retries on SQLSTATE `40001` (serialization_failure) unconditionally.
2. Usually also retries `40P01` (deadlock_detected).
3. Retries the **complete transaction**, including all the reads and logic that chose what to write. PostgreSQL has no automatic retry because it cannot do this correctly for you.
4. Caps attempts and adds backoff, since high contention may need several tries.

Unique violations (`23505`) can sometimes be retried too, for example when the app picks a new key after reading existing ones, but they may also be permanent errors, so handle them deliberately.

keyPoints: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is the concurrency-safe upsert; EXCLUDED is the proposed row.
Deduplicate batch input: a row cannot be affected twice by one ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.
MERGE (with NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE in 17) suits syncs but is not a drop-in replacement for ON CONFLICT under concurrency.
Session advisory locks survive rollback; use transaction-level ones behind a transaction pooler.
Retry the whole transaction on 40001 (and usually 40P01), with a cap and backoff.

gotchas.trap: Check with SELECT, then INSERT if the row is missing.
gotchas.correct: Two sessions can both see "missing" and one hits a unique violation. Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT.

gotchas.trap: Use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for a counter upsert.
gotchas.correct: DO NOTHING silently drops the increment for an existing row. Use DO UPDATE with EXCLUDED.

gotchas.trap: Retry only the statement that raised 40001.
gotchas.correct: The earlier reads are stale too. Retry the entire transaction.

lessons.lab: Write an upsert counter with ON CONFLICT and hit it from many concurrent clients (for example pgbench with a custom script); confirm the final count is exact. Then write a MERGE that syncs a staging table into a target, deleting target rows missing from staging, and return `merge_action()`. Finally write a small retry wrapper in your language of choice that reruns a serializable transaction on 40001.

lessons.title: jsonb done right
lessons.summary: How jsonb stores and compares documents, which GIN operator class answers which operator, how jsonpath fits in, and the signs that a JSON column should have been ordinary columns.

sections.heading: What jsonb stores
sections.body:
`jsonb` stores a parsed binary form of the document. That has visible consequences:

- Whitespace and **key order are not kept**, and when a key appears twice **the last value wins**.
- Numbers are kept as `numeric`, so `1.230e-5` comes back as `0.00001230`.
- Subscripting is zero-based for arrays and works on keys too: `doc['tags'][0]`.

Use plain `json` only when you must keep the exact input text. For anything you query, use `jsonb`.

sections.heading: Containment and existence
sections.body:
The two operator families behave differently, and both look only at the **top level** unless you nest the pattern.

| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `'{"a":1,"tags":["x","y"]}' @> '{"tags":["y"]}'` | true |
| `'{"a":{"b":1}}' @> '{"b":1}'` | false (the key is nested) |
| `'[1,2,[1,3]]' @> '[1,3]'` | false |
| `'["foo","bar"]' @> '"bar"'` | true (special case for arrays) |

To match a nested value, mirror the nesting in the pattern: `doc @> '{"profile":{"city":"Oslo"}}'`.

The existence operators `?`, `?|` and `?&` test **top-level keys or array elements** only. `doc ? 'city'` is false when `city` lives under `profile`.

sections.heading: GIN operator classes
sections.body:
A GIN index is the usual way to index jsonb. Pick the operator class from the operators you need:

| Operator class | Supports | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| `jsonb_ops` (default) | `? ?\| ?& @> @? @@` | Larger, one index entry per key and value |
| `jsonb_path_ops` | `@> @? @@` only | Smaller and faster for containment, **cannot answer `?`** |

The query expression must match the indexed expression. An index on `(doc -> 'tags')` helps `doc -> 'tags' ? 'x'` but not `doc @> '{"tags":["x"]}'`, and an index on `doc` does not help a query written against `doc -> 'tags'`.

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"type":"signup"}';
```

sections.heading: jsonpath and SQL/JSON
sections.body:
`@?` asks whether a jsonpath returns any item, and `@@` evaluates a jsonpath predicate. Both can use either GIN operator class:

```sql
SELECT * FROM api WHERE jdoc @? '$.tags[*] ? (@ == "qui")';
```

Functions such as `jsonb_path_query` and `jsonb_path_exists` expose the same language. PostgreSQL 17 added the SQL-standard `JSON_TABLE`, `JSON_EXISTS`, `JSON_QUERY` and `JSON_VALUE`, and `JSON_TABLE` is the cleanest way to turn an array of objects into rows.

sections.heading: When a JSON column is a mistake
sections.body:
The docs warn that an update **locks and rewrites the whole row**, so documents should stay small and change as a unit. Warning signs that data belongs in real columns:

- You filter, join or sort on the same keys in most queries.
- The value needs a **foreign key** or **NOT NULL** guarantee. Those are declared on columns, not on keys inside a document; CHECK constraints and unique expression indexes on extracted keys are possible but awkward compared with a typed column.
- One hot field (a counter, a status) changes often inside a large document, so every change rewrites everything.
- Every row has the same shape. That is a table, not a document.

A common healthy design is typed columns for the core fields plus one `jsonb` column for sparse, vendor-specific or rarely queried attributes.

keyPoints: jsonb drops whitespace and key order; the last duplicate key wins.
@> is a nested, top-level-anchored match; ?, ?| and ?& see only top-level keys or elements.
jsonb_ops supports ? ?| ?& @> @? @@; jsonb_path_ops supports only @> @? @@ and is smaller.
The query expression must match the index expression to use a GIN index.
Keys that need constraints, joins or frequent updates belong in ordinary columns.

gotchas.trap: Creating a jsonb_path_ops index and expecting it to speed up doc ? 'key'.
gotchas.correct: jsonb_path_ops cannot answer ?. Use the default jsonb_ops class, or rewrite the filter as containment when that is equivalent.

gotchas.trap: Writing doc @> '{"city":"Oslo"}' to find a city nested under profile.
gotchas.correct: Containment is anchored at the top level. Mirror the nesting: doc @> '{"profile":{"city":"Oslo"}}'.

gotchas.trap: Keeping customer_id inside a jsonb payload to stay "flexible".
gotchas.correct: A foreign key needs a real column. Promote keys you join or constrain on.

lessons.lab: Create a table with a jsonb column and a few documents with nested objects and arrays. Compare `@>` results for nested and flat patterns, then create a `jsonb_path_ops` GIN index, disable sequential scans in your session and check with EXPLAIN which of `@>`, `?` and `@?` can use it.

lessons.title: Text, fuzzy and vector search
lessons.summary: Full-text search with tsvector and tsquery, fuzzy matching with pg_trgm, nearest-neighbour search with pgvector, and how to combine them into hybrid search.

sections.heading: tsvector and tsquery
sections.body:
`to_tsvector` parses text into normalized lexemes with positions; stop words disappear and words are stemmed:

```sql
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'a fat  cat sat on a mat - it ate a fat rats');
-- 'ate':9 'cat':3 'fat':2,11 'mat':7 'rat':12 'sat':4
```

Pick the query parser by the input source:

| Function | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `to_tsquery` | Full operator syntax; malformed input raises an error |
| `plainto_tsquery` | Joins words with `&` |
| `phraseto_tsquery` | Joins words with `<->` (followed by) |
| `websearch_to_tsquery` | Web-style quotes, `or` and `-`; **never raises a syntax error** |

`websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"supernovae stars" -crab')` gives `'supernova' <-> 'star' & !'crab'`, which makes it the safe choice for a search box.

sections.heading: Indexing and ranking
sections.body:
Index full-text search with GIN. Either index an expression, for example `to_tsvector('english', body)`, and write queries with the **same expression including the configuration**, or keep a **stored** generated `tsvector` column. In PostgreSQL 18 generated columns are virtual by default and virtual columns cannot be indexed, so say `STORED`.

`to_tsvector(NULL)` is NULL and concatenating NULL yields NULL, so wrap optional fields in `coalesce(col, '')`.

Ranking:

- `ts_rank` scores by how often terms occur. `ts_rank_cd` (cover density) also rewards terms that appear close together.
- `setweight` labels lexemes A–D. The default weights for `{D,C,B,A}` are `{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0}`, so title words marked A count ten times more than body words marked D.
- Normalization option 32 rescales the rank into 0–1 but does not change the order.

sections.heading: Fuzzy matching with pg_trgm
sections.body:
`pg_trgm` splits each word into three-character pieces after padding it with two leading spaces and one trailing space, so `show_trgm('cat')` is `"  c"`, `" ca"`, `"cat"`, `"at "`.

- `similarity(a, b)` returns 0–1, and `a % b` is true above `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` (0.3 by default). `<->` is the distance, 1 − similarity.
- `<%` and `<<%` are word-similarity operators with their own thresholds.
- Both `gin_trgm_ops` and `gist_trgm_ops` speed up `%` and **unanchored** `LIKE`, `ILIKE` and regex searches such as `ILIKE '%son%'`, which a B-tree cannot help.
- Nearest-neighbour ordering, `ORDER BY name <-> 'jonh' LIMIT 10`, is supported by the **GiST** operator class only.

sections.heading: Vector search with pgvector
sections.body:
pgvector adds the `vector` type and distance operators. Smaller is closer for every operator:

| Operator | Distance | Index operator class |
|---|---|---|
| `<->` | L2 (Euclidean) | `vector_l2_ops` |
| `<#>` | **Negative** inner product | `vector_ip_ops` |
| `<=>` | Cosine | `vector_cosine_ops` |
| `<+>` | L1 | `vector_l1_ops` |

Because `<#>` returns the negative inner product, `ORDER BY emb <#> :q` ascending already puts the largest inner product first. An index is used only when the query operator matches its operator class.

Two approximate index types:

- **HNSW** (`m` 16, `ef_construction` 64, `hnsw.ef_search` 40 by default): better speed–recall trade-off, slower to build and more memory, and can be created on an empty table.
- **IVFFlat**: faster to build and smaller. Create it **after** loading data, start with `lists` around rows/1000 (up to 1M rows) and `ivfflat.probes` around sqrt(lists); probes defaults to 1.

The `vector` type can be indexed up to 2,000 dimensions; `halfvec` goes further when you need larger embeddings. Exact limits change between releases, so check the README.

sections.heading: Filtering and hybrid search
sections.body:
Approximate indexes apply the `WHERE` clause **after** the index scan. With `ef_search` 40, a selective filter can leave fewer rows than your `LIMIT`. Options from the pgvector README:

- Turn on **iterative index scans** (0.8.0 and later): `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order` or `relaxed_order` (and `ivfflat.iterative_scan`), bounded by settings such as `hnsw.max_scan_tuples`.
- Create a **partial index** per common filter value, or **partition** by the filter column.
- Use an ordinary B-tree on the filter column when the filter is very selective, and let exact search run on the few matching rows.

**Hybrid search** runs a full-text query and a vector query separately and merges the two ranked lists, typically with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion**, so exact keyword hits and semantic neighbours both surface.

keyPoints: websearch_to_tsquery is the safe parser for raw user input.
Expression GIN indexes need the same expression, including the text search configuration, in the query.
pg_trgm GIN or GiST indexes serve unanchored LIKE/ILIKE; KNN ordering with <-> needs GiST.
pgvector operator and index operator class must match; <#> is the negative inner product.
HNSW can be built empty and has better recall/speed; IVFFlat must be built after loading data.
Filtered approximate search can under-return rows; use iterative scans, partial indexes or partitioning.

gotchas.trap: Passing a search box string straight to to_tsquery.
gotchas.correct: Malformed input raises an error. Use websearch_to_tsquery or plainto_tsquery.

gotchas.trap: Building a GIN index on to_tsvector('english', body) and querying to_tsvector(body).
gotchas.correct: The expressions differ, so the index is not used. Use the two-argument form in both places, or a stored tsvector column.

gotchas.trap: Ordering by emb <#> :q DESC to get the most similar vectors first.
gotchas.correct: <#> already returns the negative inner product; order ascending.

gotchas.trap: Creating an IVFFlat index on an empty table before the bulk load.
gotchas.correct: IVFFlat picks its list centres from existing rows. Load first, then build, or use HNSW.

lessons.lab: Load a few hundred short articles. Then add `pg_trgm`, a GiST `gist_trgm_ops` index on the title, and compare `ORDER BY title <-> 'postgress'` results.

lessons.title: Queues, events and the outbox
lessons.summary: Running job queues on a table with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, using LISTEN/NOTIFY as a wake-up signal, and making event publishing reliable with an outbox table.

sections.heading: A SKIP LOCKED job queue
sections.body:
Plain `FOR UPDATE` makes every worker wait for the first one's lock. `SKIP LOCKED` skips rows another transaction has locked; the docs describe it as giving "an inconsistent view" that is meant for "multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table".

```sql
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE state = 'queued'
  ORDER BY id
  LIMIT 10
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs SET state = 'running', started_at = now()
FROM next WHERE jobs.id = next.id
RETURNING jobs.*;
```

Put the locking clause **inside the CTE**. A locking clause on the outer query does not lock rows read inside a `WITH` query. Keep the claiming transaction short, and add a partial index such as `ON jobs (id) WHERE state = 'queued'` so workers do not scan finished jobs.

sections.heading: LISTEN and NOTIFY
sections.body:
`NOTIFY channel, 'payload'` (or `pg_notify(channel, payload)`) sends an event to every session that has already run `LISTEN channel` in the same database.

- Notifications are delivered **only when the sending transaction commits**, in commit order. A rolled-back transaction sends nothing.
- Identical channel-and-payload notifications in one transaction may be collapsed into one.
- The payload must be shorter than 8000 bytes; send an id, not a document.
- The notification queue is large but finite (8GB in a standard build). When it fills, `NOTIFY` fails at commit, and a long transaction in a listening session stops the queue from being cleaned up.
- Only sessions listening at the time receive the event. Treat it as a wake-up signal and keep the real work in a table.

Connection poolers matter: PgBouncer's **transaction pooling** mode does not support `LISTEN`, because the server connection changes between transactions. Listeners need a direct connection or session pooling.

sections.heading: The transactional outbox
sections.body:
Writing to the database and then publishing to a broker is a dual write: a crash between the two loses or duplicates the event. The outbox pattern puts the event in the same transaction as the business change:

```sql
WITH o AS (
  INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (42, 99.50)
  RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO outbox (topic, payload)
SELECT 'order.created', jsonb_build_object('order_id', id) FROM o;
```

A relay process claims outbox rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, publishes them and marks or deletes them. Delivery is **at least once**, so consumers should be idempotent (for example, keyed on the outbox id). `NOTIFY` in the same transaction can wake the relay instead of polling.

PostgreSQL has no single outbox feature; the pattern is built from data-modifying `WITH` queries, which run in one statement and one snapshot, and the row-locking clauses.

keyPoints: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many workers claim different rows without waiting.
Place the locking clause inside the CTE that selects the rows.
NOTIFY delivers on commit only, to current listeners, with a payload under 8000 bytes.
PgBouncer transaction pooling does not support LISTEN.
An outbox row written in the same transaction removes the dual-write problem; consumers must be idempotent.

gotchas.trap: Using LISTEN/NOTIFY as the job queue itself.
gotchas.correct: Sessions that are not listening miss events. Store jobs in a table and use NOTIFY only to wake workers.

gotchas.trap: Putting FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on the outer UPDATE while the CTE picks the rows.
gotchas.correct: The outer locking clause does not lock rows inside the WITH query. Lock in the CTE.

gotchas.trap: Publishing to the broker after COMMIT from application code.
gotchas.correct: A crash in between loses the event. Write an outbox row in the same transaction and relay it.

lessons.lab: Create a jobs table with 1,000 queued rows. In two psql sessions, run the claiming CTE inside BEGIN without committing and confirm that each session gets different ids. Then remove SKIP LOCKED and watch the second session wait.

lessons.title: Roles, RLS and security definer
lessons.summary: Layering GRANTs and row-level security, writing USING and WITH CHECK correctly, the bypass rules, safe SECURITY DEFINER functions, and how Supabase applies RLS to anon and authenticated users.

sections.heading: Privileges first, then policies
sections.body:
Row-level security works **in addition to** the normal privilege system. A role needs `GRANT SELECT` on the table before any policy is considered, and a policy cannot give access that a GRANT withholds. Policies narrow which rows a granted command sees or changes.

For passwords, `password_encryption` defaults to `scram-sha-256`, and MD5 password support is deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 (creating or altering an MD5 password warns).

sections.heading: How RLS policies evaluate
sections.body:
```sql
ALTER TABLE docs ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON docs
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint);
```

- **Default deny**: with RLS enabled and no policy for a command, no rows are visible or modifiable.
- `USING` filters existing rows (SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE). `WITH CHECK` validates new or changed rows (INSERT, UPDATE). If you omit `WITH CHECK`, the `USING` expression is used for it.
- **Permissive** policies (the default) combine with OR; **restrictive** policies combine with AND. One broad permissive policy therefore opens access for every role it applies to.
- Scope policies with `TO role` and `FOR command`.

sections.heading: Who bypasses RLS
sections.body:
- Superusers and roles with `BYPASSRLS` always bypass policies.
- The **table owner** bypasses them too, unless you run `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. If your application connects as the owner, enabling RLS alone protects nothing.
- Unique, primary key and foreign key checks bypass RLS, so a constraint error can reveal that a hidden row exists. Avoid secrets in key values.
- `TRUNCATE` is not subject to RLS.
- Setting `row_security = off` makes a query **error** instead of silently returning filtered results, which is useful for backups.
- Policies containing subqueries on other tables can race with concurrent changes under READ COMMITTED; the docs suggest locking the referenced rows.

sections.heading: SECURITY DEFINER functions
Supabase-style RLS
sections.body:
Supabase exposes tables through an API, so RLS is the security boundary:

- Requests run as `anon` (signed out) or `authenticated`. `auth.uid()` returns the user id, NULL when signed out, and `auth.jwt()` returns the token claims.
- Keep authorization data in `raw_app_meta_data`, which users cannot change, not in user metadata, which they can.
- Write `(select auth.uid())` so the value is evaluated once per statement, add `TO authenticated`, and index the columns the policy filters on.
- `service_role` has `BYPASSRLS`; its key belongs on servers only.
- Views bypass RLS by default because they run as their owner. Create them `with (security_invoker = true)` (PostgreSQL 15+) so the caller's policies apply.
- An UPDATE also needs a SELECT policy, because the rows must be visible to be updated.

```sql
CREATE POLICY "own todos" ON todos
FOR SELECT TO authenticated
USING ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
```

keyPoints: RLS adds to GRANTs; it never replaces them.
RLS enabled with no policy means default deny.
Owners bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set; superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass.
Permissive policies OR together; restrictive policies AND together.
SECURITY DEFINER: SET search_path with pg_temp last, and REVOKE EXECUTE FROM PUBLIC in the same transaction.
Supabase: (select auth.uid()), TO authenticated, indexed policy columns, security_invoker views, raw_app_meta_data for roles.

gotchas.trap: Enabling RLS while the application still connects as the table owner.
gotchas.correct: The owner bypasses RLS. Use a separate non-owner role or FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

gotchas.trap: Adding a permissive admin policy without TO admin.
gotchas.correct: Permissive policies OR together, so it applies to everyone. Scope it with TO, or use a restrictive policy for the tenant rule.

gotchas.trap: Exposing a plain view over an RLS table through the Supabase API.
gotchas.correct: The view runs as its owner and bypasses RLS. Create it with security_invoker = true.

gotchas.trap: Checking a role claim stored in user metadata inside a policy.
gotchas.correct: Users can edit that metadata. Store authorization data in raw_app_meta_data.

lessons.lab: Create a non-owner role app_user and a docs table with tenant_id. Enable RLS with a tenant policy based on current_setting('app.tenant_id'). As app_user, set the tenant and confirm you see only your rows and cannot insert another tenant's row. Then query as the owner, add FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and query again.

lessons.title: Connections, pooling and monitoring
lessons.summary: Why connection count is a scarce resource, how PgBouncer and Supabase poolers change what a session means, and how to find the queries and sessions that hurt.

sections.heading: Connections are a budget
sections.body:
Every client connection is a separate server backend process. In PostgreSQL 18 the default `max_connections` is 100, and `superuser_reserved_connections` (default 3) keeps the last slots for superusers, so ordinary roles are refused at 97 connections.

Raising `max_connections` is not free. Memory settings such as `work_mem` apply **per sort or hash operation**, not per server, so one complex query can use several multiples of it, and hash operations may use `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0 by default). Many busy backends multiply that further. The usual fix for "too many connections" is a pooler, not a larger limit.

sections.heading: Pooling modes and their pitfalls
sections.body:
PgBouncer offers three pool modes:

| Mode | Server connection is held for | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| session | the whole client session | apps that rely on session state |
| transaction | one transaction | most web and serverless traffic |
| statement | one statement | autocommit-only workloads |

In **transaction mode**, the next transaction from the same client may run on a different server connection. Features that keep state on the session therefore break: `SET`/`RESET`, `LISTEN`, `WITH HOLD` cursors, SQL-level `PREPARE`/`DEALLOCATE`, temp tables with `PRESERVE`/`DELETE ROWS`, `LOAD`, and session-level advisory locks. Use `SET LOCAL` inside the transaction and transaction-level advisory locks (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`) instead.

Protocol-level prepared statements (the kind drivers send) are supported in transaction mode since PgBouncer 1.21 and are on by default in recent versions through `max_prepared_statements`. SQL `PREPARE` is still not.

sections.heading: Supabase connection options
sections.body: Supabase documents a **direct** connection (port 5432 on the database host), a **shared pooler (Supavisor)** in session mode (port 5432) or transaction mode (port 6543), and a **dedicated pooler (PgBouncer)**. The shared pooler in transaction mode does not support prepared statements, so turn them off in the driver. For serverless and edge functions, the docs recommend transaction mode, a pool size of 1 per function instance, and creating the client once at module scope. Ports and names can change, so check the page before you hard-code them.

sections.heading: Finding the problem: pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements
sections.body:
`pg_stat_activity` shows one row per backend. Watch `state` (`active`, `idle`, `idle in transaction`, `idle in transaction (aborted)`), `wait_event_type`/`wait_event`, `xact_start` and `backend_xmin`. A session sitting in **idle in transaction** keeps its locks and its snapshot, which can block DDL and stop vacuum from removing dead rows.

`pg_stat_statements` aggregates statistics per normalized statement (constants become `$1`, `$2`). It must be in `shared_preload_libraries` (a restart is needed) and needs query IDs; the default `compute_query_id = auto` turns them on when the module is loaded. Sort by `total_exec_time` to find what costs the most overall, not only by mean time. `temp_blks_written` shows sorts and hashes spilling to disk, a hint that `work_mem` is too small for that query.

```sql
SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time, temp_blks_written
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

sections.heading: Key settings
sections.body:
- `shared_buffers`: the docs suggest about 25% of RAM on a dedicated server as a starting point; going above 40% rarely helps because PostgreSQL also relies on the OS cache.
- `work_mem` (4MB default): per operation, so raise it per role or per session for reporting queries rather than globally.
- `maintenance_work_mem` (64MB default): used by VACUUM, CREATE INDEX and similar.
- In 18, asynchronous I/O arrived: `io_method` defaults to `worker`, and `effective_io_concurrency` now defaults to 16.
- Find unused indexes with `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0`, but first check how long statistics have been collecting since the last reset.

keyPoints: max_connections defaults to 100 with 3 slots reserved for superusers; fix connection storms with a pooler, not a bigger limit.
work_mem is per sort or hash operation, so a single query can use several multiples of it.
Transaction pooling breaks session state: SET, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors, SQL PREPARE, session advisory locks.
pg_stat_statements needs shared_preload_libraries; rank by total_exec_time.
Sessions idle in transaction hold locks and snapshots; watch pg_stat_activity.

gotchas.trap: Raise max_connections to 2000 so the serverless app stops getting "too many clients" errors.
gotchas.correct: Put a transaction-mode pooler in front and keep the server connection count modest; each backend costs memory and work_mem multiplies per operation.

gotchas.trap: Use SET search_path or SET statement_timeout once at connect time behind a transaction pooler.
gotchas.correct: Session SETs leak to whoever gets that server connection next. Use SET LOCAL inside each transaction, or per-role settings.

gotchas.trap: Sort pg_stat_statements by mean_exec_time to find the biggest load.
gotchas.correct: A fast query called millions of times can dominate; total_exec_time shows overall cost.

lessons.lab: On a dev database, run `SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, xact_start, left(query, 60) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';`. Open a second session, run `BEGIN; SELECT 1;` and leave it. Re-run the first query and find the session in state `idle in transaction`. Then, in the second session, run `SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s';`, wait a few seconds, and confirm that session has been terminated.

lessons.title: Zero-downtime schema migrations
lessons.summary: Which DDL rewrites or locks a table, and the safe patterns: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID then VALIDATE, and lock_timeout with retries.

sections.heading: The real danger is the lock queue
sections.body:
Most `ALTER TABLE` forms take an **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE** lock, which conflicts with everything, even plain `SELECT`. The statement may finish in milliseconds, but it first has to **wait** for the lock. While it waits behind a long-running transaction, new queries on the table queue up behind it, and the application stalls.

This follows from the lock conflict table and the fact that lock requests wait in order. The defence is `lock_timeout`: if the lock cannot be taken quickly, the DDL fails instead of blocking everyone, and the migration tool retries later.

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
```

`lock_timeout` applies to each separate lock wait. Setting it equal to or higher than `statement_timeout` is pointless, because the statement timeout would fire first. All these timeouts default to 0 (off). Set them per session or per role, not globally in postgresql.conf. PostgreSQL 17 added `transaction_timeout`.

sections.heading: Adding columns
sections.body:
`ADD COLUMN` with no default, or with a **non-volatile** default, does not rewrite the table; the default is stored in the catalog. `DEFAULT now()` is fine (it is stable, evaluated once). A **volatile** default such as `DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` or `clock_timestamp()` forces a full table rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

`ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` usually rewrites the table and rebuilds indexes. Binary-coercible changes (for example `varchar(n)` to `text`) can skip the rewrite.

Table rewrites are also not MVCC-safe: a concurrent transaction with an older snapshot may see the rewritten table as empty.

sections.heading: Indexes without blocking writes
sections.body:
Plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on the table for the whole build. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` lets writes continue. It costs more: two table scans plus waiting for transactions that could use the index.

Rules to remember:
- It **cannot run inside a transaction block**, so many migration tools need a "no transaction" flag for it.
- If it fails (deadlock, unique violation, cancel), it leaves an **INVALID** index. The planner ignores it, but it still adds write overhead. Drop it with `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` or rebuild it with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
- To add a primary key or unique constraint without a long lock: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, then `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX ...`.

sections.heading: Constraints: NOT VALID, then VALIDATE
sections.body:
Adding a CHECK or foreign key normally scans the whole table while holding a strong lock. Split it in two:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id) NOT VALID;  -- fast, new rows checked

ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk;          -- scans old rows
```

`NOT VALID` makes the constraint apply to new and updated rows right away without checking existing rows. `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` then scans the table under only a **SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE** lock, so reads and writes continue. Note that adding a foreign key takes a SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE lock on both tables, so still use `lock_timeout` for the first step.

For **NOT NULL**: `SET NOT NULL` normally scans the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, but it skips the scan if a valid `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL)` constraint already proves it. So add that CHECK as NOT VALID, validate it, then run `SET NOT NULL` and drop the CHECK. PostgreSQL 18 also allows NOT NULL constraints to be added as `NOT VALID` directly.

keyPoints: A DDL waiting for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE queues all later queries; always set lock_timeout and retry.
ADD COLUMN with a non-volatile default is instant; a volatile default rewrites the table.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction block and leaves an INVALID index on failure.
NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT; validation takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE.
A validated CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) lets SET NOT NULL skip the full scan.

gotchas.trap: The ALTER TABLE only takes a few milliseconds, so it is safe at peak traffic.
gotchas.correct: Lock wait time is the problem. Behind a long transaction it blocks every later query. Use lock_timeout.

gotchas.trap: A failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY leaves nothing behind.
gotchas.correct: It leaves an INVALID index that still slows writes. Drop it or REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

gotchas.trap: ADD COLUMN id uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() is instant like any default.
gotchas.correct: gen_random_uuid() is volatile, so the table is rewritten under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

lessons.lab: In a scratch database, create a table with a million rows. Time `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN a timestamptz DEFAULT now();` and then `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN b uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid();` and compare. Then add a CHECK constraint with NOT VALID, validate it, and check `pg_constraint.convalidated` before and after.

lessons.title: Backups, replication and upgrades
lessons.summary: Logical dumps versus physical backups with WAL archiving, point-in-time recovery, streaming and logical replication, replica lag, and how major upgrades work.

sections.heading: pg_dump versus physical backups
sections.body:
**pg_dump** makes a *logical* backup: SQL or an archive of the objects and data, consistent as of one snapshot. It is portable across major versions and good for copying one database. It **cannot** be combined with WAL to replay to a later moment, so it gives you only the state at dump time.

A **physical** backup copies the data directory files. `pg_basebackup` takes one from a running server. Combined with archived WAL, a base backup can be rolled forward to any point after it. Since PostgreSQL 17, `pg_basebackup --incremental` with `pg_combinebackup` (and `summarize_wal` on) supports incremental backups.

sections.heading: WAL archiving and point-in-time recovery
sections.body:
Setup:
1. `archive_mode = on` and an `archive_command` (or archive library) that copies each finished WAL segment to safe storage. The command must return 0 **only** on success, and should refuse to overwrite an existing file.
2. Take base backups regularly.

Recovery: restore a base backup, set `restore_command`, set a target (`recovery_target_time`, a named restore point, or a transaction ID), create `recovery.signal`, and start the server. It replays WAL to the target. Each recovery that ends starts a **new timeline**, so later WAL does not mix with the old history.

Monitor archiving. If `archive_command` keeps failing, WAL piles up in `pg_wal`; if the disk fills, the server shuts down with a PANIC. A backup you have never restored is not a tested backup.

sections.heading: Streaming and logical replication
sections.body:
**Streaming (physical) replication** sends WAL to standbys, which are byte-for-byte copies of the whole cluster. Standbys can serve read-only queries (hot standby). With asynchronous replication the standby can lag, so a user who writes on the primary and immediately reads from a replica may not see their change. Send read-your-own-writes traffic to the primary, or measure lag (`pg_stat_replication` shows `write_lag`, `flush_lag`, `replay_lag`).

**Logical replication** publishes row changes for chosen tables to subscribers, which are normal writable databases, possibly on another major version. Restrictions in 18:
- Schema and DDL are **not** replicated; apply schema changes on the subscriber yourself.
- Sequence data and large objects are not replicated. TRUNCATE is.
- Only tables can be published.
- UPDATE and DELETE need a **replica identity** (the primary key by default) on published tables.

PostgreSQL 17 added failover slots and `pg_createsubscriber`; 18 makes `streaming = parallel` the subscription default and adds `idle_replication_slot_timeout`. An unused replication slot keeps WAL forever, so drop or time out abandoned slots.

sections.heading: Upgrades
sections.body:
Minor releases (for example 18.5 to 18.6) are bug and security fixes; you install new binaries and restart. Major upgrades change the on-disk format and need one of:
- **pg_upgrade**: fast, in place (copy, link, clone, or `--swap` in 18). In 18 it keeps planner statistics.
- **dump and restore**: simple, slow for big databases.
- **logical replication** to a new-version server, then switch over: lowest downtime, but mind the restrictions above.

In 18, `initdb` enables data checksums by default, and pg_upgrade needs the old and new clusters to match on checksums. Track the end-of-life dates on the versioning page; each major gets about five years of support.

keyPoints: pg_dump is logical and point-in-time only; PITR needs a base backup plus archived WAL.
archive_command must return 0 only on success; failing archiving can fill pg_wal and crash the server.
Each completed recovery starts a new timeline.
Async replicas lag: route read-your-writes to the primary.
Logical replication does not copy DDL or sequences, and needs a replica identity for UPDATE/DELETE.

gotchas.trap: Nightly pg_dump lets us restore to 14:32 yesterday.
gotchas.correct: pg_dump restores only to the dump time. PITR needs physical base backups plus continuous WAL archiving.

gotchas.trap: Logical replication will carry our ALTER TABLE to the subscriber.
gotchas.correct: DDL is not replicated. Apply schema changes to the subscriber (usually first, for added columns).

gotchas.trap: An archive_command that always exits 0 is safe because it never blocks.
gotchas.correct: PostgreSQL then deletes WAL that was never archived, silently breaking PITR.

lessons.lab: Read the "Making a Base Backup" and "Recovering Using a Continuous Archive Backup" sections of the PITR docs. On a dev server, enable archiving to a local directory, take a `pg_basebackup`, insert a row, note the time, delete it, then restore to the noted time and confirm the row is back.

flashcards.front: Why can `x NOT IN (SELECT col FROM t)` return zero rows?
flashcards.back: If the subquery yields any NULL, `x NOT IN (...)` is false or NULL for every row, never true. Use `NOT EXISTS` instead.

flashcards.front: How do you write a semi join in SQL?
flashcards.back: `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM child WHERE child.fk = parent.id)`. Each parent row is returned at most once.

flashcards.front: Two correct ways to write an anti join
flashcards.back: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)`, or `LEFT JOIN child ON ... WHERE child.join_col IS NULL`.

flashcards.front: What happens when you filter the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE?
flashcards.back: The NULL-extended rows are removed, so the outer join behaves like an inner join. Put the condition in `ON`.

flashcards.front: What does `LATERAL` allow?
flashcards.back: A subquery in FROM may reference columns of FROM items that appear before it; it is evaluated per row of those items.

flashcards.front: Top 3 orders per customer, keeping customers with none
flashcards.back: `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3) o ON true`

flashcards.front: Difference between `WHERE` and `HAVING`
flashcards.back: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.

flashcards.front: What does `FILTER (WHERE ...)` do on an aggregate?
flashcards.back: Only rows satisfying the condition feed that aggregate, e.g. `count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')`.

flashcards.front: `count(*)` vs `count(x)` on the values (1), (NULL)
flashcards.back: `count(*)` = 2 (rows); `count(x)` = 1 (non-NULL values).

flashcards.front: `ROLLUP (a, b)` expands to which grouping sets?
flashcards.back: `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())`: detail, subtotal per a, grand total.

flashcards.front: How many grouping sets does `CUBE (a, b)` produce?
What does `GROUPING(col)` return?
flashcards.back: 1 when `col` is not part of the current row's grouping set (a subtotal or total row), 0 otherwise. It separates subtotal NULLs from real NULLs.

flashcards.front: Rule for `DISTINCT ON` and `ORDER BY`
flashcards.back: The DISTINCT ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions; later sort keys decide which row of each group is kept.

flashcards.front: Default window frame when `OVER` has `ORDER BY`
flashcards.back: `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which includes the current row's peers.

flashcards.front: Why does `last_value(x) OVER (ORDER BY t)` seem to return the current row?
flashcards.back: The default frame ends at the current row (and its peers). Use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.

flashcards.front: `rank`, `dense_rank`, `row_number` on 10, 20, 20, 30
flashcards.back: rank 1,2,2,4; dense_rank 1,2,2,3; row_number 1,2,3,4 (order among the tied 20s is arbitrary).

flashcards.front: Where are window functions allowed?
flashcards.back: Only in the select list and `ORDER BY`. To filter on one, compute it in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.

flashcards.front: Is `IGNORE NULLS` for `lag`/`lead` available in PostgreSQL 18?
flashcards.back: No. RESPECT/IGNORE NULLS and `nth_value ... FROM LAST` are not implemented in 18 (planned for 19).

flashcards.front: Gaps and islands key for consecutive days
flashcards.back: `day - (row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day))::int` is constant within a run; group by it.

flashcards.front: When is a non-recursive CTE inlined vs materialized by default?
flashcards.back: Inlined if side-effect-free and referenced once; materialized if referenced more than once. Override with `MATERIALIZED` / `NOT MATERIALIZED`.

flashcards.front: How is a recursive CTE evaluated?
flashcards.back: Iteratively: start with the non-recursive term, run the recursive term against the previous step's rows, stop when a step yields no rows.

flashcards.front: What does the `CYCLE` clause of a recursive CTE do?
flashcards.back: `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path` tracks visited keys, marks a row that revisits one, and stops recursing from it.

flashcards.front: What can the main query see after `WITH t AS (UPDATE ... RETURNING *)`?
flashcards.back: The base table as of the shared snapshot (old values). New values are visible only through `t` (RETURNING).

flashcards.front: `NULL AND false`, `NULL OR true`, `NOT NULL::boolean`
flashcards.back: false, true, NULL.

flashcards.front: Null-safe "not equal" operator
flashcards.back: `a IS DISTINCT FROM b`: never returns NULL; `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL` is false.

flashcards.front: `7/2`, `-7/2` and `7/2.0` in PostgreSQL
flashcards.back: 3, -3 (integer division truncates toward zero), and 3.5 (numeric).

flashcards.front: Default NULL position in ORDER BY
flashcards.back: NULLs sort as larger than any value: last for ASC, first for DESC. Override with `NULLS FIRST`/`NULLS LAST`.

flashcards.front: Row appears 3 times left, once right: `EXCEPT ALL` and `INTERSECT ALL`?
flashcards.back: `EXCEPT ALL` returns it twice (max(m−n,0)); `INTERSECT ALL` once (min(m,n)). Plain `EXCEPT` returns nothing.

flashcards.front: What is the practical working rule for third normal form?
flashcards.back: Every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

flashcards.front: How do you model a many-to-many relationship in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: A junction table with foreign keys to both sides, a composite primary key on the pair, and an extra index on the second column for reverse lookups.

flashcards.front: Why not store related ids in an int[] column?
flashcards.back: Array elements cannot be foreign keys, and the Arrays docs suggest a separate table with a row per item when you search for elements.

flashcards.front: What is the default way to model and query a tree of arbitrary depth?
flashcards.back: An adjacency list (nullable parent_id referencing the same table) queried with WITH RECURSIVE, ideally with a CYCLE clause.

flashcards.front: GENERATED ALWAYS vs BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY?
flashcards.back: ALWAYS rejects explicit values unless the INSERT says OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE; BY DEFAULT accepts explicit values.

flashcards.front: Which UUID functions are new in PostgreSQL 18?
flashcards.back: uuidv7([shift]) (timestamp-ordered) and uuidv4() (an alias of gen_random_uuid()).

flashcards.front: How do you read the creation time from a uuidv7?
flashcards.back: uuid_extract_timestamp(uuid), which works for version 1 and version 7 UUIDs. This also means a v7 id reveals when it was created.

flashcards.front: Does PostgreSQL index the referencing column of a foreign key automatically?
flashcards.back: No. Index it yourself, or every delete or key update on the parent scans the child table.

flashcards.front: ON DELETE NO ACTION vs RESTRICT?
flashcards.back: Both reject deleting a referenced parent. NO ACTION (the default) can be deferred to commit; RESTRICT cannot.

flashcards.front: What does MATCH SIMPLE mean for a composite foreign key?
flashcards.back: It is the default: if any referencing column is NULL, the row is not checked against the parent.

flashcards.front: Does CHECK (qty > 0) reject a NULL qty?
flashcards.back: No. A CHECK passes when its expression is true or NULL. Add NOT NULL.

flashcards.front: What does UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT do?
flashcards.back: Treats NULLs as equal for the constraint, so only one row per key may contain NULL (available since PostgreSQL 15).

flashcards.front: How do you forbid overlapping bookings per room?
flashcards.back: EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&), which needs btree_gist for the scalar column. In PostgreSQL 18, a WITHOUT OVERLAPS key is a declarative alternative.

flashcards.front: What does adding a constraint NOT VALID do?
flashcards.back: It enforces the constraint for new and updated rows but skips checking existing rows until ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, which takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE.

flashcards.front: timestamptz or timestamp for event times stored in UTC?
flashcards.back: timestamptz. The wiki says to use it for points in time even if you only store UTC.

flashcards.front: Why use numeric rather than double precision for money?
flashcards.back: numeric is exact; floating point is not (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 is false in float8). Also avoid the money type.

flashcards.front: Is varchar(255) faster than text?
flashcards.back: No. The docs state there is no performance difference; use text and a CHECK for real length rules.

flashcards.front: What can you not do to an existing enum value?
flashcards.back: Remove it or change its sort order, short of dropping and recreating the type. Adding and renaming values is supported.

flashcards.front: In PostgreSQL 18, what kind of generated column do you get without STORED or VIRTUAL?
flashcards.back: VIRTUAL (computed on read). Virtual generated columns cannot be indexed.

flashcards.front: What must a PRIMARY KEY on a partitioned table include?
flashcards.back: All partition key columns. There is no global unique index across partitions.

flashcards.front: What does partition pruning need from a query?
flashcards.back: A predicate on the partition key. Pruning happens at plan time and at execution time.

flashcards.front: How should old data be removed from a time-partitioned table?
flashcards.back: DROP TABLE the old partition or DETACH PARTITION [CONCURRENTLY], instead of a large DELETE.

flashcards.front: When does hash partitioning fit better than range or list?
flashcards.back: When you want rows spread evenly and there is no natural range or small list of values, for example many tenant ids.

flashcards.front: Range partition bounds: inclusive or exclusive?
flashcards.back: The lower bound is inclusive and the upper bound exclusive, so FROM (2026-11-01) TO (2026-12-01) covers November exactly.

flashcards.front: Which operators can a B-tree index serve?
flashcards.back: <, <=, =, >=, >, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, and anchored LIKE 'abc%' (with C collation or a pattern operator class).

flashcards.front: In a B-tree on (a, b, c), which conditions narrow the scanned index range?
flashcards.back: Equality on the leading columns plus one inequality on the first column without an equality. Later-column conditions are checked in the index but do not shrink the range.

flashcards.front: What is B-tree skip scan (PostgreSQL 18)?
flashcards.back: Using an index on (a, b) for WHERE b = ? by running one search per distinct a. It pays off only when a has few distinct values.

flashcards.front: Can one index on (x) serve ORDER BY x DESC?
flashcards.back: Yes. A B-tree can be scanned backwards.

flashcards.front: What index serves ORDER BY x ASC, y DESC?
flashcards.back: One declared with matching directions: (x ASC, y DESC), or (x DESC, y ASC) scanned backwards. An index on (x, y) cannot.

flashcards.front: Default NULL ordering in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: NULLs sort as larger than any value: NULLS LAST for ASC, NULLS FIRST for DESC.

flashcards.front: Two requirements for an index-only scan?
flashcards.back: The index type supports it (B-tree yes, GIN never), and every column the query references is in the index.

flashcards.front: What does Heap Fetches mean on an Index Only Scan?
flashcards.back: How many rows needed a heap visit because their page was not marked all-visible in the visibility map. VACUUM keeps that map current.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't WHERE lower(email) = 'x' use an index on email?
flashcards.back: The index stores email, not lower(email). Create an expression index on lower(email).

flashcards.front: Rules for an expression index to be used?
flashcards.back: The query must use the same expression, and the functions must be IMMUTABLE.

flashcards.front: When can the planner use a partial index?
flashcards.back: When it can prove at plan time that the query's WHERE clause implies the index predicate. Parameterized clauses in generic plans do not match.

flashcards.front: Use case for a partial unique index?
flashcards.back: Uniqueness within a subset, e.g. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON subs (user_id) WHERE active: one active row per user.

flashcards.front: What do INCLUDE columns do?
flashcards.back: They add payload to leaf entries for index-only scans. They are not searchable, are ignored for uniqueness, cannot be expressions, and are never deduplicated.

flashcards.front: Which index types support INCLUDE?
flashcards.back: B-tree, GiST and SP-GiST.

flashcards.front: Which index type for jsonb @> or array &&?
flashcards.back: GIN (an inverted index).

flashcards.front: jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops?
flashcards.back: jsonb_ops (the default) supports ? ?| ?& @> @? @@. jsonb_path_ops is smaller and faster but supports only @> @? @@, not key existence ?.

flashcards.front: Which index type for ranges, exclusion constraints and KNN ORDER BY <->?
flashcards.back: GiST.

flashcards.front: When is a BRIN index effective?
flashcards.back: When column values correlate with physical row order, e.g. created_at on an append-only table. It stores per-block-range summaries.

flashcards.front: What does a hash index support?
flashcards.back: Only equality (=).

flashcards.front: Does EXPLAIN ANALYZE execute the statement?
flashcards.back: Yes. Wrap UPDATE, DELETE or INSERT in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.

flashcards.front: actual rows=40 loops=500: how many rows did the node produce?
flashcards.back: About 20,000. Actual rows and time are per loop.

flashcards.front: EXPLAIN changes in PostgreSQL 18?
flashcards.back: EXPLAIN ANALYZE includes BUFFERS by default (BUFFERS OFF to disable), row counts are fractional, and index scan nodes show Index Searches.

flashcards.front: First thing to check in a slow plan?
flashcards.back: Estimated vs actual rows per node. A big mismatch usually points to stale or missing statistics, or to correlated columns the planner treats as independent.

flashcards.front: Fix for underestimated rows on correlated columns (city, country)?
flashcards.back: CREATE STATISTICS (dependencies / ndistinct / mcv) on the columns, then ANALYZE.

flashcards.front: Are partitioned parent tables analyzed by autovacuum?
flashcards.back: No. Run ANALYZE on the parent manually.

flashcards.front: Why is OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 slow?
flashcards.back: Skipped rows are still computed in the server. Use keyset pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20.

flashcards.front: What is an N+1 query and its fix?
flashcards.back: One query for a list plus one query per row. Replace it with a join, = ANY(array) or LATERAL.

flashcards.front: How does SELECT * hurt index use?
flashcards.back: It references every column, which rules out index-only scans on a narrower covering index.

flashcards.front: How does PostgreSQL handle WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2 with separate indexes on a and b?
flashcards.back: It can combine them with a BitmapOr of two Bitmap Index Scans. Otherwise rewrite as a UNION.

flashcards.front: What is the default transaction isolation level in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: READ COMMITTED. Each statement sees data committed before that statement began.

flashcards.front: How does READ UNCOMMITTED behave in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: Exactly like READ COMMITTED. PostgreSQL never shows dirty reads.

flashcards.front: Does REPEATABLE READ prevent phantom reads in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: Yes. PostgreSQL's repeatable read is stricter than the SQL standard requires and prevents phantoms. It still allows serialization anomalies such as write skew.

flashcards.front: What SQLSTATE do serialization failures use, and what should the client do?
flashcards.back: 40001 (serialization_failure). Roll back and retry the entire transaction, including its reads.

flashcards.front: Do SSI predicate locks (SIReadLock) block other transactions?
flashcards.back: No. They never block and cannot cause deadlocks. Conflicts are resolved by aborting a transaction with 40001.

flashcards.front: What does SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE do?
flashcards.back: It may wait at start for a safe snapshot, then runs without risk of being cancelled by a serialization failure. Good for long reports.

flashcards.front: Under READ COMMITTED, what happens when UPDATE finds its target row was changed by a concurrent transaction?
flashcards.back: It waits for that transaction, then re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the new row version and updates it only if it still matches.

flashcards.front: What are xmin and xmax on a row version?
flashcards.back: xmin is the ID of the transaction that inserted the version; xmax is the ID of the transaction that deleted or updated (or locked) it, zero if none.

flashcards.front: Why does a row's ctid change after UPDATE?
flashcards.back: UPDATE writes a new row version at a new physical location; the old version is kept until VACUUM. ctid is therefore not a stable identifier.

flashcards.front: What does plain VACUUM do with the space from dead tuples?
flashcards.back: Marks it reusable within the table. It generally does not return it to the OS, except empty pages at the end of the table.

flashcards.front: What lock does VACUUM FULL take?
flashcards.back: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. It rewrites the table, blocks all reads and writes, and needs extra disk for the new copy.

flashcards.front: Name three things that hold back the xmin horizon and stop VACUUM removing dead tuples.
flashcards.back: Long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions, old prepared transactions, and stale replication slots.

flashcards.front: What is the default autovacuum vacuum trigger in PostgreSQL 18?
flashcards.back: Dead tuples > min(autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold, 50 + 0.2 x reltuples). The max threshold (new in 18) defaults to 100 million.

flashcards.front: What two conditions allow a HOT (heap-only tuple) update?
flashcards.back: No column referenced by an index changes (summarizing indexes like BRIN excepted), and the same page has free space for the new version.

flashcards.front: Which statistic shows how many updates were HOT?
