flashcards.back: n_tup_hot_upd in pg_stat_all_tables (or pg_stat_user_tables), compared with n_tup_upd.

flashcards.front: Why can transaction ID wraparound happen?
flashcards.back: XIDs are 32-bit. If tuples are not frozen for about two billion transactions, old rows could appear to be in the future and data loss could result.

flashcards.front: Does disabling autovacuum stop anti-wraparound vacuums?
flashcards.back: No. Once a table exceeds autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200 million by default), autovacuum runs on it even if autovacuum is disabled.

flashcards.front: Which table lock levels block a plain SELECT?
flashcards.back: Only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, most ALTER TABLE).

flashcards.front: What table lock does plain CREATE INDEX take versus CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY?
flashcards.back: CREATE INDEX takes SHARE (blocks writes, allows reads). CONCURRENTLY takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE.

flashcards.front: Which row lock does a plain UPDATE take if it does not change key columns?
flashcards.back: FOR NO KEY UPDATE, which does not conflict with the FOR KEY SHARE locks taken by foreign-key checks.

flashcards.front: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED vs FOR UPDATE NOWAIT?
flashcards.back: SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows (queue consumers). NOWAIT raises an error immediately instead of waiting.

flashcards.front: How does PostgreSQL handle a deadlock?
flashcards.back: After deadlock_timeout (1s default) it detects the cycle and aborts one transaction (unpredictable which) with SQLSTATE 40P01. Prevent with consistent lock ordering.

flashcards.front: In INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, what is EXCLUDED?
flashcards.back: The row that was proposed for insertion, so SET n = t.n + EXCLUDED.n can use the incoming values.

flashcards.front: Why does a batch ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE fail with "cannot affect row a second time"?
flashcards.back: The input contains duplicate conflict keys. Deduplicate the batch before the statement.

flashcards.front: Session vs transaction advisory locks?
flashcards.back: Session locks (pg_advisory_lock) persist until unlocked or disconnect and survive ROLLBACK. Transaction locks (pg_advisory_xact_lock) release at commit or rollback.

flashcards.front: What does WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE do in MERGE?
flashcards.back: Added in 17, it acts on target rows that have no matching source row, for example to DELETE them during a sync.

flashcards.front: What happens to key order and duplicate keys in jsonb?
flashcards.back: Key order and whitespace are not kept, and the last value of a duplicated key wins.
No. Containment is anchored at the top level; the pattern must mirror the nesting: `'{"a":{"b":1}}'`.

flashcards.front: Which operators does GIN `jsonb_path_ops` support?
flashcards.back: Only `@>`, `@?` and `@@`. It is smaller and faster than `jsonb_ops` but cannot answer the existence operators `?`, `?|`, `?&`.

flashcards.front: What do jsonb `?`, `?|` and `?&` test?
flashcards.back: Whether a string exists as a top-level key or array element (one, any, all). They do not look into nested objects.

flashcards.front: What do the jsonb operators `@?` and `@@` take?
flashcards.back: A jsonpath. `@?` asks whether the path returns any item; `@@` evaluates a jsonpath predicate. Both can use a GIN index.

flashcards.front: Which SQL/JSON functions arrived in PostgreSQL 17?
flashcards.back: `JSON_TABLE`, `JSON_EXISTS`, `JSON_QUERY` and `JSON_VALUE`.

flashcards.front: Why does a frequently updated field inside a big jsonb document hurt?
flashcards.back: Every update locks and rewrites the whole row, so each small change rewrites the entire document.

flashcards.front: Which tsquery parser is safe for raw search-box input?
flashcards.back: `websearch_to_tsquery`. It accepts quotes, `or` and `-` and never raises a syntax error.

flashcards.front: `ts_rank` vs `ts_rank_cd`?
flashcards.back: `ts_rank` scores by term frequency; `ts_rank_cd` (cover density) also rewards terms that occur close together.

flashcards.front: Default weights for tsvector labels `{D,C,B,A}`?
Why `coalesce` when building a tsvector from several columns?
flashcards.back: `to_tsvector(NULL)` is NULL and concatenating NULL yields NULL, so one missing field would drop the whole document from search.

flashcards.front: What trigrams does `show_trgm('cat')` return?
flashcards.back: Four: `"  c"`, `" ca"`, `"cat"`, `"at "` (two leading spaces and one trailing space are added to each word).

flashcards.front: Which pg_trgm index class supports `ORDER BY col <-> 'x' LIMIT n`?
flashcards.back: GiST (`gist_trgm_ops`) only. GIN trigram indexes support `%` and unanchored LIKE/ILIKE but not nearest-neighbour ordering.

flashcards.front: Default `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` used by `%`?
pgvector: what do `<->`, `<#>` and `<=>` compute?
flashcards.back: L2 distance, negative inner product, and cosine distance.

flashcards.front: Why does `ORDER BY emb <#> :q` ascending return the most similar vectors first?
flashcards.back: `<#>` returns the negative inner product, so the largest inner product is the smallest value.

flashcards.front: HNSW vs IVFFlat in one line each?
flashcards.back: HNSW: better speed–recall trade-off, slower build, more memory, can be built on an empty table. IVFFlat: faster build and smaller, but must be built after the data is loaded.

flashcards.front: What is the default `ivfflat.probes` and a starting value to try?
flashcards.back: Default 1; start around sqrt(lists).

flashcards.front: Why can a filtered pgvector query return fewer rows than its LIMIT?
flashcards.back: Approximate indexes apply the filter after the index scan; with HNSW that is about `hnsw.ef_search` (40 by default) candidates. Use iterative index scans, partial indexes or partitioning.

flashcards.front: What does `SKIP LOCKED` do in a queue query?
flashcards.back: Skips rows locked by other transactions, so several workers can claim different rows without waiting on each other.

flashcards.front: When is a NOTIFY delivered?
flashcards.back: When the sending transaction commits, in commit order, to sessions currently listening. A rollback sends nothing.

flashcards.front: Maximum NOTIFY payload size?
flashcards.back: Shorter than 8000 bytes by default. Send an id and look the data up.

flashcards.front: Does PgBouncer transaction pooling support LISTEN?
flashcards.back: No. Listeners need a direct connection or session pooling.

flashcards.front: What problem does the outbox table solve?
flashcards.back: The dual write: the event row is inserted in the same transaction as the business change, so both commit or neither does. A relay publishes it later.

flashcards.front: RLS is enabled and no policy exists. What can a normal role see?
flashcards.back: Nothing. RLS without policies is default deny.

flashcards.front: Who bypasses row-level security?
flashcards.back: Superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS, and the table owner unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set.

flashcards.front: `USING` vs `WITH CHECK` in a policy?
flashcards.back: `USING` filters existing rows; `WITH CHECK` validates new or modified rows. Without WITH CHECK, the USING expression is used.

flashcards.front: How do permissive and restrictive policies combine?
flashcards.back: Permissive policies combine with OR; restrictive policies combine with AND (and must all pass).

flashcards.front: Two must-dos for a SECURITY DEFINER function?
flashcards.back: Set `search_path` with `pg_temp` last, and REVOKE EXECUTE FROM PUBLIC in the same transaction as the CREATE.

flashcards.front: Supabase: why write `(select auth.uid())` in a policy?
flashcards.back: Wrapping it in a select lets the value be computed once per statement instead of once per row.

flashcards.front: Supabase: how do you make a view respect RLS?
flashcards.back: Create it `with (security_invoker = true)` (PostgreSQL 15+); otherwise it runs as its owner and bypasses RLS.

flashcards.front: Default `password_encryption` and MD5 status in PostgreSQL 18?
flashcards.back: `scram-sha-256`; MD5 passwords are deprecated and creating one raises a warning.

flashcards.front: Default max_connections in PostgreSQL 18, and how many are reserved for superusers?
flashcards.back: 100, with superuser_reserved_connections = 3, so ordinary roles are refused at 97.

flashcards.front: Is work_mem a per-query, per-session or per-operation limit?
flashcards.back: Per sort or hash operation. A complex query can use several multiples; hash operations may use work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier (2.0).

flashcards.front: Name PgBouncer's three pool modes.
flashcards.back: session, transaction and statement.

flashcards.front: Name four features that break under transaction pooling.
flashcards.back: Any of: SET/RESET, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors, SQL PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, temp tables with PRESERVE/DELETE ROWS, LOAD, session advisory locks.

flashcards.front: What does Supabase's shared pooler in transaction mode not support?
flashcards.back: Prepared statements; disable them in the driver. Use it for serverless and edge functions with a small pool.

flashcards.front: Why can a fast ALTER TABLE take the app down?
flashcards.back: It waits for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind a long transaction, and new queries queue behind it. Use lock_timeout and retry.

flashcards.front: Does ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT now() rewrite the table? DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()?
flashcards.back: now() is non-volatile: no rewrite. gen_random_uuid() is volatile: full table rewrite.

flashcards.front: Two key rules for CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
flashcards.back: It cannot run in a transaction block, and on failure it leaves an INVALID index that must be dropped or reindexed concurrently.

flashcards.front: Lock taken by ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT?
flashcards.back: SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so normal reads and writes continue during the scan.

flashcards.front: How do you add NOT NULL to a big table without a long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE scan?
flashcards.back: Add CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, VALIDATE it, then SET NOT NULL (which skips the scan), then drop the CHECK. In 18 NOT NULL itself can be NOT VALID.

flashcards.front: Can pg_dump backups be used for point-in-time recovery?
flashcards.back: No. They are logical snapshots. PITR needs a physical base backup plus archived WAL.

flashcards.front: What must archive_command return?
flashcards.back: Exit 0 only when the WAL file was safely archived; anything else makes PostgreSQL retry and keep the segment.

flashcards.front: What happens to the timeline after a point-in-time recovery?
flashcards.back: A new timeline starts, keeping the new WAL history separate from the old one.

flashcards.front: What does logical replication not replicate?
flashcards.back: Schema/DDL, sequence data and large objects (as of 18). TRUNCATE is replicated.

flashcards.front: What do published tables need for UPDATE and DELETE to replicate logically?
flashcards.back: A replica identity, which is the primary key by default.

flashcards.front: Setup requirements for pg_stat_statements.
flashcards.back: Add it to shared_preload_libraries (restart), make sure query IDs are computed (compute_query_id, default auto, enables them when the module loads), then CREATE EXTENSION. Rank by total_exec_time.

flashcards.front: Starting point for shared_buffers on a dedicated server?
flashcards.back: About 25% of RAM; more than 40% rarely helps.

flashcards.front: Three ways to do a major-version upgrade.
flashcards.back: pg_upgrade, dump and restore, or logical replication to a new-version server and switch over.

questions.scenario: A retention report must list customers who have never ordered. It uses `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`. Guest checkouts store `orders.customer_id` as NULL, and the report has returned no rows since guest checkout launched.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Add `DISTINCT` to the subquery so duplicate customer ids do not interfere.
Rewrite as `LEFT JOIN orders o ON true WHERE o.customer_id <> customers.id`.
Replace `NOT IN` with `<> ALL (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`.
Rewrite as `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = customers.id)`.
questions.explanation: One NULL in the subquery makes `x NOT IN (...)` false or NULL for every row, so nothing passes WHERE. `NOT EXISTS` only asks whether a matching row exists, so NULL customer ids just fail to match. The PostgreSQL wiki recommends `NOT EXISTS` over `NOT IN` with subqueries, both for this reason and for performance.
rationales: Duplicates are not the problem. A single NULL still makes every comparison unknown.
This pairs every customer with every order and keeps pairs that differ, so almost every customer survives. It is not an anti join.
`<> ALL` is equivalent to `NOT IN` and has the same NULL behaviour.
Correct. `NOT EXISTS` is a true anti join and is unaffected by NULLs in `orders.customer_id`.

questions.scenario: An account dashboard should show every customer with the number of orders they placed in 2026, including customers with zero. The query is `SELECT c.id, count(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-01-01' GROUP BY c.id`. Customers with no 2026 orders are missing.
questions.stem: Which change returns every customer with a correct count?
options: Change `count(o.id)` to `count(*)`.
Change `LEFT JOIN` to `FULL JOIN`.
Move the date condition into the join: `ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at >= '2026-01-01'`.
Add `OR o.created_at IS NULL` to the WHERE clause.
questions.explanation: WHERE runs after the join and removes NULL-extended rows, so the outer join acts as an inner join. Putting the condition in ON changes only which orders match, and customers without a match keep one NULL-extended row that `count(o.id)` counts as 0.
rationales: The missing rows were already removed by WHERE. Also, `count(*)` would count the NULL-extended row as 1.
A full join does not fix it, because the WHERE clause still removes the NULL rows.
Correct. Conditions on the nullable side of an outer join belong in ON.
This keeps customers with no orders at all, but still drops customers whose only orders are from before 2026.

questions.scenario: A support screen needs each customer's three most recent orders. Customers without orders must still appear, with NULL order columns.
questions.stem: Which FROM clause does this correctly?
options: `FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) o ON true`
`FROM customers c LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3) o ON true`
`FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) o`
`FROM orders o RIGHT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM customers c WHERE c.id = o.customer_id) c ON true LIMIT 3`
questions.explanation: LATERAL lets the subquery reference `c` and runs it per customer, so `LIMIT 3` applies per customer. A LEFT join with `ON true` keeps customers whose subquery returns nothing. The id tiebreaker makes the choice deterministic.
rationales: Without LATERAL a FROM subquery cannot reference `c`, so this fails.
Correct. `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` is the top-N-per-group pattern and keeps customers with no orders.
CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops customers for whom the subquery returns no rows.
In a RIGHT JOIN LATERAL the lateral item cannot reference the left side, and the outer LIMIT caps the whole result at 3 rows.

questions.scenario: A marketing export lists customers who have at least one order. `SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id` returns a customer once per order, and the team keeps adding DISTINCT.
questions.stem: Which rewrite expresses the intent directly, returning each qualifying customer once with no de-duplication step?
options: `SELECT c.* FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`
`SELECT c.* FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL`
`SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id LIMIT 1`
`SELECT c.* FROM customers c CROSS JOIN orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id`
questions.explanation: EXISTS is a semi join: the result depends only on whether the subquery returns any row, so each customer appears at most once. The join-based versions still produce one row per matching order.
rationales: Correct. EXISTS returns each outer row at most once and needs no DISTINCT.
This is an inner join written the long way and still returns one row per order.
LIMIT 1 caps the whole result at a single row, not one row per customer.
This is the same inner join with the condition moved to WHERE, so it has the same duplicates.

questions.scenario: You need products that have never been ordered. `order_items.product_id` is nullable because legacy imports left some line items unlinked.
questions.stem: Which two queries return the correct set? (Select two.)
options: `SELECT p.* FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)`
`SELECT p.* FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL`
`SELECT p.* FROM products p WHERE p.id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items)`
`SELECT p.* FROM products p JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL`
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS and the LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern are both correct anti joins. In the LEFT JOIN form, matched rows always have a non-NULL `product_id` (equality was true), so only unmatched products remain. NOT IN returns nothing once the subquery contains a NULL.
rationales: Correct. NOT EXISTS is the recommended anti join and ignores NULLs in the subquery.
Correct. Only NULL-extended rows have `oi.product_id IS NULL`, because a match requires equality.
The NULL `product_id` values make `NOT IN` never true, so this returns no rows.
An inner join only keeps rows where the equality is true, so `product_id` is never NULL and the result is empty.

questions.scenario: A finance query should return customers whose paid orders total more than 1000. A developer wrote `SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND sum(amount) > 1000 GROUP BY customer_id`, and it fails.
questions.stem: What is the correct form?
options: Keep both conditions in WHERE and wrap the query in a subquery.
Move both conditions to HAVING: `HAVING status = 'paid' AND sum(amount) > 1000`.
Keep `status = 'paid'` in WHERE and move `sum(amount) > 1000` to `HAVING`.
Replace `sum(amount) > 1000` with `amount > 1000` in WHERE.
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it cannot use aggregates ("aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE"). HAVING filters groups after aggregation. The row-level status filter stays in WHERE, where it also reduces the rows fed into grouping.
rationales: Wrapping does not help. The aggregate is still in a WHERE clause.
`status` is not grouped, so HAVING cannot reference it directly. Even if it could, it is a row filter and belongs in WHERE.
Correct. Row filters go in WHERE and group filters go in HAVING.
This keeps individual orders over 1000 instead of customers whose total is over 1000.

questions.scenario: A daily operations report needs total orders, paid orders and refunded orders per day in one pass over `orders`. A draft uses `count(status = 'paid') AS paid`, and the paid number always equals the total.
questions.stem: Which expression gives the correct paid count?
options: `count(DISTINCT status = 'paid')`
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')`
`count(status) HAVING status = 'paid'`
`count(status = 'paid' IS NOT NULL)`
questions.explanation: count(expr) counts non-NULL values, and the boolean `status = 'paid'` is non-NULL (true or false) for every row with a status. `FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts which rows feed the aggregate, so each conditional count comes from the same single scan.
rationales: This counts the distinct boolean values (at most 2), not paid orders.
Correct. FILTER limits the aggregate to paid rows.
HAVING is a clause for whole groups, not a modifier for one aggregate, so this is not valid syntax.
This boolean is never NULL, so it counts every row.

questions.scenario: A sales report uses `GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product)` and labels subtotal rows with `COALESCE(product, 'All products')`. Some sales have a NULL product (uncategorised), and those detail rows are also being labelled "All products".
questions.stem: How should the query tell subtotal rows apart from real NULL-product groups?
options: Use `CASE WHEN GROUPING(product) = 1 THEN 'All products' ELSE product END`.
Add `ORDER BY product NULLS LAST` so subtotals come after detail rows.
Switch to `GROUP BY DISTINCT ROLLUP (region, product)`.
Replace ROLLUP with `CUBE (region, product)`.
questions.explanation: `GROUPING(col)` returns 1 when the column is not part of the current row's grouping set, so it marks subtotal and total rows even when the data contains NULL keys. COALESCE cannot tell the two kinds of NULL apart.
rationales: Correct. GROUPING() tells a subtotal NULL from a data NULL.
Sorting does not change the labels, and both kinds of row still show NULL.
GROUP BY DISTINCT removes duplicate grouping sets. It does not label rows.
CUBE adds more grouping sets, such as per-product totals, and has the same labelling problem.

questions.scenario: A notification job needs the latest order of each customer. A developer writes `SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, id, created_at FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC`.
questions.stem: What happens, and what is the fix?
options: It works, but returns the oldest order. Change DESC to ASC.
It fails because DISTINCT ON cannot be combined with ORDER BY. Use GROUP BY customer_id instead.
It returns one arbitrary row per customer. Add LIMIT 1.
It fails because DISTINCT ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions. Use `ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC`.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL requires the DISTINCT ON expressions to match the initial ORDER BY expressions. The remaining sort keys then decide which row of each group is kept. Here that is the newest order (add `id DESC` as a tiebreaker for determinism).
rationales: The query does not run at all, and the sort direction is not the issue.
DISTINCT ON needs an ORDER BY to pick the row. GROUP BY customer_id alone cannot select the other columns of the latest row.
The query errors rather than returning rows, and LIMIT 1 would cap the whole result at one row.
Correct. Lead the ORDER BY with the DISTINCT ON key.

questions.stem: Which two statements about grouping sets in PostgreSQL are correct? (Select two.)
options: `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((region), (product), ())` returns the same rows as a UNION ALL of the three corresponding GROUP BY queries, with ungrouped columns NULL.
`ROLLUP (a, b)` is equivalent to `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())`.
`CUBE (a, b)` produces three grouping sets: `(a, b)`, `(a)` and `()`.
`GROUP BY DISTINCT` removes duplicate output rows produced by the grouping sets.
questions.explanation: Grouping sets behave like a UNION ALL of one grouping per set. ROLLUP is the hierarchical shorthand (detail, prefixes, grand total). CUBE produces every subset, which is four sets for two columns. GROUP BY DISTINCT removes duplicate grouping sets, not duplicate rows.
rationales: Correct. This is how the docs define grouping sets.
Correct. ROLLUP produces the list prefixes plus the empty set.
CUBE (a, b) also includes (b), so it produces four sets.
DISTINCT here removes duplicate grouping sets created when you combine ROLLUP, CUBE or GROUPING SETS. It does not touch output rows.

questions.scenario: For each session, an analytics query shows the final page visited next to every event: `last_value(page) OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY ts)`. Every row shows its own page instead of the session's last page.
questions.stem: What is the most direct fix?
options: Add a frame: `OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)`.
Remove `PARTITION BY session_id`.
Use `last_value(page) IGNORE NULLS OVER (...)`.
Change `ORDER BY ts` to `ORDER BY ts DESC` and keep the default frame.
questions.explanation: With ORDER BY, the default frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, so the frame ends at the current row (and its peers). The docs warn that last_value with this frame "is likely to give unhelpful results". Extending the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING makes the whole partition visible.
rationales: Correct. The frame must reach the end of the partition.
This mixes all sessions together and still has the default frame problem.
IGNORE NULLS is not implemented in PostgreSQL 18 and does not change the frame anyway.
Reversing the order makes last_value return the current row's value again. To get the final page this way you would need first_value.

questions.scenario: A ledger has several entries per day. `sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY entry_date)` shows the same running total on every row of a given day, and reviewers want a total that increases row by row.
questions.stem: Which window definition produces a strict per-row running total?
options: `OVER (ORDER BY entry_date RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
`OVER (PARTITION BY entry_date ORDER BY entry_date)`
`OVER (ORDER BY entry_date, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
`OVER (ORDER BY entry_date GROUPS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
questions.explanation: The default RANGE frame includes all peers of the current row. On 10, 20, 20, 30 it gives 10, 50, 50, 80, while ROWS gives 10, 30, 50, 80. ROWS counts physical rows, and the unique `id` tiebreaker fixes the order within a day.
rationales: This is just the default frame written out, so peers still share one total.
Partitioning by day restarts the total every day, and every row of a day is still a peer.
Correct. ROWS mode plus a unique tiebreaker gives a strictly increasing per-row total.
GROUPS mode works in whole peer groups, so rows of the same day still share a total.

questions.scenario: A contest leaderboard sorts by score. Tied players must share a place, and the next player gets the next consecutive place (1, 2, 2, 3), not a skipped one.
questions.stem: Which function fits?
options: `row_number() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)`
`rank() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)`
`ntile(3) OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)`
`dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)`
questions.explanation: dense_rank gives peers the same rank and leaves no gaps. rank leaves gaps after ties (1, 2, 2, 4). row_number gives every row a different number and orders tied rows arbitrarily.
rationales: row_number never gives tied players the same place.
rank would give 1, 2, 2, 4.
ntile splits rows into buckets. It is not a ranking of places.
Correct. dense_rank gives 1, 2, 2, 3.

questions.scenario: To keep only each customer's newest order, a developer writes `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) = 1`. It fails.
questions.stem: What is the correct approach in PostgreSQL?
options: Move the condition to `HAVING row_number() OVER (...) = 1`.
Add `GROUP BY customer_id` so the window function is allowed in WHERE.
Add a `QUALIFY row_number() OVER (...) = 1` clause.
Compute `row_number()` as a column in a subquery or CTE and filter `WHERE rn = 1` in the outer query.
questions.explanation: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, and are allowed only in the select list and ORDER BY. The standard pattern is to compute the rank in an inner query and filter on it outside.
rationales: HAVING is also evaluated before window functions, so the error stays.
Grouping does not change where window functions may appear.
QUALIFY is not part of PostgreSQL 18's SELECT syntax.
Correct. Compute it in the inner query and filter in the outer one.

questions.scenario: Product wants each user's login streaks: runs of consecutive calendar days with a start date, end date and length. `logins(user_id, day date)` can contain several rows per user per day. The database runs PostgreSQL 18.
questions.stem: Which approach is correct?
options: Use `lag(day) IGNORE NULLS OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day)` to skip missing days, then group.
Group by `dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day)`.
De-duplicate to one row per user per day, compute `day - (row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day))::int` as a group key, then GROUP BY user_id and that key.
Group by `ntile(7) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day)` to bucket days into weeks.
questions.explanation: Within a run of consecutive days, the date and its row_number both go up by 1, so their difference is constant and identifies the island. On Jan 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 this gives two islands of 2 and 3 days. You must de-duplicate first, because repeated days advance row_number without advancing the date.
rationales: IGNORE NULLS is not implemented in PostgreSQL 18, and missing days are absent rows, not NULLs.
dense_rank numbers each distinct day, so every day becomes its own group.
Correct. This is the classic gaps-and-islands technique.
ntile makes buckets of equal size and ignores whether the days are consecutive.

questions.stem: Which two statements about window frames in PostgreSQL 18 are correct? (Select two.)
options: When `OVER` has ORDER BY and no frame clause, the frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` and includes the current row's peers.
`GROUPS` frame mode counts offsets in peer groups rather than individual rows.
When `OVER` has no ORDER BY, the default frame contains only the current row.
`lag(x) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY t)` returns the previous non-NULL value.
questions.explanation: The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE from the partition start to the current row, including peers. GROUPS mode measures offsets in peer groups. Without ORDER BY all rows are peers, so the frame is the whole partition. IGNORE NULLS is not implemented in 18.
rationales: Correct. This is why running totals repeat across tied rows.
Correct. ROWS counts rows, RANGE uses value offsets, and GROUPS counts peer groups.
Without ORDER BY every row is a peer, so aggregates cover the whole partition.
RESPECT/IGNORE NULLS are not implemented in PostgreSQL 18.

questions.scenario: A revenue report shows month-over-month change as `revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)`. Finance wants the first month to show its full revenue as the change (treat the previous month as 0) instead of NULL.
questions.stem: Which expression does this?
options: `revenue - lag(revenue, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month)`
`revenue - lead(revenue, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month)`
`revenue - first_value(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)`
`revenue - lag(revenue) IGNORE NULLS OVER (ORDER BY month)`
questions.explanation: lag takes an optional offset (default 1) and a default value (NULL by default) that is returned when the offset row does not exist. Passing 0 as the default makes the first month's change equal its revenue.
rationales: Correct. The third argument replaces the missing previous row.
lead reads the next month, not the previous one.
first_value subtracts the first month's revenue from every row. That is a change since the start, not month over month.
IGNORE NULLS is not implemented in 18, and it would not supply a default anyway.

questions.scenario: A recursive CTE walks `referrals(user_id, referred_by)` upward and carries a `depth` column. A data bug created a referral loop, and the query now runs until it is cancelled.
questions.stem: What is the most robust way to make the query terminate correctly?
options: Change `UNION ALL` to `UNION` so repeated rows are discarded.
Add `LIMIT 1000` to the outer query.
Mark the CTE `MATERIALIZED`.
Add `CYCLE user_id SET is_cycle USING path` and filter `WHERE NOT is_cycle`.
questions.explanation: The CYCLE clause tracks visited keys in a path column and stops recursing when a key repeats. UNION only drops rows that are exact duplicates, and the increasing depth makes every lap distinct. The docs describe LIMIT as a trick for testing only.
rationales: Because depth changes on every lap, no row is an exact duplicate and the loop continues.
LIMIT may cut off the output, but it is a testing trick only and does not detect cycles.
Materialization controls inlining and has nothing to do with recursion termination.
Correct. CYCLE detects revisited keys and stops recursing from them.

questions.scenario: A query defines `WITH recent AS (SELECT * FROM events WHERE ts > now() - interval '7 days')` and then references `recent` twice, each time with a selective `WHERE account_id = $1`. `events(account_id, ts)` has a suitable index, but the plan scans all recent events once and filters afterwards.
questions.stem: What explains this, and what is the targeted fix?
options: CTEs are always inlined, so the index is simply not selective enough. Run ANALYZE.
A CTE referenced more than once is materialized by default, so outer filters are not pushed into it. Declare it `AS NOT MATERIALIZED`.
CTEs can never use indexes. Rewrite the query with a temporary table.
A CTE referenced more than once is inlined, so it runs twice. Declare it `AS MATERIALIZED`.
questions.explanation: A non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE is inlined only when it is referenced once. With two references it is materialized by default, so each outer reference filters the materialized rows. NOT MATERIALIZED forces inlining, so each reference can push `account_id = $1` down to the index.
rationales: Inlining happens only for a single reference, so the premise is wrong.
Correct. NOT MATERIALIZED overrides the default for a CTE with several references.
Inlined CTEs use indexes like any subquery. A temporary table adds work.
This reverses the default rule. MATERIALIZED would keep the slow plan.

questions.scenario: A price-change script runs `WITH upd AS (UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.05 WHERE category = 'tools' RETURNING *) SELECT id, price FROM products WHERE category = 'tools'`. The output shows the old prices, and the developer suspects the update failed.
questions.stem: What is happening?
options: The UPDATE did not run because the main query never reads `upd`.
The UPDATE is deferred until commit, so no query in this transaction can see it.
All sub-statements share one snapshot, so the main query sees the table as it was before the update. Read the new values with `SELECT id, price FROM upd`.
Data-modifying statements inside WITH are executed only when marked MATERIALIZED.
questions.explanation: Data-modifying CTEs and the main query run with the same snapshot, so they cannot see each other's changes to the tables. RETURNING is the only way to pass changed rows along. The update still runs exactly once and to completion, whether or not its output is read.
rationales: Data-modifying CTEs run to completion even when nothing reads their output.
Later statements in the same transaction do see the change. Only this statement's snapshot does not.
Correct. Use RETURNING to observe the modified rows.
MATERIALIZED does not affect whether a data-modifying CTE executes.

questions.scenario: An org-chart page needs an indented tree in which each manager is immediately followed by all of their reports, recursively. The recursive CTE already returns `id, manager_id, name, depth`.
questions.stem: Which addition produces that order most directly?
options: `ORDER BY depth, id` in the outer query.
`SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ord` on the CTE, then `ORDER BY ord`.
Change the recursive `UNION ALL` to `UNION`.
`SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` on the CTE, then `ORDER BY ord`.
questions.explanation: SEARCH DEPTH FIRST adds an ordering column that places every node directly before its descendants, which is the order an indented tree needs. Ordering by depth, or using BREADTH FIRST, lists the tree level by level.
rationales: This lists all level-1 rows, then all level-2 rows, so reports are separated from their managers.
Breadth-first order is level by level, not each subtree in turn.
UNION only removes duplicates. It does not define an output order.
Correct. Depth-first order puts each subtree under its root.

questions.scenario: An audit query must find orders where `discount` is anything other than exactly 0, including orders where the discount is unknown (NULL). `WHERE discount <> 0` misses the NULL rows.
questions.stem: Which predicate is correct?
options: `WHERE discount IS DISTINCT FROM 0`
`WHERE NOT (discount = 0)`
`WHERE discount != 0`
`WHERE discount <> 0 AND discount IS NULL`
questions.explanation: Comparing NULL with an ordinary operator gives NULL, and WHERE keeps only rows whose condition is true. IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a comparable value, so `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 0` is true and `0 IS DISTINCT FROM 0` is false.
rationales: Correct. This is the null-safe comparison.
`NOT NULL` is still NULL, so NULL rows are still excluded.
`!=` is just another spelling of `<>`.
No value is both non-zero and NULL, so this returns nothing. Using OR would work, but IS DISTINCT FROM is the direct form.

questions.scenario: A KPI tile shows conversion as `(paid_orders / total_orders)::numeric`, where both columns are `bigint` counts. It always shows 0, even though about 30% of orders are paid.
questions.stem: Which expression fixes it?
options: `round(paid_orders / total_orders, 2)`
`paid_orders::numeric / NULLIF(total_orders, 0)`
`(paid_orders / total_orders)::float8`
`CAST(paid_orders / total_orders AS numeric(5,2))`
questions.explanation: Dividing two integers truncates toward zero, so 3/10 is already 0 before any cast of the result. Casting an operand to numeric makes the division exact, and NULLIF guards against division by zero when there are no orders.
rationales: The integer division has already truncated to 0, so rounding cannot recover the fraction.
Correct. Cast before dividing.
Casting the truncated result still gives 0.
Casting after the division keeps the truncated 0.

questions.scenario: Table `a` contains the value 'x' three times. Table `b` contains 'x' once. Both are single-column text tables.
questions.stem: Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: `SELECT v FROM a EXCEPT ALL SELECT v FROM b` returns 'x' twice.
`SELECT v FROM a INTERSECT ALL SELECT v FROM b` returns 'x' once.
`SELECT v FROM a UNION SELECT v FROM b` returns 'x' four times.
`SELECT v FROM a EXCEPT SELECT v FROM b` returns 'x' twice.
questions.explanation: With ALL, a row seen m times on the left and n times on the right appears max(m − n, 0) times in EXCEPT ALL and min(m, n) times in INTERSECT ALL. Without ALL, set operations remove duplicates, so UNION returns 'x' once and EXCEPT removes it completely.
rationales: Correct. max(3 − 1, 0) = 2.
Correct. min(3, 1) = 1.
UNION removes duplicates and returns 'x' once. UNION ALL would return it four times.
Plain EXCEPT works on distinct rows. 'x' exists in b, so it is removed entirely.

questions.scenario: An `orders` table stores `customer_id` and also `customer_email`, copied from the customer at checkout so a report can avoid a join. After customers update their email, support finds old addresses on new invoices that read from `orders`.
questions.stem: What is the best schema change?
options: Add a trigger on customers that updates customer_email in every matching orders row
Drop orders.customer_email and read the email from customers through customer_id
Add a UNIQUE constraint on orders.customer_email
Move customer_email into a jsonb column on orders
questions.explanation: The email is a fact about the customer, not the order, so storing it on orders violates normalization and causes update anomalies. Keeping it once on customers and joining through the foreign key removes the inconsistency. A copy would be correct only if it were a deliberate snapshot, and here the invoices need the current email.
rationales: A trigger keeps copies in sync but adds write amplification and locks for a problem that normalization removes.
Correct: one fact in one place, reached through the existing foreign key.
Uniqueness on orders is wrong: one customer has many orders with the same email.
Changing the storage type does not remove the duplicated fact.

questions.scenario: Students can enroll in many courses and each course has many students. The team needs to store the enrollment date and quickly answer both "courses for a student" and "students in a course".
questions.stem: Which design fits best?
options: A course_ids bigint[] column on students with a GIN index
A comma-separated text column of course codes on students
An enrollments table with student_id and course_id foreign keys, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id), an enrolled_at column and an index on course_id
A jsonb column on courses holding an array of enrolled student objects
questions.explanation: A junction table is the standard many-to-many model: it supports foreign keys to both sides, per-link attributes like enrolled_at, and indexes in both directions. The composite PK serves lookups by student, and the extra index serves lookups by course.
rationales: Arrays cannot hold foreign keys and have nowhere natural to store the per-enrollment date.
Delimited text cannot be constrained or indexed for element lookups.
Correct: foreign keys, a place for enrollment attributes and indexes for both directions.
jsonb cannot enforce referential integrity, and every enrollment change rewrites the course row.

questions.scenario: A `categories(id, parent_id, name)` table stores a product taxonomy whose depth varies from 2 to 9 levels and changes over time. A page must list every descendant of a chosen category.
questions.stem: Which query approach is most appropriate?
options: A recursive CTE starting from the chosen category and joining children on parent_id, with a CYCLE clause to guard against loops
Five chained self-joins on parent_id, covering the typical depth
A window function partitioned by parent_id
A LATERAL join from categories to itself on parent_id
questions.explanation: For an adjacency list of arbitrary depth, WITH RECURSIVE walks the tree level by level until no more rows are found. The CYCLE clause marks and stops loops created by bad data. Fixed self-join chains silently miss deeper levels.
rationales: Correct: recursion handles any depth, and CYCLE protects against loops.
Hard-coded self-joins miss descendants beyond the chosen depth.
Window functions compute over rows already selected; they do not traverse parent links.
A single LATERAL join only reaches one level of children.

questions.scenario: A reporting team proposes several denormalizations for a busy OLTP database.
questions.stem: Which two proposals are reasonable? (Select two.)
options: Copy customer_name into every orders row before any query has been measured, to avoid joins
Serve a dashboard of daily totals from a materialized view refreshed every 10 minutes, after profiling showed the aggregate query dominates load and 10 minutes of staleness is acceptable
Replace the order_tags junction table with a text[] of tag ids so that tags no longer need a foreign key
Add a STORED generated column for a value computed from other columns in the same row, so that it can be indexed
questions.explanation: Denormalization is reasonable when it answers a measured read problem and a mechanism keeps the copy correct. A materialized view with an accepted refresh interval and a stored generated column (always derived by the database) both meet that bar. Copying mutable parent attributes without measurement and dropping foreign keys trade integrity for an unproven gain.
rationales: Premature: it creates update anomalies without evidence that the join is a problem.
Correct: a measured hotspot, staleness explicitly accepted, and the refresh keeps it consistent.
This removes referential integrity; array elements cannot be foreign keys.
Correct: the database computes the value, so it cannot drift, and STORED makes it indexable.

questions.scenario: A mobile app creates records offline and syncs later, so ids must be generated on devices and in several services without a central sequence. The team also wants new ids to sort roughly by creation time. The database is PostgreSQL 18.
questions.stem: Which key choice best meets the requirements?
options: bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
uuid values generated with gen_random_uuid()
uuid values generated as version 7 (uuidv7()), with the timestamp exposure considered acceptable
A text key made by concatenating the device name and a local counter
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL 18 adds uuidv7(), whose values embed a millisecond Unix timestamp and are described as timestamp-ordered, while still being generatable without a central sequence. The trade-off is that uuid_extract_timestamp can read the creation time back. Random v4 UUIDs meet the decentralized requirement but carry no time order.
rationales: Identity values come from a database sequence, which offline devices cannot use.
gen_random_uuid() produces random version 4 values with no time ordering.
Correct: decentralized generation plus timestamp ordering.
Ad hoc text keys are larger, harder to keep unique and not time-sortable across devices.

questions.scenario: A new table must have an auto-generated primary key. A past incident happened because a script inserted explicit ids that later collided with sequence-generated ones.
questions.stem: Which column definition best prevents a repeat?
options: id serial PRIMARY KEY
id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
id bigint DEFAULT nextval('t_id_seq') PRIMARY KEY
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
questions.explanation: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY rejects explicit values in INSERT unless the statement deliberately adds OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, which blocks accidental collisions. The PostgreSQL wiki recommends identity columns over serial.
rationales: serial is discouraged by the wiki and accepts explicit values.
BY DEFAULT accepts explicit values, which is how the collision happened.
A plain sequence default also accepts explicit values.
Correct: explicit ids are rejected unless overridden on purpose.

questions.scenario: Deleting a single row from `accounts` takes several seconds. The table `ledger_entries` (80M rows) has `account_id bigint REFERENCES accounts(id)`. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the delete (inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK) shows the delete node itself is fast and almost all the time is reported under the foreign key constraint trigger.
questions.stem: What is the most effective fix?
options: Change the foreign key to ON DELETE CASCADE
Raise work_mem for the session that runs the delete
Make the foreign key DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
Create an index on ledger_entries(account_id), using CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the live table
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL does not index the referencing column of a foreign key automatically. Each parent delete must search ledger_entries for matching rows, which is a full scan without an index on account_id. Building that index concurrently avoids blocking writes during the build.
rationales: CASCADE changes behaviour (deleting children) and still needs to find them with a scan.
Memory settings do not replace the missing index for this lookup.
Deferring moves the same scan to commit time; it does not make it cheaper.
Correct: the missing child-side index is why every delete scans 80M rows.

questions.scenario: When a user deletes their account, their forum posts must remain visible but shown as written by a deleted user. `posts.author_id` references `users(id)`.
questions.stem: Which foreign key action fits?
options: ON DELETE CASCADE
ON DELETE RESTRICT
ON DELETE SET NULL, with author_id nullable
ON DELETE NO ACTION
questions.explanation: SET NULL keeps the child rows and clears the reference when the parent is deleted, which matches "keep the posts, drop the author". CASCADE would delete the posts, and RESTRICT and NO ACTION would block the account deletion.
rationales: This deletes the posts along with the user.
This blocks deleting a user who has posts.
Correct: posts remain and the author reference becomes NULL.
The default action also rejects the delete while posts exist (it can only be deferred).

questions.scenario: `users` uses `email text PRIMARY KEY`, and twelve tables reference it. Users regularly change their email, and each change currently requires coordinated updates across all twelve tables.
questions.stem: What is the best long-term design?
options: Keep email as the key and add ON UPDATE CASCADE to all twelve foreign keys
Add a bigint identity surrogate primary key, point the foreign keys at it, and keep a UNIQUE constraint on email
Change the key to a composite of (email, created_at)
Forbid email changes in the application
questions.explanation: A natural key is a safe primary key only if it never changes, and email does change. A surrogate key never needs updating, so references stay stable, while the UNIQUE constraint still enforces one account per email. ON UPDATE CASCADE automates the fan-out but keeps rewriting and locking rows in twelve tables on every change.
rationales: This automates the problem rather than removing it: every change still rewrites rows in twelve tables.
Correct: stable references plus the business rule enforced by UNIQUE.
A composite that includes email still changes when the email changes.
This changes a legitimate product requirement to work around a schema choice.

questions.scenario: A table has `discount_pct numeric CHECK (discount_pct BETWEEN 0 AND 100)`. A data audit finds rows where `discount_pct` is NULL, although the business says every row must have a discount (0 if none).
questions.stem: Why did the CHECK constraint allow these rows, and what fixes it?
options: The CHECK only applies to UPDATE, so add a trigger for INSERT
BETWEEN excludes NULL only in strict mode, so enable standard_conforming_strings
A CHECK passes when its expression is NULL; add NOT NULL (and DEFAULT 0) to the column
The constraint was created NOT VALID, so run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT
questions.explanation: A CHECK constraint is satisfied when its expression evaluates to true or NULL, and a comparison with NULL yields NULL. Requiring a value is the job of NOT NULL, and a default of 0 matches the business rule.
rationales: CHECK constraints apply to both INSERT and UPDATE.
This setting is about string literal escapes and has nothing to do with constraints.
Correct: NULL passes CHECK; NOT NULL is the missing rule.
A NOT VALID constraint still checks new rows, and it would not reject NULL either.

questions.scenario: In `accounts(tenant_id, external_ref)`, `external_ref` is optional. The rule is: within a tenant, each external_ref is unique, and at most one account may have no external_ref.
questions.stem: Which constraint enforces the rule?
options: UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_ref)
UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (tenant_id, external_ref)
A unique index on (tenant_id, external_ref) WHERE external_ref IS NOT NULL
CHECK (external_ref IS NOT NULL OR tenant_id IS NOT NULL)
questions.explanation: By default UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct, so any number of rows per tenant could have NULL. NULLS NOT DISTINCT, available since PostgreSQL 15, treats NULLs as equal so only one NULL per tenant is allowed.
rationales: Default NULL handling allows unlimited NULL external_ref rows per tenant.
Correct: NULLs compare equal for this constraint.
This index ignores NULL rows entirely, so many NULLs remain allowed.
A row-level CHECK cannot compare rows with each other.

questions.scenario: A booking service must guarantee that the same room is never booked for overlapping time ranges, even when two requests arrive at the same moment. Bookings store `room_id int` and `during tstzrange`.
questions.stem: Which approach enforces this correctly?
options: In the application, SELECT for overlapping bookings and INSERT only if none are found, inside a READ COMMITTED transaction
UNIQUE (room_id, lower(during), upper(during))
A CHECK constraint with a subquery that looks for overlapping rows
CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist and add EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
questions.explanation: An exclusion constraint rejects any new row for which another row has an equal room_id and an overlapping range, and the database enforces it under concurrency. The scalar equality on room_id inside a GiST constraint needs btree_gist. PostgreSQL 18 also offers WITHOUT OVERLAPS keys for the same rule.
rationales: Two concurrent transactions can both see no conflict and both insert.
Uniqueness only blocks identical bounds, not overlapping ranges.
CHECK constraints cannot run subqueries against other rows.
Correct: the overlap rule is enforced by the database for every writer.

questions.scenario: A team must add a foreign key and a NOT NULL rule to a 2 TB table that serves production traffic on PostgreSQL 18, with minimal blocking.
questions.stem: Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Adding the foreign key with NOT VALID and later running VALIDATE CONSTRAINT avoids holding a long blocking lock while existing rows are checked
A NOT VALID constraint is not enforced at all until it is validated
In PostgreSQL 18 a NOT NULL constraint can also be added as NOT VALID and validated later
ADD FOREIGN KEY takes only an ACCESS SHARE lock, so validating in one step is already non-blocking
questions.explanation: NOT VALID adds the constraint quickly and enforces it for new writes, and VALIDATE CONSTRAINT scans existing rows under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which allows normal reads and writes. PostgreSQL 18 extends NOT VALID to NOT NULL constraints. ADD FOREIGN KEY takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE, which blocks writes.
rationales: Correct: the slow validation is split out and runs under a weaker lock.
New and updated rows are checked immediately; only existing rows are skipped.
Correct: NOT NULL NOT VALID is new in 18.
ADD FOREIGN KEY takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both tables, which blocks writes during a one-step validation.

questions.scenario: Application servers in three regions write `created_at` values into a `timestamp without time zone` column, each in its local time. Cross-region reports now order events incorrectly.
questions.stem: What column type should the team use?
options: timestamp without time zone, with a convention that every writer converts to UTC first
timestamptz, so each value is stored as an absolute instant
text holding ISO 8601 strings with offsets
date plus a separate time column
questions.explanation: timestamptz represents a point in time: input with a zone or offset is converted to UTC, and output is shown in the session time zone. The PostgreSQL wiki recommends timestamptz for points in time even when you only ever store UTC, because timestamp ignores zone information.
rationales: A convention is easy to break, and the type still cannot tell instants apart from wall-clock readings.
Correct: the type itself stores an absolute instant.
Text loses date arithmetic, range queries and validation.
Splitting date and time still lacks zone information.

questions.scenario: An invoicing table stores amounts as `double precision`. Finance reports totals that are off by fractions of a cent compared with the source system.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Store amounts as numeric (with a separate currency column if needed)
Switch to the money type
Keep double precision and wrap every SUM in round(..., 2)
Switch to real to reduce storage
questions.explanation: Floating point types are inexact binary approximations, so sums of decimal amounts drift (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 is false for float8 but true for numeric). The numeric type is exact decimal arithmetic, and the wiki recommends it over the money type.
rationales: Correct: exact decimal storage and arithmetic.
The wiki advises against the money type; use numeric.
Rounding hides some symptoms but each stored value is still inexact.
real is less precise than double precision.

questions.scenario: Order statuses are currently an enum. Product now wants to retire two statuses, add a display label and an is_terminal flag to each status, and let operations staff manage the list without schema migrations.
questions.stem: What is the best design?
options: Keep the enum and use ALTER TYPE to drop the retired values
Replace the enum with a CHECK (status IN (...)) constraint
Store statuses as free text with no constraint
Create an order_status lookup table (code, label, is_terminal, active) and reference it from orders with a foreign key
questions.explanation: Enum values can be added and renamed, but existing values cannot be removed or reordered without recreating the type, and enums cannot carry attributes. A lookup table referenced by a foreign key supports metadata and changes through ordinary DML.
rationales: Enums do not support removing existing values.
A CHECK list still needs DDL to change and holds no metadata.
Free text loses all validation.
Correct: metadata, retirement and changes without DDL.

questions.scenario: On PostgreSQL 18 a developer runs `ALTER TABLE order_lines ADD COLUMN total numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * unit_price);` and then `CREATE INDEX ON order_lines (total);` The index creation fails.
questions.stem: Why does it fail?
options: Generated columns can never be indexed in PostgreSQL
The table must be rewritten with VACUUM FULL before the index can be built
Multiplying two numeric columns is not immutable
Without STORED, the column is VIRTUAL by default in PostgreSQL 18, and virtual generated columns cannot be indexed
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL 18 makes VIRTUAL the default for generated columns, computed when read, and indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported. Declaring the column STORED (or indexing the expression qty * unit_price directly) solves it.
rationales: Stored generated columns can be indexed.
No rewrite is required; the problem is the column kind.
The expression is immutable; otherwise the ALTER itself would have failed.
Correct: the 18 default is virtual, which cannot be indexed.

questions.scenario: An e-commerce catalogue has a few fields used by every query (sku, price, category_id, in_stock) and many attributes that differ per category (voltage, fabric, screen size).
questions.stem: Which model fits best?
options: Typed columns for the common fields, plus a jsonb column for per-category attributes with a GIN index if they are searched
A single jsonb document per product holding every field
An entity-attribute-value table (product_id, attr_name, attr_value text)
One nullable column on products for every attribute of every category
questions.explanation: Fields that are filtered, joined or constrained should be typed columns so they can have foreign keys, CHECKs and ordinary indexes. Genuinely variable attributes fit jsonb, and GIN supports containment and existence queries. Keeping documents small also limits the cost of whole-row rewrites on update.
rationales: Correct: typed columns where it matters, jsonb where data varies.
Core fields lose types and foreign keys, and every change rewrites the whole document.
EAV stores everything as text and makes simple queries into many self-joins.
Hundreds of sparse columns are hard to manage and still need DDL for each new attribute.

questions.scenario: A schema review lists several type and query choices.
questions.stem: Which two follow the PostgreSQL wiki guidance? (Select two.)
options: Use char(2) for country codes because fixed-length types are faster
Use text by default rather than varchar(n), adding a CHECK where a length limit is a real rule
Query time ranges with created_at >= start AND created_at < end rather than BETWEEN
Use the money type for currency amounts
questions.explanation: The wiki recommends text over char(n) and varchar(n) by default, and the docs state there is no performance difference apart from char(n) padding. It also recommends half-open >= / < ranges because BETWEEN includes the end point. It advises numeric instead of money.
rationales: char(n) pads with spaces and is not faster.
Correct: text by default, constraints for real rules.
Correct: half-open ranges avoid double counting the boundary.
The wiki says not to use money.

questions.scenario: `events` is range-partitioned by month on `created_at` (36 partitions). A query `SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50` shows every partition in EXPLAIN, and it is slower than before partitioning.
questions.stem: What explains this and what is the best fix?
options: enable_partition_pruning is off by default; turn it on
Range partitioning cannot prune; switch to hash partitioning on created_at
Pruning needs a predicate on the partition key; add a created_at lower bound that matches the feature (for example the last 90 days), and keep an index on (user_id, created_at) in each partition
Add more, smaller partitions so each scan is cheaper
questions.explanation: Partition pruning removes partitions only when the query constrains the partition key, so a filter on user_id alone visits all 36 partitions. Adding a created_at bound lets the planner or executor prune, and per-partition indexes find the rows within the remaining partitions. enable_partition_pruning is on by default.
rationales: It is on by default.
Range partitions prune fine when the key is constrained; hash would not help range filters.
Correct: give the planner a key predicate and index within partitions.
More partitions means more to scan and more planning overhead without a key predicate.

questions.scenario: A developer runs `CREATE TABLE events (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);` and it fails.
questions.stem: The team must keep range partitioning on created_at for pruning and monthly retention. What is the correct fix?
options: Use PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at), because unique constraints on a partitioned table must include the partition key
Replace PRIMARY KEY with UNIQUE (id), which has no such restriction
Create a global unique index on id across all partitions
Switch to PARTITION BY HASH (id) so the key can stay on id alone
questions.explanation: A primary key or unique constraint on a partitioned table must include all partition key columns, because each partition enforces uniqueness only locally and there is no global unique index. Including created_at satisfies the rule. Hash partitioning by id would allow PRIMARY KEY (id) but gives up time-based pruning and retention.
rationales: Correct: the key includes the partition column.
UNIQUE has exactly the same restriction.
PostgreSQL has no global unique index across partitions.
It works syntactically, but it abandons the time-based design the table needs for pruning and retention.

questions.scenario: A nightly job runs `DELETE FROM metrics WHERE ts < now() - interval '13 months'` on a 3 TB table. It runs for hours, and the table bloats until vacuum catches up.
questions.stem: Which redesign best fixes retention?
options: Run VACUUM FULL after each delete
Hash-partition metrics into 64 partitions on series_id
Range-partition metrics by month on ts and remove old months with DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY and DROP TABLE
Replace the DELETE with TRUNCATE metrics
questions.explanation: With range partitions aligned to the retention window, removing a month is a metadata operation (DETACH or DROP of a partition) instead of a mass DELETE that leaves dead tuples. DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking ongoing queries.
rationales: VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and rewrites 3 TB, which makes the outage worse.
Hash partitions spread every month across all partitions, so old data still needs DELETE.
Correct: retention becomes dropping a partition.
TRUNCATE removes all data, not only old data.

questions.scenario: An architect is deciding whether to partition several tables.
questions.stem: In which two situations is declarative partitioning most likely to help? (Select two.)
options: A 2 GB users table where most queries look up a single row by primary key
A time-series table far larger than server memory, where almost all queries touch the most recent few days
A table where every month of data older than two years must be removed regularly
A table where an email column must be unique across all rows, but the partition key is signup_date
questions.explanation: The partitioning docs say benefits normally appear when a table would be larger than physical memory and queries concentrate on a few partitions, and that bulk removal is much cheaper by dropping or detaching partitions. A small table looked up by primary key gains nothing. A unique constraint must include the partition key, so cross-partition uniqueness on email cannot be enforced.
rationales: An index lookup on a small table is already fast; partitioning adds planning overhead.
Correct: pruning keeps the working set to the recent partitions.
Correct: retention becomes DROP or DETACH of old partitions.
There is no global unique index, so this requirement conflicts with partitioning by signup_date.

questions.scenario: A support dashboard runs SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE org_id = $1 AND created_at >= $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50. The table has 40M rows across thousands of orgs.
questions.stem: Which single index best serves this query?
options: CREATE INDEX ON tickets (created_at, org_id)
CREATE INDEX ON tickets USING brin (org_id)
CREATE INDEX ON tickets (org_id, created_at)
CREATE INDEX ON tickets USING hash (org_id)
questions.explanation: Equality on the leading column plus a range on the next column bounds the B-tree scan, and the entries for one org come out already ordered by created_at, so LIMIT can stop early. With created_at first, the scan covers every org in the time range.
rationales: With created_at leading, the scan covers all orgs in the time range and filters org_id inside it.
BRIN depends on physical correlation, and org_id is unlikely to follow insert order. It also gives no ordering.
Correct: equality first, then the range and sort column, so the scan is bounded and sorted.
Hash indexes support only equality. They cannot provide the range or the ordering.

sources.title: Indexes and ORDER BY — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: An index exists on events (tenant_id, kind). A new report filters only WHERE kind = 'refund'. tenant_id has about 200,000 distinct values. The team runs PostgreSQL 18.
questions.stem: What should they expect, and what should they do?
options: Reverse the column order with ALTER INDEX.
The index can never be used for a non-leading column in any version.
Skip scan makes the existing index as good as an index on (kind). No change needed.
The planner can use skip scan only when tenant_id has few distinct values. With 200,000 it will likely avoid the index, so add an index leading with kind if the report matters.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL 18 skip scan runs one search per distinct value of the leading column, which pays off only when that column has few distinct values. With very many tenants the planner prefers another plan, so a dedicated index is the reliable fix.
rationales: ALTER INDEX cannot reorder key columns. You must create a new index.
Wrong for 18: skip scan does allow such use in some cases.
Skip scan is not equivalent to a leading-column index, and its benefit depends on the leading column's cardinality.
Correct: skip scan helps only with low-cardinality leading columns, so add an index that leads with kind.

questions.stem: A leaderboard query runs ORDER BY score DESC, player_name ASC LIMIT 10. Which index lets PostgreSQL return rows in order without a Sort node?
options: (score, player_name)
(player_name, score DESC)
(score DESC, player_name)
(score DESC, player_name DESC)
questions.explanation: Mixed sort directions need an index whose column directions match the ORDER BY, or are all reversed for a backward scan. (score DESC, player_name ASC) matches exactly. (score ASC, player_name ASC) scanned backwards gives score DESC, player_name DESC, which is the wrong order for the tiebreaker.
rationales: Scanned forwards it gives score ASC. Scanned backwards it gives score DESC, player_name DESC. Neither matches.
The leading column is wrong, so it cannot produce score order.
Correct: the directions match the ORDER BY exactly.
Gives score DESC, player_name DESC (or the exact reverse), not the mixed order requested.

sources.title: Indexes and ORDER BY — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) of SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'open' shows: Index Only Scan using orders_status_id_idx ... Heap Fetches: 48210, with about 48,500 rows returned. The table gets heavy UPDATE traffic.
questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Most pages are not marked all-visible in the visibility map, so the scan must visit the heap to check visibility. A VACUUM, or more frequent autovacuum, would reduce the heap fetches.
The planner chose the wrong index type. Switch to GIN.
The index does not contain the id column.
Index-only scans always fetch every row from the heap. The counter is informational.
questions.explanation: Visibility information lives in the heap. An index-only scan skips the heap only for pages marked all-visible in the visibility map. Heavy updates clear those bits until VACUUM sets them again, so Heap Fetches climbs.
rationales: Correct: the visibility map is not current, and VACUUM restores all-visible pages.
GIN never supports index-only scans.
If id were missing, the plan could not be an Index Only Scan at all.
When pages are all-visible, the heap is skipped. That is the whole point of the optimization.

sources.title: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: A login query is SELECT id FROM users WHERE lower(email) = lower($1). There is a B-tree index on users(email), but the plan shows a Seq Scan on 8M rows.
questions.stem: Which change lets the query use an index without changing the query?
options: CREATE INDEX ON users USING hash (email);
Run ANALYZE users.
SET enable_seqscan = off for the application role.
CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email));
questions.explanation: The index stores email, but the predicate compares lower(email), so the plain index cannot be searched. An expression index on exactly lower(email) matches the query's expression.
rationales: A hash index on email has the same problem as the B-tree: it stores email, not lower(email).
Fresh statistics cannot make an index on email answer a lower(email) predicate.
Disabling seq scans does not make the email index usable for this predicate. It only distorts other plans.
Correct: the expression index matches the expression in the WHERE clause.

questions.scenario: A daily report filters WHERE created_at::date = '2026-11-01' on a 200M-row events table that has a B-tree index on created_at (timestamptz).
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Change the filter to created_at BETWEEN '2026-11-01' AND '2026-11-02'.
Add a hash index on created_at.
Change the filter to created_at >= '2026-11-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-02'.
Increase work_mem so the cast is cheaper.
questions.explanation: Casting the column hides it from the index on created_at. A half-open range on the bare column can use the B-tree. The wiki recommends >= and < over BETWEEN because BETWEEN includes both endpoints.
rationales: BETWEEN includes midnight of the next day, so it can pick up rows from the wrong day.
Hash supports only equality, and the cast still hides the column.
Correct: the bare column, a sargable half-open range, and exact day boundaries.
Memory settings do not change whether the index can be searched.

questions.scenario: A job queue table has 50M rows. Fewer than 1,000 are ever in status 'pending'. Workers poll SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100.
questions.stem: Which index is the best fit?
options: CREATE INDEX ON jobs (status, created_at) INCLUDE (payload);
CREATE INDEX ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
CREATE INDEX ON jobs (status);
CREATE INDEX ON jobs USING brin (status);
questions.explanation: A partial index holds only the tiny pending subset, already ordered by created_at, so it stays small and cheap to maintain. The planner can use it because the query's literal predicate matches the index predicate.
rationales: It indexes every row and adds a wide payload column. Bigger and slower to maintain for no gain.
Correct: small, ordered, and matches the literal predicate.
It works, but it indexes all 50M rows and still needs a sort or extra work for the created_at order.
BRIN on a low-cardinality, uncorrelated status column skips almost nothing.

questions.scenario: Following the previous design, a partial index exists ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'. The ORM sends the query as a prepared statement: WHERE status = $1 ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100. The connection pooler sets plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan, so the server always uses a generic plan, and EXPLAIN EXECUTE shows a seq scan.
questions.stem: Why?
options: Partial indexes are ignored for prepared statements in every case.
The index became invalid after autovacuum.
LIMIT prevents partial index use.
Partial-index predicate matching happens at plan time. A generic plan with a parameter cannot be proven to imply status = 'pending'.
questions.explanation: The planner must prove that the query's WHERE clause implies the index predicate, and it does that at plan time. With a parameter in a generic plan the value is unknown, so the partial index cannot be chosen. Sending the literal 'pending' (or allowing custom plans) fixes it.
rationales: Custom plans, which know the parameter value, can still use the index. The problem is the generic plan.
Autovacuum does not invalidate indexes.
LIMIT has no effect on whether a partial index qualifies.
Correct: plan-time predicate proof fails for a parameter in a generic plan.

questions.stem: A table has CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON accounts (account_no) INCLUDE (owner_id). Which statement is true?
options: Only account_no must be unique. owner_id is payload that supports index-only scans.
The pair (account_no, owner_id) must be unique.
WHERE owner_id = 5 can do an index range scan on this index.
INCLUDE columns can be expressions such as lower(owner_name).
questions.explanation: INCLUDE columns are stored in leaf entries but are not part of the search key. They are ignored for uniqueness and cannot be expressions. Their purpose is to let more queries run as index-only scans.
rationales: Correct.
INCLUDE columns are ignored for uniqueness.
INCLUDE columns are not searchable keys.
INCLUDE columns cannot be expressions.

sources.title: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: A SaaS app must allow many cancelled subscriptions per user but at most one with status 'active'.
questions.stem: Which DDL enforces this?
options: ALTER TABLE subs ADD CHECK (status = 'active');
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON subs (user_id) WHERE status = 'active';
ALTER TABLE subs ADD UNIQUE (user_id, status);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON subs (user_id) INCLUDE (status);
questions.explanation: A partial unique index enforces uniqueness only among rows that match its predicate, so each user can have one active row and any number of others. A unique constraint on (user_id, status) would also wrongly limit users to one cancelled row each.
rationales: A CHECK constraint would forbid any non-active row.
Correct: uniqueness applies only to the active subset.
This would allow only one cancelled subscription per user.
INCLUDE columns are ignored for uniqueness, so this makes user_id unique across all rows.

questions.scenario: A product catalog stores attributes in a jsonb column attrs and filters with WHERE attrs @> '{"color":"red"}'.
questions.stem: Which index supports this operator?
options: CREATE INDEX ON products USING brin (attrs);
CREATE INDEX ON products (attrs);
CREATE INDEX ON products USING hash (attrs);
CREATE INDEX ON products USING gin (attrs);
questions.explanation: The containment operator @> on jsonb is supported by GIN operator classes. B-tree and hash indexes on jsonb support only comparison or equality of whole values, not containment.
rationales: BRIN does not support jsonb containment.
A B-tree on jsonb compares whole documents. It cannot answer @>.
Hash supports only whole-value equality.
Correct: GIN (jsonb_ops by default) supports @>.

questions.scenario: A team wants the smallest, fastest GIN index for jsonb, and their queries use both @> and the key-existence operator ? (WHERE attrs ? 'discount').
questions.stem: Which operator class should they choose?
options: jsonb_ops (the default), because jsonb_path_ops does not support ?.
jsonb_path_ops, because it supports every jsonb operator.
gin_trgm_ops.
jsonb_path_ops for ? and a B-tree for @>.
questions.explanation: jsonb_path_ops is smaller and faster but supports only @>, @? and @@. The default jsonb_ops also supports ?, ?| and ?&. Because the workload needs key existence, jsonb_ops is required.
rationales: Correct: only jsonb_ops covers both operators.
jsonb_path_ops cannot answer ?.
gin_trgm_ops is for text similarity and LIKE, not jsonb.
jsonb_path_ops cannot do ?, and a B-tree cannot do @>.

questions.scenario: A 3-billion-row append-only sensor table is always queried by a recent time window on recorded_at. Rows arrive roughly in time order. A B-tree on recorded_at is very large.
questions.stem: Which index type gives most of the benefit at a tiny fraction of the size?
options: GIN
GiST
BRIN
Hash
questions.explanation: BRIN stores min/max summaries per block range and skips ranges that cannot match. It works well when values correlate with physical row order, as with time-ordered appends.
rationales: GIN is an inverted index for multi-element values, not for scalar time ranges.
GiST is aimed at ranges, geometry and nearest-neighbour search. It does not offer BRIN's per-block-range summaries, so it stays large.
Correct: tiny, and effective on physically correlated data.
Hash cannot answer range queries.

questions.scenario: A booking system stores reservations with a tstzrange column during and needs queries like WHERE during && tstzrange($1, $2), plus a constraint that no two reservations overlap.
questions.stem: Which index type serves both needs?
options: B-tree
BRIN
Hash
GiST
questions.explanation: GiST supports range operators such as && and is the access method used by exclusion constraints like EXCLUDE USING gist (during WITH &&).
rationales: B-tree has no overlap operator for ranges.
BRIN cannot back an exclusion constraint.
Hash supports equality only.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A search box suggests the 10 product names most similar to user input with ORDER BY name <-> $1 LIMIT 10 (pg_trgm).
questions.stem: Which index lets PostgreSQL answer this with an ordered index scan?
options: CREATE INDEX ON products (name text_pattern_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON products USING gist (name gist_trgm_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON products USING hash (name);
questions.explanation: pg_trgm supports nearest-neighbour ordering by the <-> distance operator with GiST indexes only. GIN trigram indexes speed up similarity and LIKE filters but cannot return rows in distance order.
rationales: Pattern operator classes support anchored LIKE, not similarity distance.
GIN supports trigram filtering but not KNN ordering.
Correct: GiST supports ORDER BY <->.
