Hash supports only equality.

questions.stem: Which statements about PostgreSQL index types are correct? (Select two.)
options: Hash indexes can serve range predicates like col > 10.
B-tree indexes can serve jsonb containment queries (@>).
GIN indexes never support index-only scans.
BRIN works best when column values correlate with the table's physical order.
questions.explanation: GIN never supports index-only scans, and BRIN relies on physical correlation to skip block ranges. Hash supports only equality, and B-tree does not support jsonb containment.
rationales: Hash supports only =.
Containment needs GIN.
Correct: GIN never returns index-only results.
Correct: BRIN skips ranges only when the data is physically clustered.

sources.title: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: A plan fragment reads: Nested Loop (actual time=0.05..2900 rows=48000 loops=1) -> Index Scan on order_items (rows=1) (actual time=0.010..0.012 rows=4 loops=12000).
questions.stem: How many rows did the inner index scan produce in total, and what does the estimate tell you?
options: 12,000 rows, one per loop.
About 48,000 rows in total. The estimate of 1 per loop against 4 actual is a modest per-loop miss. The real cost driver is the 12,000 loops.
It cannot be determined from EXPLAIN output.
4 rows. The estimate is close.
questions.explanation: Actual rows and time are reported per loop, so 4 rows x 12,000 loops is about 48,000 rows, which matches the Nested Loop's own rows=48000. The per-loop estimate of 1 against 4 actual is a small miss; the cost comes from repeating the inner scan 12,000 times.
rationales: That confuses loops with rows.
Correct: multiply per-loop values by loops.
The totals follow directly from rows × loops.
4 is the per-loop figure, not the total.

questions.scenario: An engineer wants actual run times for a DELETE that removes millions of rows, without losing the data.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Run BEGIN; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) DELETE ...; ROLLBACK;
Run EXPLAIN DELETE ... because EXPLAIN never executes.
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF) DELETE ..., since turning off buffers prevents execution.
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a SELECT count(*) with the same WHERE instead. It has identical costs.
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the statement, so a DELETE would remove rows unless it is rolled back. Plain EXPLAIN shows only estimates.
rationales: Correct: you get actual timing and the delete is undone.
Plain EXPLAIN gives estimates only, not the actual times they asked for.
BUFFERS OFF only hides buffer counts. The statement still runs.
A SELECT skips the deletion work, index maintenance and trigger costs.

questions.scenario: After a nightly bulk load of 20M rows into a staging table, the first report queries choose Nested Loops with estimates of rows=1 where tens of thousands of rows come back. Later in the day the same queries are fast.
questions.stem: What is the most effective fix?
options: Add SET enable_nestloop = off to the reports.
Run ANALYZE on the table right after the bulk load.
Raise random_page_cost.
Rebuild every index with REINDEX.
questions.explanation: The planner relies on statistics gathered by ANALYZE. Right after a bulk load they are stale until autovacuum's analyze threshold is reached and it runs. Running ANALYZE immediately gives the planner correct row estimates.
rationales: This is a blunt override that hides the cause and can hurt other queries.
Correct: fresh statistics fix the estimates that drive join choice.
Cost constants do not fix wrong row estimates.
Reindexing does not refresh table statistics.

sources.title: Statistics Used by the Planner — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: A query filters WHERE city = 'Lyon' AND country = 'FR'. The planner estimates 12 rows, but 9,800 come back, because the two columns are strongly correlated. Statistics are fresh.
questions.stem: Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: Run VACUUM FULL addresses.
Increase work_mem.
Create a hash index on city.
CREATE STATISTICS addr_dep (dependencies) ON city, country FROM addresses; ANALYZE addresses;
questions.explanation: By default the planner treats conditions as independent and multiplies their selectivities, which underestimates correlated columns. Extended statistics capture functional dependencies so the combined estimate is realistic.
rationales: Rewriting the table does not affect how column correlation is estimated.
Memory does not affect selectivity estimates.
An index does not change the estimate for the combined condition.
Correct: extended statistics teach the planner about the correlation.

sources.title: Statistics Used by the Planner — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: A team on PostgreSQL 18 has a partitioned measurements table. Queries spanning many partitions have poor estimates, even though each partition is analyzed regularly.
questions.stem: What is the likely cause?
options: Partitions cannot have statistics.
EXPLAIN in 18 hides estimates for partitions.
Autovacuum does not analyze partitioned parent tables, so the parent-level statistics are missing or stale. Run ANALYZE on the parent.
Partition pruning disables statistics.
questions.explanation: The routine vacuuming docs note that partitioned parents are not processed by autovacuum's analyze. Statistics for the whole hierarchy must be gathered with a manual ANALYZE on the parent.
rationales: Each leaf partition is a normal table and is auto-analyzed.
Estimates are still shown.
Correct.
Pruning does not disable statistics.

questions.scenario: An API lists posts newest-first with ?page=N using ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET (N-1)*20. Page 5,000 takes seconds, and users report duplicate posts while new ones are being added.
questions.stem: Which redesign fixes both problems?
options: Keyset pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_created_at, $last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, with an index on (created_at DESC, id DESC).
Use ORDER BY random() to spread load.
Add an index on created_at and keep OFFSET.
Cache the full result set in the application.
questions.explanation: Rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed inside the server, so cost grows with page depth, and inserts shift rows between pages. Keyset pagination seeks directly past the last row seen, with a unique tiebreaker for a stable order.
rationales: Correct: constant cost per page and a stable cursor.
Random order breaks pagination entirely.
The index helps ordering, but OFFSET still reads and discards every skipped row, and page drift remains.
Caching moves the problem elsewhere and goes stale as posts arrive.

sources.title: Indexes and ORDER BY — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.stem: A team is implementing keyset pagination over orders sorted by created_at. Which two practices are required for correct, efficient pages? (Select two.)
options: Back the ORDER BY with a matching multicolumn index such as (created_at, id).
Use OFFSET for the first page and keyset afterwards, without ORDER BY.
Wrap created_at in date_trunc('second', created_at) in the predicate to normalize timestamps.
Add a unique tiebreaker such as id to both ORDER BY and the seek predicate.
questions.explanation: Without a unique tiebreaker, rows with equal timestamps can be skipped or repeated across pages. A matching index lets each page seek and stop after LIMIT rows.
rationales: Correct: the index makes each page a bounded seek.
LIMIT without ORDER BY returns an unpredictable subset.
A function on the column prevents the plain index from being searched.
Correct: it gives a total, stable order.

sources.title: Indexes and ORDER BY — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: An order page runs one query for 50 orders, then a separate SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ? for each order. Each item query takes 0.3 ms, but the page takes 80 ms.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Increase max_connections so the queries run in parallel.
Fetch all items in one statement, for example WHERE order_id = ANY($1) with the 50 ids, or a join.
Add a second index on order_items(order_id).
Switch order_items to a hash index.
questions.explanation: This is an N+1 pattern. The per-query cost is small, but round trips and per-statement overhead multiply with N. Fetching the children in one set-based statement removes the extra round trips.
rationales: More connections do not remove the per-statement overhead and add contention.
Correct: one set-based query instead of N.
The lookups are already fast. The overhead is the number of round trips.
The index type is not the bottleneck.

sources.title: Table Expressions (joins and LATERAL) — PostgreSQL Docs
Row and Array Comparisons (= ANY) — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: A covering index exists: CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (status, total). The ORM issues SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1, and the plan shows an Index Scan with heap access rather than an Index Only Scan.
questions.stem: Why?
options: INCLUDE indexes cannot be used by ORMs.
SELECT * references columns that are not in the index, so an index-only scan is impossible. Select only customer_id, status and total.
The visibility map is disabled for INCLUDE indexes.
Index-only scans require a hash index.
questions.explanation: An index-only scan is possible only when every column the query references is stored in the index. SELECT * pulls every table column, so the heap must be visited. Naming the needed columns allows the covering index to answer the query.
rationales: Any client can benefit. It depends only on the query text.
Correct.
Visibility-map checks apply normally.
Hash indexes do not support index-only scans.

sources.title: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes — PostgreSQL Docs

questions.scenario: A lookup runs WHERE email = $1 OR phone = $2 on a 30M-row customers table. There are separate B-tree indexes on email and on phone.
questions.stem: Which plans or rewrites can avoid a full sequential scan? (Select two.)
options: Replacing both indexes with one index on (email, phone).
Wrapping both columns in coalesce() so a single index applies.
Rewriting as SELECT ... WHERE email = $1 UNION SELECT ... WHERE phone = $2.
A BitmapOr combining Bitmap Index Scans on both indexes.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL can combine separate indexes with a BitmapOr for OR conditions across columns. Alternatively, a UNION of two individually indexed queries works. A composite index cannot bound the phone branch, and wrapping columns in functions prevents index use.
rationales: With email leading, phone-only matches are not bounded.
Functions on the columns stop the indexes from being searched.
Correct: each branch uses its own index.
Correct: bitmap scans can combine multiple indexes.

questions.stem: A team upgrading to PostgreSQL 18 compares EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) output with their old runbooks. Which changes should they expect? (Select two.)
options: Index scan nodes report Index Searches.
Buffer usage is reported by default, without writing BUFFERS.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE no longer executes the statement.
Actual rows are now totals across all loops instead of per loop.
questions.explanation: In PostgreSQL 18, EXPLAIN ANALYZE includes buffer counts by default (BUFFERS OFF disables them), and index scan nodes show Index Searches. The statement is still executed, and actual figures are still per loop.
rationales: Correct: index scan nodes report the number of index searches.
Correct: BUFFERS is on by default with ANALYZE in 18.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE still runs the statement.
Actual rows remain per loop. Multiply by loops.

questions.scenario: An inventory service runs at the default isolation level. To sell an item it runs `SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id = $1`, computes `stock - 1` in application code, then runs `UPDATE items SET stock = $2 WHERE id = $1`. Under load, two concurrent sales of the last unit both succeed.
questions.stem: Which change prevents the lost update while staying at READ COMMITTED?
options: Wrap the SELECT and the UPDATE in a single BEGIN ... COMMIT block.
Add a B-tree index on items(id, stock) so the UPDATE finds the row faster.
Run the transaction at READ UNCOMMITTED so each session sees the other's pending change.
Replace both statements with `UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock > 0 RETURNING stock`.
questions.explanation: A single UPDATE that computes from the current value is atomic: if another session changed the row, read committed waits and re-evaluates the WHERE clause on the new version. A transaction block alone does not lock what the SELECT read, and READ UNCOMMITTED behaves like READ COMMITTED in PostgreSQL.
rationales: Incorrect: under read committed both sessions can still read the same stock value before either writes.
Incorrect: an index changes speed, not the race between read and write.
Incorrect: PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED; dirty reads never happen.
Correct: the read and write happen in one statement, and the stock > 0 check is re-evaluated against the latest version.

questions.scenario: Table `website` has two rows with `hits` = 9 and `hits` = 10. Session A runs `BEGIN; UPDATE website SET hits = hits + 1;` and has not committed. Session B, at READ COMMITTED, then runs `DELETE FROM website WHERE hits = 10;`, which waits. Session A commits.
questions.stem: What does session B's DELETE do?
options: Deletes the row that originally had hits = 10, using its snapshot value.
Deletes the row that now has hits = 10 (formerly 9).
Deletes no rows.
Fails with SQLSTATE 40001 because of the concurrent update.
questions.explanation: B's snapshot saw the first row as 9, so it was never a candidate. The row it waited on is re-checked after A commits and now holds 11, so it no longer matches. This is the example the PostgreSQL docs use to show read committed re-evaluation.
rationales: Incorrect: after waiting, read committed re-evaluates WHERE on the updated version (11), which does not match.
Incorrect: that row was 9 in B's snapshot, so the scan never selected it.
Correct: neither row matches at the moment it is examined, so nothing is deleted.
Incorrect: read committed does not raise serialization failures; it waits and re-evaluates.

questions.scenario: A billing job runs at REPEATABLE READ. It reads an invoice, does some calculations, then updates the invoice. Occasionally it fails with `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update`.
questions.stem: What is the correct way to handle this error?
options: Re-run only the failing UPDATE statement inside the same transaction.
Switch the job to READ UNCOMMITTED so the conflict cannot occur.
Roll back and retry the whole transaction from the beginning, including the initial read.
Ignore it: repeatable read already guarantees the update is applied once the lock is free.
questions.explanation: This error has SQLSTATE 40001 and means the row changed after the transaction's snapshot was taken. The transaction is aborted, and its earlier reads are stale, so the complete transaction must be retried. PostgreSQL does not retry automatically because only the application can redo the logic correctly.
rationales: Incorrect: the transaction is already aborted, and the calculation was based on stale reads.
Incorrect: READ UNCOMMITTED is the same as READ COMMITTED in PostgreSQL and would reintroduce lost updates.
Correct: retrying the whole transaction gets a fresh snapshot and recomputes from current data.
Incorrect: the statement failed; nothing is applied.

questions.scenario: A hospital app requires at least one doctor on call. Two transactions each run `SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call` (result: 2), then each sets a different doctor's `on_call = false` and commits. Both use REPEATABLE READ, and afterwards nobody is on call.
questions.stem: Which change makes PostgreSQL itself reject one of the two transactions, without adding explicit locks?
options: Keep REPEATABLE READ; it already prevents phantom reads, so the count is safe.
Run both at READ COMMITTED so each statement sees the other's commit.
Run both at SERIALIZABLE; the second transaction will block until the first commits and then succeed.
Run both at SERIALIZABLE and retry on SQLSTATE 40001.
questions.explanation: This is write skew, a serialization anomaly that repeatable read allows. Serializable snapshot isolation detects the read/write dependency and aborts one transaction with 40001, which the app must retry. SSI predicate locks never block, so the other transaction is not simply delayed.
rationales: Incorrect: preventing phantoms does not prevent write skew; each transaction writes a different row.
Incorrect: read committed allows the same anomaly and more.
Incorrect: SSI does not block on predicate locks; it aborts a transaction instead.
Correct: SSI aborts one of the two, and a retry sees the updated count.

questions.stem: Which statements about PostgreSQL isolation levels are true? (Select two.)
options: READ UNCOMMITTED behaves the same as READ COMMITTED.
REPEATABLE READ prevents phantom reads.
REPEATABLE READ prevents all serialization anomalies.
SERIALIZABLE predicate locks block concurrent writers until the reader commits.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL implements three distinct levels; READ UNCOMMITTED maps to READ COMMITTED. Its repeatable read uses one snapshot per transaction and so prevents phantoms, but still allows anomalies such as write skew. SSI predicate locks never block.
rationales: Correct: PostgreSQL never exposes uncommitted data.
Correct: PostgreSQL's repeatable read is stricter than the SQL standard minimum here.
Incorrect: serialization anomalies are possible at repeatable read; only serializable prevents them.
Incorrect: SIReadLocks never block and cannot cause deadlocks.

questions.scenario: A finance team runs a 20-minute report on a busy primary where all writers use SERIALIZABLE. The report must see a state consistent with some serial order of those writers, and it is costly if it gets cancelled by a serialization failure near the end.
questions.stem: How should the report transaction start?
options: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE, then LOCK every table in SHARE mode.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ, then retry on 40001 until it completes.
questions.explanation: A serializable, read-only, deferrable transaction may wait when it takes its snapshot, but then runs without the overhead of serializable checks and with no risk of being cancelled by a serialization failure. Read committed gives no single consistent view, and locking every table would block all writers for 20 minutes.
rationales: Incorrect: each statement sees a different snapshot, so the report is not consistent.
Correct: it waits for a safe snapshot and then cannot fail with a serialization error.
Incorrect: SHARE locks block all writes on those tables for the whole report.
Incorrect: a read-only repeatable read snapshot is not guaranteed to match any serial order of the serializable writers, and retrying would not fix that.

questions.scenario: A developer runs `SELECT ctid, xmin, * FROM t WHERE id = 1` and sees ctid `(0,1)`. After `UPDATE t SET note = 'x' WHERE id = 1`, the same query shows ctid `(0,2)` and a different xmin.
questions.stem: What explains this?
options: The UPDATE overwrote the row in place and then compacted the page.
xmin records the last time the row was read, so it changes on every access.
ctid is a logical row ID, so a change indicates corruption.
The UPDATE wrote a new row version created by the updating transaction; the old version remains until VACUUM removes it.
questions.explanation: Under MVCC an UPDATE never modifies a tuple in place: it inserts a new version (new ctid, xmin = updating transaction) and marks the old version's xmax. The old version stays on disk so older snapshots can still read it, until VACUUM reclaims it.
rationales: Incorrect: PostgreSQL does not update tuples in place.
Incorrect: xmin is the inserting transaction ID, not a read timestamp.
Incorrect: ctid is the physical location of a version and is expected to change.
Correct: this is how MVCC row versioning works.

questions.scenario: To speed up lookups, an engineer proposes storing each order row's `ctid` in an audit table and later fetching orders with `WHERE ctid = $1`.
questions.stem: What is the main problem with this design?
options: ctid is not unique within a table.
ctid cannot be used in a WHERE clause.
ctid changes when the row is updated or the table is rewritten (for example VACUUM FULL), so stored values go stale.
Reading ctid requires superuser privileges.
questions.explanation: ctid is the physical location of the current row version. Every UPDATE writes a new version elsewhere and VACUUM FULL rewrites the table, so a stored ctid soon points to the wrong version or nothing. Use the primary key for durable references.
rationales: Incorrect: at any moment a ctid identifies one tuple; the problem is that it moves.
Incorrect: ctid can be filtered on; it is just not durable.
Correct: it is not a stable identifier and should not be persisted.
Incorrect: system columns are readable by anyone who can read the table.

questions.scenario: Session A starts `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ` and reads a product price (10). Session B then runs `UPDATE products SET price = 12` and commits immediately, without waiting. Session A reads the price again.
questions.stem: What does A see, and why was B not blocked?
options: A sees 12; B was not blocked because A holds no locks.
A gets an error because the row changed after its snapshot.
A sees 10 because A holds a shared row lock that B queued behind.
A sees 10; A reads the old row version from its snapshot, and readers do not block writers under MVCC.
questions.explanation: MVCC keeps the old version, so A keeps reading the version visible to its snapshot while B writes a new one. Plain reads take no row locks, so B never waits. A would only get a serialization error if it tried to update or lock that row.
rationales: Incorrect: repeatable read keeps one snapshot for the transaction, so the new value is not visible.
Incorrect: reads never fail this way; only an update or lock of the changed row would.
Incorrect: plain SELECT does not take row locks, and B did not wait.
Correct: snapshot reads see the old version and never block writers.

questions.scenario: Autovacuum runs on the `orders` table every few minutes, yet `n_dead_tup` keeps growing and VACUUM VERBOSE reports many dead row versions that "cannot be removed yet". `pg_stat_activity` shows a session in state `idle in transaction` whose `xact_start` was six hours ago.
questions.stem: What is the most effective fix?
options: Run VACUUM FULL on orders to force the dead tuples out.
End the idle session and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout for the application role.
Raise autovacuum_max_workers so more workers vacuum the table.
Lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor on orders to 0.01.
questions.explanation: VACUUM cannot remove versions that an open snapshot might still see, and the idle transaction holds back the xmin horizon for the database. Ending it lets the next vacuum clean up, and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout stops it recurring. More or earlier vacuums hit the same wall.
rationales: Incorrect: VACUUM FULL cannot drop versions still visible to an old snapshot and would block all access.
Correct: removing the old snapshot releases the horizon so dead tuples can be reclaimed.
Incorrect: workers are not the bottleneck; the horizon is.
Incorrect: vacuuming more often still cannot remove tuples the old transaction might see.

questions.scenario: After deleting 90% of a 200 GB logging table, the team runs plain VACUUM. The table file stays about 200 GB on disk. They need the disk space back for the operating system.
questions.stem: Which statement is accurate?
options: Plain VACUUM always returns freed space to the OS; the size will drop after a checkpoint.
ANALYZE reclaims the space once statistics are updated.
VACUUM FULL runs concurrently with inserts, so it can run at any time.
VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and returns space to the OS, but holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration and needs disk for the new copy.
questions.explanation: Plain VACUUM makes dead space reusable inside the table but generally does not shrink the file, except for empty pages at the end. VACUUM FULL writes a compact new copy and returns space, at the cost of an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks reads and writes, plus temporary extra disk.
rationales: Incorrect: plain VACUUM only truncates fully empty trailing pages.
Incorrect: ANALYZE only collects statistics.
Incorrect: VACUUM FULL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and blocks all access.
Correct: that is the trade-off the docs describe.

questions.scenario: A `sessions` table is updated thousands of times per second, each update setting `last_seen_at = now()`. There is a B-tree index on `last_seen_at` that a weekly cleanup job uses. `n_tup_hot_upd` is close to zero and the indexes are bloating.
questions.stem: Which two changes, applied together, would let most of these updates be HOT? (Select two.)
options: Drop the index on last_seen_at (for example, let the weekly job scan instead).
Lower the table's fillfactor so pages keep free space for new versions.
Replace the index with a covering index on (user_id) INCLUDE (last_seen_at).
Increase autovacuum_max_workers.
questions.explanation: A HOT update requires that no column referenced by an index changes and that the page has room for the new version. While last_seen_at is indexed, no update can be HOT whatever the fillfactor, so the index must go; a lower fillfactor then keeps room on each page for the new versions. INCLUDE columns are still referenced by the index, so they block HOT.
rationales: Correct: last_seen_at would no longer be an indexed column.
Correct: once the indexed-column condition is met, free space on the same page is the other HOT condition.
Incorrect: an INCLUDE column is still an indexed column for HOT purposes.
Incorrect: more workers do not change whether an update qualifies as HOT.

questions.scenario: Logs show `WARNING: database "app" must be vacuumed within 30000000 transactions`. Investigation finds a prepared transaction from three weeks ago in `pg_prepared_xacts` and a replication slot for a replica that was decommissioned.
questions.stem: What is the recommended response?
options: Stop the server and run VACUUM in single-user mode immediately.
Run VACUUM FULL on every table to reset transaction IDs.
Commit or roll back the old prepared transaction, drop the stale slot, then run a database-wide plain VACUUM.
Set autovacuum = off so that maintenance does not compete with the application.
questions.explanation: Freezing cannot advance past whatever holds the horizon back, so old prepared transactions and stale slots must be cleared first. The docs then advise a normal database-wide VACUUM and say single-user mode should be avoided because it takes the system down and disables wraparound safeguards.
rationales: Incorrect: current docs say single-user mode is no longer needed in typical cases and is riskier.
Incorrect: VACUUM FULL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks and is not the documented remedy.
Correct: remove the blockers, then vacuum normally.
Incorrect: disabling autovacuum removes routine freezing and makes the situation worse.

questions.scenario: To avoid I/O during business hours, a team set `autovacuum_enabled = false` on a large append-mostly table. Weeks later they still see an autovacuum worker on it, labelled "to prevent wraparound".
questions.stem: Why is autovacuum still running on this table?
options: The storage parameter only takes effect after a server restart.
autovacuum_enabled = false only applies to TOAST tables.
The worker is ANALYZE, which ignores autovacuum_enabled.
Anti-wraparound autovacuum runs on any table older than autovacuum_freeze_max_age, even when autovacuum is disabled.
questions.explanation: To prevent data loss from XID wraparound, PostgreSQL forces an autovacuum on any table whose unfrozen XIDs are older than autovacuum_freeze_max_age, regardless of autovacuum settings. The fix is to let regular vacuums freeze the table, not to try to block this one.
rationales: Incorrect: per-table storage parameters apply without a restart.
Incorrect: the parameter applies to the table itself.
Incorrect: the "to prevent wraparound" label indicates an anti-wraparound vacuum.
Correct: the wraparound safeguard runs even when autovacuum is disabled.

questions.scenario: A 2-billion-row `events` table receives millions of updates per day. With default settings autovacuum visits it rarely, and dead tuples reach hundreds of millions before each run. Other tables are fine.
questions.stem: What is the best targeted fix?
options: Set autovacuum_naptime to 1s globally.
ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01), optionally with a lower threshold.
Schedule a nightly VACUUM FULL on events.
Raise vacuum_freeze_min_age so fewer tuples need freezing.
questions.explanation: The trigger is a threshold plus a scale factor times the row count, so on very large tables the default fraction allows a large dead-tuple backlog. Lowering the scale factor as a per-table storage parameter makes autovacuum visit this table sooner without affecting others. (PostgreSQL 18 also caps the trigger with autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold.)
rationales: Incorrect: naptime affects how often the launcher checks, not the per-table trigger, and changes every database.
Correct: per-table autovacuum storage parameters are the documented tuning point.
Incorrect: VACUUM FULL locks the table every night and does not address the trigger.
Incorrect: freezing settings do not change when dead tuples are cleaned.

questions.scenario: During peak traffic an engineer runs `CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id)` on a large table. Checkout requests that insert orders start timing out, while dashboards that only read orders keep working.
questions.stem: What explains this, and what should be used instead?
options: CREATE INDEX takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; use VACUUM first to make it faster.
Index builds lock individual rows as they scan them; lower maintenance_work_mem.
CREATE INDEX takes ROW EXCLUSIVE, which conflicts only with inserts; run it inside a transaction block instead.
CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock, which blocks writes but allows reads; use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE.
questions.explanation: Plain CREATE INDEX holds SHARE on the table, which conflicts with the ROW EXCLUSIVE lock writers need but not with readers' ACCESS SHARE. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE so writes continue, at the cost of a slower build that cannot run inside a transaction block.
rationales: Incorrect: if it took ACCESS EXCLUSIVE the dashboards would have blocked too.
Incorrect: index builds take a table lock, not row locks.
Incorrect: ROW EXCLUSIVE is what writers take; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction block anyway.
Correct: this matches the lock table and the observed symptoms.

questions.scenario: Eight workers each run `BEGIN; SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE;` then process the job and mark it done. Throughput does not improve beyond one worker, because the others wait on the same row.
questions.stem: Which change lets the workers take different jobs in parallel?
options: Add NOWAIT to the locking clause.
Add SKIP LOCKED to the locking clause.
Run the workers at SERIALIZABLE.
Take pg_advisory_lock(0) before selecting a job.
questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED makes each worker skip rows that another worker has already locked, which the docs describe as the way to avoid contention among multiple consumers of a queue-like table. NOWAIT would make the waiting workers fail instead of picking other jobs.
rationales: Incorrect: NOWAIT raises an error rather than moving to the next unlocked row.
Correct: each worker locks the first row nobody else holds.
Incorrect: serializable adds aborts; it does not spread workers across rows.
Incorrect: one global advisory lock makes the workers fully serial.

questions.scenario:
A worker claims jobs with:

```sql
WITH picked AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY id LIMIT 10
)
SELECT * FROM picked FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
```

Two workers sometimes process the same jobs.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: Move `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside the WITH query so the job rows themselves are locked.
Add `MATERIALIZED` to the CTE.
Change `SKIP LOCKED` to `NOWAIT`.
Raise the isolation level to REPEATABLE READ.
questions.explanation: A locking clause in the main query does not lock rows produced by a WITH query; the docs say to put the clause inside the WITH query if those rows should be locked. With the clause inside the CTE, each worker locks and skips rows on the jobs table itself.
rationales: Correct: the lock must be applied where the jobs table is scanned.
Incorrect: materialization does not add row locks.
Incorrect: NOWAIT still would not lock the CTE's rows and would add errors.
Incorrect: isolation level does not substitute for locking the job rows.

questions.scenario: A payments service runs `SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE` and then updates `accounts.balance`. Meanwhile, inserts into `orders` (which has a foreign key to accounts.id) for the same account stall until the payment transaction commits. The primary key is never changed.
questions.stem: Which change removes the stall while still serializing balance updates?
options: Use `FOR SHARE` instead of `FOR UPDATE`.
Use `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` in the payments query.
Drop the foreign key from orders to accounts.
Use `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` instead of `FOR UPDATE`.
questions.explanation: Foreign-key checks on child inserts take FOR KEY SHARE on the parent row, which conflicts only with FOR UPDATE. FOR NO KEY UPDATE, the lock a plain non-key UPDATE takes anyway, still conflicts with other FOR NO KEY UPDATE lockers, so balance updates stay serialized while FK checks proceed.
rationales: Incorrect: FOR SHARE lets two payment transactions hold the lock together, and they would conflict when updating.
Incorrect: skipping a locked account would silently skip the payment.
Incorrect: this gives up referential integrity to fix a lock-strength choice.
Correct: it does not conflict with FOR KEY SHARE but does conflict with other updaters.

questions.scenario: Two transfer transactions run at the same time: one updates account 1 and then account 2, the other updates account 2 and then account 1. One of them fails with `deadlock detected`.
questions.stem: What is the best prevention?
options: Raise deadlock_timeout to 60s so the transactions have time to finish.
Add NOWAIT to every UPDATE.
Always update (or lock) the accounts in a consistent order, for example lowest id first, and retry on 40P01.
Increase max_locks_per_transaction.
questions.explanation: A deadlock is a cycle of waits; PostgreSQL detects it and aborts one transaction. Acquiring locks in the same order in every transaction makes the cycle impossible, and treating 40P01 as retryable handles any remaining cases. deadlock_timeout only controls how long PostgreSQL waits before checking.
rationales: Incorrect: this delays detection and makes both sessions wait longer.
Incorrect: UPDATE has no NOWAIT option, and failing fast does not remove the ordering problem.
Correct: consistent lock ordering is the documented prevention.
Incorrect: lock table capacity is not the cause.

questions.stem: Which commands take a lock that blocks a concurrent plain SELECT on the same table? (Select two.)
options: TRUNCATE orders
CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at)
VACUUM FULL orders
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON orders (created_at)
questions.explanation: Only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE conflicts with the ACCESS SHARE lock of a plain SELECT. TRUNCATE and VACUUM FULL take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, while plain CREATE INDEX takes SHARE and the concurrent build takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE.
rationales: Correct: TRUNCATE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.
Incorrect: SHARE blocks writers but allows readers.
Correct: VACUUM FULL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE while it rewrites the table.
Incorrect: SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE allows both reads and writes.

questions.scenario: An admin UI lets a user open a record for editing. If another user is already editing it, the UI should immediately say "record is busy" instead of hanging.
questions.stem: Which query pattern fits?
options: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT`, treating the lock-not-available error as "busy".
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, treating an empty result as "busy".
`SELECT ... FOR KEY SHARE`.
A plain `SELECT` at SERIALIZABLE.
questions.explanation: NOWAIT raises an error instead of waiting when the row is already locked, which maps directly to a "busy" message. SKIP LOCKED is designed for queue consumers and returns an empty result, which is ambiguous with "record not found".
rationales: Correct: it fails immediately with a clear error when the row is locked.
Incorrect: an empty result cannot be told apart from a missing record; SKIP LOCKED is meant for queues.
Incorrect: FOR KEY SHARE is the weakest row lock; it does not conflict with FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE or another FOR KEY SHARE, and it waits rather than failing fast.
Incorrect: plain reads take no row locks and never detect another editor.

questions.scenario: A page-view counter is implemented as: `SELECT n FROM page_views WHERE page = $1`; if no row, `INSERT`; otherwise `UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1`. Under load it logs duplicate-key errors for new pages.
questions.stem: What is the concurrency-safe replacement?
options: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (page) DO UPDATE SET n = page_views.n + EXCLUDED.n`.
`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (page) DO NOTHING`.
Run the existing logic at SERIALIZABLE without a retry loop.
A MERGE statement, which is guaranteed never to raise a unique violation.
questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT guarantees an atomic insert-or-update outcome under concurrency, and EXCLUDED supplies the proposed row. DO NOTHING would drop increments for existing rows, and MERGE does not offer the same guarantee against concurrent inserts.
rationales: Correct: atomic upsert that adds the incoming count.
Incorrect: existing pages would never be incremented.
Incorrect: serializable converts races into 40001 errors that still need retries.
Incorrect: the MERGE docs point to ON CONFLICT for handling concurrent inserts.

questions.scenario: A nightly import upserts 50,000 rows with one `INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...) ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET price = EXCLUDED.price`. It fails with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`.
questions.stem: What is the cause and fix?
options: Another session updated the same sku; retry with SERIALIZABLE.
DO UPDATE cannot use EXCLUDED in a multi-row VALUES list; switch to DO NOTHING.
There is no unique index on sku; add one.
The batch contains the same sku more than once; deduplicate the input (for example keep the latest row per sku) before upserting.
questions.explanation: One ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE statement may not update the same existing row twice, which happens when the proposed rows contain duplicate conflict keys. Deduplicating the batch, for example with DISTINCT ON over a staging table, resolves it.
rationales: Incorrect: this is a cardinality error within one statement, not a concurrency conflict.
Incorrect: EXCLUDED works with multi-row inserts.
Incorrect: without a matching unique index the statement would fail with a different error about the conflict target.
Correct: duplicate keys in the input trigger it.

questions.scenario: A nightly MERGE syncs `staging_customers` into `customers`. Meanwhile the web app inserts new customers. Occasionally the MERGE fails with a unique violation on `customers.email` for a row that did not exist when MERGE started.
questions.stem: What best explains this?
options: MERGE is not atomic and commits each WHEN clause separately.
MERGE follows normal isolation rules; a concurrent insert can make its NOT MATCHED INSERT collide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is the statement that can switch to UPDATE when a concurrent insert occurs.
MERGE ignores unique indexes unless WHEN MATCHED is listed first.
The source has duplicate emails, which MERGE always reports as a unique violation.
questions.explanation: MERGE decides matched or not matched from the rows it can see, so a concurrent insert can lead to a unique violation on its INSERT action. The MERGE docs point to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT as the alternative that can run an UPDATE if a concurrent INSERT occurs, and note the two are not interchangeable.
rationales: Incorrect: MERGE is a single statement and is atomic.
Correct: this matches the documented concurrency behaviour.
Incorrect: constraints are enforced regardless of clause order.
Incorrect: the scenario says the conflicting row came from a concurrent session.

questions.scenario: A sync job must make `target` match `source`: update matching rows, insert new ones, and delete target rows that no longer exist in source, in one statement on PostgreSQL 17 or later.
questions.stem: Which construct handles the deletes?
options: `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN DELETE`
`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO DELETE`
`WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE`
`WHEN MATCHED AND source.id IS NULL THEN DELETE`
questions.explanation: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE (added in 17) applies to target rows with no matching source row, so DELETE there removes rows missing from the source. WHEN NOT MATCHED (BY TARGET) can only INSERT, and ON CONFLICT has no DELETE action.
rationales: Incorrect: NOT MATCHED [BY TARGET] rows exist only in the source and can only be inserted.
Incorrect: ON CONFLICT supports only DO NOTHING and DO UPDATE.
Correct: it targets rows present only in the target.
Incorrect: a MATCHED row always has a source row.

questions.scenario: A cron service ensures only one instance runs a job by calling `SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42)` and later `pg_advisory_unlock(42)`. After moving behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode, unlock sometimes returns false and the lock appears stuck.
questions.stem: What should the service do?
options: Switch to `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(42)` inside the job's transaction, so the lock is released at commit or rollback.
Call `pg_advisory_unlock_all()` at the start of every request.
Wrap the session-level lock in SAVEPOINTs.
Use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on pg_locks.
questions.explanation: Session-level advisory locks belong to a server connection, and in transaction pooling mode consecutive transactions can run on different connections, so lock and unlock may hit different sessions. PgBouncer lists session advisory locks as unsupported in transaction mode. Transaction-level advisory locks are released automatically at transaction end.
rationales: Correct: the lock lives and dies with one transaction on one server connection.
Incorrect: this runs on whichever pooled connection you get and can release other clients' locks.
Incorrect: session-level advisory locks are not released by rollback, so savepoints do not scope them.
Incorrect: pg_locks is a view and cannot be row-locked.

sources.title: Pooling modes and features — PgBouncer docs

questions.scenario: A developer writes `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM tasks WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100` to lock a batch of 100 task ids.
questions.stem: What is wrong with it?
options: Advisory locks only accept constant arguments.
LIMIT is not guaranteed to apply before the lock function runs, so more locks than rows returned can be taken; apply the LIMIT in a subquery first.
pg_advisory_lock cannot be called in a SELECT list.
The query locks the task rows themselves, blocking updates.
questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs call this pattern dangerous because the planner may evaluate the function on rows that LIMIT later discards, leaving session locks the application does not know about. Selecting the ids in a subquery with LIMIT and calling the lock function in the outer query avoids it.
rationales: Incorrect: column values are fine as advisory lock keys.
Correct: this is the documented pitfall.
Incorrect: calling it in a select list is normal; the issue is evaluation order.
Incorrect: advisory locks do not lock table rows.

questions.stem: A client library retries transactions automatically. Which SQLSTATEs should trigger a retry of the whole transaction? (Select two.)
options: 40001 serialization_failure
40P01 deadlock_detected
42601 syntax_error
22012 division_by_zero
questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs recommend retrying serialization failures unconditionally and say it may also be advisable to retry deadlock failures. Syntax errors and data errors are deterministic and would fail again on retry.
rationales: Correct: it signals a transient conflict; retry the complete transaction.
Correct: a deadlock victim can usually succeed on retry.
Incorrect: the same SQL will fail again.
Incorrect: the same data will fail again.

questions.scenario: A product catalogue stores attributes in `attrs jsonb`. The team created `CREATE INDEX ON products USING gin (attrs jsonb_path_ops)`. A filter `WHERE attrs ? 'warranty'` still does a sequential scan over millions of rows.
questions.stem: What is the most direct way to make this filter use an index?
options: Run ANALYZE on products so the planner notices the GIN index
Add a GIN index on attrs with the default jsonb_ops operator class
Replace the GIN index with a B-tree index on attrs
Raise work_mem so the bitmap of the GIN index fits in memory
questions.explanation: The jsonb_path_ops operator class supports only @>, @? and @@, so it can never answer the existence operator ?. The default jsonb_ops class supports ?, ?|, ?&, @>, @? and @@. Statistics or memory changes cannot make an operator class support an operator it lacks.
rationales: Statistics do not matter; the index simply cannot serve the ? operator.
Correct. jsonb_ops supports the existence operator ?.
A B-tree on a jsonb value compares whole documents and cannot test key existence.
Memory settings do not change which operators an index supports.

questions.scenario: User profiles are stored as `{"name": ..., "profile": {"city": ..., "lang": ...}}` in `doc jsonb`, with a default GIN index on `doc`.
questions.stem: Which predicate returns users whose city is Oslo and can use that index?
options: `doc @> '{"city":"Oslo"}'`
`doc ? 'Oslo'`
`doc @> '{"profile":{"city":"Oslo"}}'`
`doc -> 'profile' ->> 'city' = 'Oslo'` with no other index
questions.explanation: jsonb containment is checked from the top level, so the pattern has to mirror the nesting. A flat pattern looks for a top-level city key, which does not exist. The extraction-and-equality form is correct but a GIN index on doc does not serve it.
rationales: This looks for a top-level city key and returns no rows.
? tests top-level keys or array elements, not nested values.
Correct. The nested pattern matches, and @> is supported by the GIN index.
Logically right, but the GIN index on doc cannot serve this expression; it would need its own expression index.

questions.scenario: To keep an index small, an engineer indexed only the tags array: `CREATE INDEX ON api USING gin ((jdoc -> 'tags'))`. The application query is `WHERE jdoc @> '{"tags":["qui"]}'` and EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan.
questions.stem: Which change lets the existing index serve the search?
options: Rewrite the filter as `jdoc -> 'tags' ? 'qui'`
Rewrite the filter as `jdoc ->> 'tags' LIKE '%qui%'`
Add `SET enable_seqscan = off` to the application session
Recreate the same index with CONCURRENTLY
questions.explanation: An expression index is used only when the query uses the same expression. The index is on jdoc -> 'tags', so the filter must be written against jdoc -> 'tags', for example with ? for an element. Disabling sequential scans cannot make a non-matching index applicable.
rationales: Correct. The expression matches the indexed expression, and ? is supported by jsonb_ops.
Text LIKE on the extracted value is a different expression and not supported by this index.
The planner still has no applicable index; this only distorts costs.
CONCURRENTLY changes how the index is built, not which queries it can serve.

questions.scenario: An orders service stores everything in one `data jsonb` column: customer_id, status, a running item_count that changes on every cart edit, and a free-form `gift_message`. Reports join on customer_id and the team wants guaranteed valid customers.
questions.stem: What is the best schema change?
options: Keep the document and add a jsonb_path_ops GIN index for the joins
Move everything into separate key-value rows (entity, attribute, value)
Switch the column from jsonb to json to make updates cheaper
Promote customer_id, status and item_count to typed columns with a foreign key and keep jsonb for sparse fields
questions.explanation: A foreign key can only be declared on a column, not on a key inside a document. The docs also note that each update locks and rewrites the whole row, so a hot counter inside a large document is costly. Typed core columns plus a jsonb column for sparse attributes keeps the flexibility where it helps.
rationales: An index speeds lookups but cannot enforce a foreign key or reduce rewrite cost.
An entity-attribute-value design loses types and constraints too and makes queries harder.
json stores the raw text; it does not make updates cheaper and is slower to query.
Correct. Typed columns can carry the foreign key and constraints, and the hot field no longer sits inside the document.

questions.stem: Which statements about jsonb are true? (Select two.)
options: It keeps the original key order of the input object
If a key appears twice in the input, the last value is kept
A default GIN index on a jsonb column supports @>, ? and the jsonpath operators @? and @@
The ? operator finds keys at any nesting depth
questions.explanation: jsonb stores a decomposed form that drops whitespace and key order and keeps the last duplicate key. The default jsonb_ops GIN class supports ?, ?|, ?&, @>, @? and @@. The existence operators look only at top-level keys and array elements.
rationales: Key order is not preserved in jsonb; only json keeps the input text.
Correct. The last duplicate key wins.
Correct. jsonb_ops supports all of these operators.
? checks top-level keys or array elements only.

questions.scenario: An articles table has `CREATE INDEX ON articles USING gin (to_tsvector('english', body))`. The search endpoint runs `WHERE to_tsvector(body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', $1)` and is slow.
questions.stem: Why is the index not used, and what fixes it?
options: GIN cannot serve @@; replace it with a GiST index
The query expression omits the configuration and does not match the index; use to_tsvector('english', body) in the query
plainto_tsquery disables index use; switch to to_tsquery
The table needs VACUUM FULL before a new GIN index becomes usable
questions.explanation: An expression index is only considered when the query contains the same expression, and the one-argument to_tsvector depends on default_text_search_config, so it is a different expression. Writing the two-argument form in the query, or storing a generated tsvector column, lets GIN serve @@.
rationales: GIN is the standard index type for tsvector @@ searches.
Correct. Matching the indexed expression, including the configuration, makes the index usable.
The query parser does not affect whether the tsvector side can use the index, and to_tsquery is riskier for user input.
A new GIN index is usable as soon as it is built; VACUUM FULL is unrelated.

sources.title: Tables and indexes for text search — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: A search box passes the raw user string to `to_tsquery('english', $1)`. Users who type `"error 500" -timeout` or an unmatched parenthesis get HTTP 500 responses.
questions.stem: Which change best handles arbitrary user input?
options: Use websearch_to_tsquery, which supports quoted phrases and minus and never raises a syntax error
Escape every non-letter character before calling to_tsquery
Replace full-text search with ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%'
Wrap the call in a PL/pgSQL exception handler that returns no rows
questions.explanation: websearch_to_tsquery accepts web-search syntax such as quotes, or and a leading minus, and it does not raise syntax errors on malformed input. It also keeps the intent of the query, which escaping or swallowing errors throws away.
rationales: Correct. It parses the intended syntax and tolerates malformed input.
Escaping avoids errors but discards the phrase and exclusion the user typed.
ILIKE loses stemming and ranking and treats the whole string as one literal.
Swallowing the error hides the problem and returns nothing for valid intent.

questions.scenario: A stored generated column is defined as `to_tsvector('english', title || ' ' || subtitle || ' ' || body)`. Articles without a subtitle never appear in search results.
questions.stem: What is the cause?
options: GIN indexes skip rows whose tsvector exceeds a size limit
The english configuration drops short documents as stop words
Generated columns are not recomputed when subtitle is NULL
Concatenating a NULL subtitle makes the whole input NULL, so the tsvector is NULL; wrap each field in coalesce
questions.explanation: String concatenation with NULL yields NULL, and to_tsvector(NULL) is NULL, so those rows have no searchable vector. Wrapping each part in coalesce(col, '') fixes it, and setweight can then weight the fields separately.
rationales: Size is not the issue here; the vector is NULL.
Stop words are individual common words, not whole documents.
Generated columns are always computed; the computed value is simply NULL.
Correct. Coalesce the optional fields so one NULL does not erase the document.

sources.title: Tables and indexes for text search — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: Search results should rank a match in the title far above a match in the body, and documents where the query words appear close together should rank higher.
questions.stem: Which approach fits?
options: Build separate indexes for title and body and UNION the results
setweight the title vector A and the body vector D, concatenate them, and order by ts_rank_cd
Order by length(body) ascending so short documents with the title words come first
Use ts_rank with normalization option 32, which boosts title matches
questions.explanation: Weight labels let ranking functions treat title and body lexemes differently; by default A counts 1.0 and D counts 0.1. ts_rank_cd uses cover density, which takes term proximity into account. Normalization 32 only rescales scores into 0 to 1 and does not change the order.
rationales: UNION combines matches but gives no relative ranking between fields.
Correct. Weights express field importance and cover density rewards proximity.
Document length is not a relevance signal for title matches.
Option 32 rescales without changing order and knows nothing about fields.

questions.scenario: A CRM needs a customer lookup that tolerates typos (`jonh smiht`) and also supports `name ILIKE '%smi%'` for partial matches. A B-tree on name does not help either query.
questions.stem: Which index best serves both needs?
options: A GIN index using gin_trgm_ops from pg_trgm on name
A B-tree index on lower(name) with text_pattern_ops
A GIN index on to_tsvector('simple', name)
A hash index on name
questions.explanation: pg_trgm trigram indexes support similarity operators such as % and also unanchored LIKE and ILIKE patterns. A pattern-ops B-tree helps only left-anchored patterns, and full-text search does not do fuzzy matching of misspellings.
rationales: Correct. Trigram GIN indexes serve similarity searches and unanchored LIKE/ILIKE.
text_pattern_ops helps prefix patterns like 'smi%', not '%smi%' or typos.
Full-text search matches whole lexemes and does not correct misspellings.
Hash indexes support only equality.

questions.scenario: An autocomplete endpoint runs `SELECT name FROM places ORDER BY name <-> $1 LIMIT 10`. The team added `CREATE INDEX ON places USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops)`, but every call still sorts the whole table.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Rewrite the ORDER BY as ORDER BY similarity(name, $1) DESC
Lower pg_trgm.similarity_threshold to 0.1
Create a GiST index with gist_trgm_ops, which supports nearest-neighbour ordering by <->
Add INCLUDE (name) to the GIN index to allow an index-only scan
questions.explanation: The pg_trgm docs state that distance ordering with <-> can be served by the GiST trigram operator class but not by the GIN one. A GiST gist_trgm_ops index lets the planner return the nearest matches without sorting every row.
rationales: Ordering by a function result still requires computing it for every row.
The threshold affects the % operator, not ORDER BY <->.
Correct. GiST trigram indexes support K-nearest-neighbour ordering.
GIN does not support INCLUDE columns, and the problem is the ordering, not heap access.

questions.scenario: An embeddings table has `CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops)`. The model provider recommends cosine similarity, so the query is `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5`. EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: Increase hnsw.ef_search to 200
Create the HNSW index with vector_cosine_ops to match the <=> operator
Switch the index type to IVFFlat, which supports every distance
Normalize the query vector in the application; the L2 index will then be used for <=>
questions.explanation: pgvector indexes are built for one distance through their operator class, and only queries using the matching operator can use them. <=> is cosine distance and needs vector_cosine_ops. Normalizing vectors makes L2 and cosine order the same, but the query still has to use the operator the index was built for.
rationales: ef_search changes recall of an index scan that is not happening.
Correct. The operator class must match the query operator.
IVFFlat also uses one operator class per index.
The planner matches operators, not vector properties; the query would need <-> to use this index.

questions.scenario: Embeddings are normalized and the team uses inner product with an HNSW index on `vector_ip_ops`. A developer writes `ORDER BY embedding <#> $1 DESC LIMIT 10` and gets the least similar items.
questions.stem: Why?
options: <#> returns the negative inner product, so ascending order already lists the most similar items first
HNSW returns results in random order unless ef_search exceeds the LIMIT
Inner product is undefined for normalized vectors; use L1 distance
<#> is the Hamming distance operator and only works on bit vectors
questions.explanation: pgvector defines <#> as the negative inner product so that, like all its distance operators, smaller means closer. ORDER BY ... <#> $1 ascending returns the highest inner products first and can use the vector_ip_ops index.
rationales: Correct. Remove DESC; the negation already flips the order.
Index results follow the distance order of the operator.
Inner product on normalized vectors equals cosine similarity and is well defined.
Hamming distance is <~>, not <#>.

questions.scenario: A multi-tenant RAG service runs `SELECT id FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 20` against an HNSW index. Small tenants often get only 2 or 3 rows back although they own thousands of chunks.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and remedy?
options: HNSW indexes cannot be combined with any WHERE clause; drop the index
The tenant filter is applied after the approximate scan of about ef_search candidates; enable hnsw.iterative_scan or use partial indexes or partitioning per tenant
Cosine distance returns NULL for small tenants; switch to L2
The index needs REINDEX after each insert to include new chunks
questions.explanation: With approximate indexes, filtering happens after the index scan, and hnsw.ef_search defaults to 40 candidates, so a selective filter can leave fewer rows than the LIMIT. pgvector 0.8.0 and later can keep scanning with iterative index scans, and partial indexes or partitioning by the filter column are the other documented options.
rationales: Filters work; they are applied after the scan, which is the issue.
Correct. Iterative scans, partial indexes or partitioning address post-filtering.
Cosine distance is defined for these vectors; the distance is not the problem.
HNSW indexes are maintained on insert without a REINDEX.

questions.stem: Which statements about pgvector index types are true? (Select two.)
options: An IVFFlat index should be created after the table contains data
HNSW builds faster and uses less memory than IVFFlat
HNSW generally offers a better speed–recall trade-off and can be created on an empty table
ivfflat.probes defaults to the number of lists, so every list is searched
questions.explanation: The pgvector README says HNSW has better query performance in terms of speed and recall but slower builds and more memory, and that it can be created without data. IVFFlat chooses its lists from existing rows, so it should be built after loading, and its probes setting defaults to 1.
rationales: Correct. IVFFlat needs data to choose its lists.
It is the other way round: IVFFlat builds faster and uses less memory.
Correct. HNSW does not need a training step.
ivfflat.probes defaults to 1; raising it trades speed for recall.

questions.scenario: Users search product docs with exact error codes such as `E1042` and with vague questions. Pure vector search misses the error codes; pure full-text search misses paraphrases.
questions.stem: Which design does the pgvector documentation suggest?
options: Embed the error codes with a larger model so vectors capture them
Store embeddings in jsonb and query them with jsonpath
Run vector search only when full-text search returns zero rows
Run full-text and vector searches separately and merge the ranked lists, for example with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
questions.explanation: pgvector describes hybrid search as combining vector search with PostgreSQL full-text search, merging results with an approach such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion. That keeps exact keyword hits and semantic neighbours in one ranked list.
rationales: A bigger model does not guarantee exact token matching.
jsonb has no vector distance operators or ANN indexes.
A fallback hides semantic results whenever any keyword match exists.
Correct. Hybrid search merges both ranked lists.

questions.scenario: Eight workers each run `BEGIN; SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE state = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE;` then process the job. Throughput does not improve beyond one worker.
questions.stem: What change lets the workers run in parallel?
options: Add SKIP LOCKED so each worker skips rows other workers have locked
Use NOWAIT and retry immediately on error
Switch the transactions to SERIALIZABLE
Remove FOR UPDATE and rely on the UPDATE to detect duplicates
questions.explanation: With plain FOR UPDATE every worker queues behind the lock on the same first row. The docs describe SKIP LOCKED as a way to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers of a queue-like table, so each worker claims the next unlocked row.
rationales: Correct. Workers claim different rows without waiting.
NOWAIT errors instead of waiting, so workers spin on the same row.
Stronger isolation adds serialization failures and does not remove the contention.
Without a lock, two workers can pick and process the same job.

questions.scenario: A worker claims jobs with `WITH next AS (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE state = 'queued' LIMIT 5) UPDATE jobs SET state = 'running' FROM next WHERE jobs.id = next.id RETURNING jobs.id`. Under load, two workers sometimes run the same job.
questions.stem: Which rewrite fixes the race?
options: Add FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED at the end of the outer UPDATE statement
Mark the CTE AS MATERIALIZED
Move FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED into the SELECT inside the CTE
Add ORDER BY random() to the CTE so workers pick different rows
questions.explanation: The rows must be locked where they are selected. The SELECT docs note that a locking clause in the main query does not lock rows read inside a WITH query, so the clause belongs in the CTE. SKIP LOCKED then lets concurrent workers take disjoint sets of jobs.
rationales: UPDATE has no FOR UPDATE clause, and a lock on the outer query would not cover the CTE anyway.
Materialization changes evaluation, not locking.
Correct. Lock and skip inside the CTE that picks the rows.
Randomness reduces collisions but does not prevent them.

questions.scenario: An order service commits the order row, then publishes `order.created` to a message broker. After a deploy restart, finance finds orders that never produced events.
questions.stem: Which design removes this failure mode?
options: Publish to the broker first, then insert the order
Insert an outbox row in the same transaction as the order and let a relay publish it and mark it sent
Send the event with NOTIFY and have the broker bridge LISTEN for it
Retry the publish three times in the application before giving up
questions.explanation: Writing to the database and a broker separately is a dual write, and a crash between them loses or duplicates the event. With an outbox row in the same transaction, the order and the event commit together, and a relay using SKIP LOCKED delivers it at least once.
rationales: Reversing the order just moves the gap: events without orders.
Correct. Both rows commit atomically and the relay retries until published.
NOTIFY is lost if the bridge is not listening at that moment.
Retries do not help when the process dies before retrying.

questions.scenario: A cache-invalidation service runs `LISTEN invalidate`. It connects through PgBouncer on the same port as the web app, which uses transaction pooling. It never receives notifications, although `NOTIFY invalidate` succeeds.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Send NOTIFY outside any transaction so it is delivered immediately
Increase the payload size limit
Call pg_notify instead of NOTIFY
Connect the listener directly to PostgreSQL or through a session-pooling pool
questions.explanation: PgBouncer lists LISTEN as unsupported in transaction pooling, because the client is not tied to one server connection between transactions. A listener needs a direct connection or session pooling so its LISTEN stays registered on one backend.
rationales: NOTIFY is always delivered on commit; a standalone NOTIFY is just an implicit transaction.
Payload size is unrelated to receiving nothing.
pg_notify is the function form of the same command.
Correct. LISTEN needs a stable server session.

sources.title: Features and pooling modes — PgBouncer docs

questions.stem: Which statements about LISTEN/NOTIFY in PostgreSQL are true? (Select two.)
options: A NOTIFY issued in a transaction that rolls back is never delivered
Notifications are stored until a disconnected listener reconnects
The payload must be shorter than 8000 bytes by default
A NOTIFY is delivered to listeners as soon as the statement runs, before commit
questions.explanation: NOTIFY events are delivered only when the sending transaction commits, in commit order, to sessions that are currently listening. The payload must be shorter than 8000 bytes in a default build. Because offline sessions miss events, durable work belongs in a table.
rationales: Correct. Rolled-back transactions send nothing.
Only sessions that are listening receive events; nothing is kept for others.
Correct. Send an id and fetch the data.
Delivery happens at commit, not when the statement executes.

questions.scenario: A team enabled row-level security on `invoices` and added a tenant policy. In testing, the application still sees every tenant's invoices. The application connects as `app`, the role that ran the migrations and owns the table.
questions.stem: What is the cause and fix?
options: Policies only apply after ANALYZE; analyze the table
The policy needs WITH CHECK to filter SELECT queries
RLS requires SERIALIZABLE isolation to take effect
The table owner bypasses RLS; connect as a separate non-owner role or set FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
questions.explanation: Table owners are normally not subject to row security policies, and superusers and BYPASSRLS roles never are. ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies the policies to the owner as well, but the cleaner setup is a non-owner application role.
rationales: Statistics have nothing to do with policy enforcement.
WITH CHECK validates new rows; USING is what filters SELECT.
RLS works at every isolation level.
Correct. The owner bypass explains why every row is visible.

questions.scenario: A documents table has a permissive tenant policy `USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int)`. To let support staff search across tenants, someone adds `CREATE POLICY support_read ON documents FOR SELECT USING (current_setting('app.is_support', true) = 'on')`. Customers can set session settings through a reporting feature.
questions.stem: What is wrong with this design?
options: Permissive policies OR together, so any session that sets app.is_support sees all tenants; scope the policy TO a support role instead of a settable flag
Two policies on one table are not allowed; the second one is ignored
FOR SELECT policies also apply to DELETE, so support staff can delete rows
current_setting cannot be used in a policy expression
questions.explanation: Permissive policies are combined with OR, so the second policy grants cross-tenant reads to anyone who can satisfy it. Tying it to a user-settable configuration value makes that anyone. Scoping the policy with TO a dedicated role, which customers cannot assume, keeps the tenant rule intact for everyone else.
rationales: Correct. The OR makes the weakest permissive policy decide.
Multiple policies per table are normal and are combined.
A FOR SELECT policy applies only to SELECT.
Policy expressions may call current_setting; the tenant policy already does.

questions.stem: You are writing a SECURITY DEFINER function that reads a protected table. Which steps follow the PostgreSQL documentation's guidance? (Select two.)
options: Give the function SET search_path with trusted schemas and pg_temp listed last
Leave search_path unset so callers can resolve their own objects
Revoke EXECUTE from PUBLIC in the same transaction that creates the function
Mark the function LEAKPROOF so non-superusers can call it safely
questions.explanation: A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with its owner's privileges, so a caller-controlled search_path could make it use a planted object; pinning search_path with pg_temp last prevents that. EXECUTE is granted to PUBLIC by default, so revoking it inside the creating transaction closes the window before anyone can call it.
rationales: Correct. Pin search_path and put pg_temp last.
An unset search_path is exactly what lets callers hijack name resolution.
Correct. Revoke PUBLIC EXECUTE before the function becomes visible.
LEAKPROOF concerns information leaks through views and can only be set by a superuser; it is not an access control.

questions.scenario: A Supabase project has RLS on `orders` so users see only their rows. A developer creates `CREATE VIEW order_summary AS SELECT user_id, sum(total) FROM orders GROUP BY user_id` and exposes it through the API. Any signed-in user can now see every customer's totals.
questions.stem: What fixes this while keeping the view?
options: Enable RLS on the view with ALTER TABLE
Grant SELECT on the view only to authenticated
Recreate the view with (security_invoker = true) so the caller's RLS policies apply to orders
Add WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL to the view
questions.explanation: Views run with the privileges of their owner by default, so they bypass the RLS policies of the underlying table. Supabase recommends creating them with security_invoker = true, available from PostgreSQL 15, so the querying user's policies are applied.
rationales: RLS policies are defined on tables; the view still reads orders as its owner.
All signed-in users are authenticated, so this still exposes everyone's totals.
Correct. The view now checks orders as the calling role.
This filters nothing that matters.

questions.scenario: A Supabase table with 5 million rows has the policy `USING (auth.uid() = user_id)` with no role list. Queries from the app are slow.
questions.stem: Which change set does the Supabase RLS guidance recommend?
options: Replace the policy with a SECURITY DEFINER function that returns all rows
Wrap the call as (select auth.uid()), add TO authenticated, and index user_id
Disable RLS and filter by user_id in the client
Use the service_role key in the app so RLS checks are skipped
questions.explanation: Wrapping auth.uid() in a select lets PostgreSQL evaluate it once per statement instead of per row. Specifying TO authenticated stops the policy being evaluated for anon requests, and an index on the policy column lets the filter use it.
rationales: Returning all rows removes the security boundary.
Correct. These are the documented performance practices.
Client-side filtering means every user can read every row.
service_role bypasses RLS and must never ship to a client.

questions.scenario: A Supabase policy grants admin access with `USING ((auth.jwt() -> 'user_metadata' ->> 'role') = 'admin')`.
questions.stem: What is the security problem?
options: auth.jwt() is NULL for authenticated users
Policies cannot read JWT claims
The ->> operator is not allowed inside policies
Users can change their own user metadata, so anyone can make themselves admin; store roles in raw_app_meta_data
questions.explanation: Supabase warns that user metadata can be updated by the user, so it must not drive authorization. Authorization data belongs in raw_app_meta_data, which users cannot modify, and policies can read it from the JWT.
rationales: auth.jwt() returns the claims of the signed-in user.
Reading JWT claims through auth.jwt() is a documented pattern.
Policies accept ordinary expressions, including jsonb operators.
Correct. Use app metadata for roles.

questions.scenario: Tenants share a `users` table with RLS that hides other tenants' rows. The `email` column has a global UNIQUE constraint. A tester notices that signing up with an email used in another tenant fails with a unique violation.
questions.stem: What does this reveal, according to the PostgreSQL docs?
options: RLS is misconfigured; correct policies would also filter unique checks
Unique, primary key and foreign key checks bypass RLS, so constraint errors can leak the existence of hidden rows
The policy needs a WITH CHECK clause that excludes other tenants' emails
Unique constraints are disabled on tables with RLS
questions.explanation: The RLS docs note that referential integrity and unique checks always bypass row security, which can act as a covert channel revealing hidden values. If that matters, design keys so they do not carry sensitive data, for example a uniqueness scope of (tenant_id, email).
rationales: No policy can make constraint checks honour RLS.
Correct. The constraint sees all rows regardless of policies.
WITH CHECK validates the new row; it cannot hide existing rows from a unique check.
The error shows the constraint is enforced.

questions.scenario: A Node API runs on a serverless platform. During traffic spikes, hundreds of function instances each open their own connection, and the database starts returning "sorry, too many clients already". The server has max_connections at its default.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Increase work_mem so each connection finishes faster and frees its slot sooner.
Raise max_connections to several thousand so every instance gets a connection.
Route the functions through a transaction-mode pooler with a small pool per instance, keeping server connections modest.
Put a session-mode pooler in front so each function instance keeps one pooled connection for its lifetime.
questions.explanation: Each connection is a backend process with its own memory, and per-operation settings like work_mem multiply across busy backends, so a huge max_connections is risky. A transaction-mode pooler lets many clients share a small number of server connections. Supabase docs recommend transaction mode and a pool size of 1 for serverless functions.
rationales: work_mem does not control connection slots and raising it increases memory risk.
Thousands of backends waste memory and can multiply work_mem usage; it treats the symptom.
Correct: transaction pooling shares few server connections among many short-lived clients.
Session mode pins a server connection to each client for its whole session, so hundreds of instances still need hundreds of server connections.

questions.scenario: An app moved from direct connections to PgBouncer in transaction mode. Since then, some requests run with the wrong search_path, and a background job that uses pg_advisory_lock() sometimes runs twice at the same time.
questions.stem: Which explanation and fix are correct?
options: Session state leaks between clients sharing a server connection; use SET LOCAL inside each transaction and pg_advisory_xact_lock() for the job.
The advisory locks are released by autovacuum; increase autovacuum_naptime.
Transaction mode does not support SET at all; move search_path into each query as a comment.
PgBouncer rewrites SET commands; upgrade PgBouncer to fix it.
questions.explanation: In transaction mode a client gets a server connection only for one transaction, so session-level SET and session advisory locks belong to a connection that other clients then reuse. PgBouncer lists both as unsupported in transaction mode. Transaction-scoped alternatives (SET LOCAL, transaction-level advisory locks) end with the transaction and are safe.
rationales: Correct: session-scoped state does not follow the client in transaction pooling.
Autovacuum does not release advisory locks.
Session-level SET is indeed unsafe in transaction mode, but a SQL comment does not change search_path; SET LOCAL or per-role settings do.
PgBouncer does not rewrite SET; the problem is how pooling reassigns connections.

questions.stem: An app connects through Supabase's shared pooler in transaction mode and logs errors such as "prepared statement already exists". What should the team do?
options: Increase max_connections on the database.
Run DEALLOCATE ALL at the start of every request.
Switch to statement pooling mode.
Disable prepared statements in the database driver for this connection.
questions.explanation: Supabase documents that the shared pooler in transaction mode does not support prepared statements and says to turn them off in the driver. Prepared statements are tied to one server connection, which transaction pooling does not keep for the client.
rationales: Connection count is not the cause of the error.
SQL DEALLOCATE is itself not supported in transaction pooling and does not solve reuse.
Statement mode is even stricter and does not support multi-statement transactions.
Correct: this is the documented fix for the shared pooler in transaction mode.

questions.scenario: A migration runs `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;` at noon. A reporting transaction has been open on orders for 20 minutes. Within seconds, every API request touching orders hangs.
questions.stem: What happened, and what prevents it next time?
